headlines.story:
I'm already getting excited for the 2027 NFL draft. This class could be really, really good. We have elite wide receivers, standout defenders and a bunch of excellent quarterback prospects. Roughly half the 2026 college football season is in the bank, and I'm updating my Big Board for 2027.

My normal disclaimer: This is not a mock draft. What follows isn't any form of prediction for when or where players will get picked once we hit Round 1 on April 29 in Washington D.C. Instead, this is simply my personal ranking of the best players in the class. The list below is based on my own evaluations from what I see on film and some conversations I've had around the NFL. And remember that a lot can change here. Players will rise and fall on the board, and some will even return to school for another year at the collegiate level before turning pro in the future.

Here is my current ranking of the top 25 prospects in the 2027 draft class, which includes a ton of QBs. And at the bottom, I've included the best players at each position. Check back regularly right through draft day -- I will keep this list updated as the class continues to take shape. But one spot that might not change at all is No. 1 ...

Jump to:
Positional rankings

1. Jeremiah Smith, WR, Ohio State

Height: 6-foot-4 | Weight: 222 pounds | Previous rank: 1

2026 stats over eight games: 62 catches, 1,067 receiving yards, 13 touchdown catches

Smith is very clearly the best player in this draft class. He's big, fast and physical, and he snatches the ball on the run cleanly. On 302 career targets, he has just six drops. And Smith has the body control to make tough catches. I love the way that he is always looking to improve, too. Smith worked on his after-the-catch skills heading into the 2026 season, and he has been able to make some things happen with the ball in his hands using his strength and speed.

Ohio State continues to feed him targets (north of 10 per game), and nobody can cover him. That was very apparent against Illinois in September, when he caught 12 balls for 217 yards and four touchdowns. In three seasons at Ohio State, he has 40 career touchdown catches, and he's averaging 16.1 yards per catch. Just an incredible football player.

2. Drew Mestemaker, QB, Oklahoma State

Height: 6-3 | Weight: 215 | Previous rank: 2

2026 stats over eight games: 65.5% completion rate, 2,649 passing yards, 25 touchdown passes, seven interceptions; 227 rushing yards, two rushing touchdowns

Mestemaker didn't even start at quarterback for his high school team; he was the punter, played some safety and was the backup QB. Then he walked on at North Texas in 2024 as a QB before becoming the starter in 2025. After throwing for more than 4,000 yards, Mestemaker transferred with coach Eric Morris to Oklahoma State. It's an incredible story.

His toolbox is also pretty incredible. I love the way he scans the field and bides his time in the pocket. Mestemaker has the big arm to make all of the throws, with 44 completions going for 20-plus yards this season (most in the FBS). But he also has the mobility to pick up nice chunks of yardage on the ground. Mestemaker shows linebacker-esque toughness and plays with a competitive edge. He doesn't turn 21 years old until January, and he has just 23 career starts to his name. So, there's a lot of untapped potential.

3. Leonard Moore, CB, Notre Dame

Height: 6-2 | Weight: 197 | Previous rank: 3

2026 stats over six games: 13 tackles, five pass breakups

Moore is exactly what NFL coaches look for in a lockdown cornerback. He has elite length and ball skills, with seven interceptions and 23 pass breakups over his three-year career. He's scheme versatile, too. Moore displays great awareness and instincts in coverage, and he's a silky smooth mover. His footwork is truly outstanding. Moore consistently performs at a high level, but he's still looking for his first pick of the season. He missed the Oct. 10 game against Stanford because of a concussion but has returned.

4. Darian Mensah, QB, Miami (Fla.)

Height: 6-3 | Weight: 205 | Previous rank: 4

2026 stats over eight games: 80.7% completion rate, 2,425 passing yards, 25 touchdown passes, 1 interception; 159 rushing yards, two rushing touchdowns

Mensah is at his third program in three years, transferring from Tulane to Duke (where he had 34 touchdown passes last season) and then on to Miami. To date, he has started 35 college games -- great experience for a kid who doesn't even turn 22 until January. He is a smooth, fluid passer with solid accuracy. He's smart in the pocket and manages the game really well. And the mobility is there for him to beat a defense as a rusher when the situation calls for it.

Mensah currently leads the nation in completion percentage (80.7%) and QBR (90.3), and he's second in yards per attempt (10.4). Scouts are getting excited for Miami's trip to South Bend this weekend to play Notre Dame -- that game is going to say a lot about Mensah's draft stock because the Hurricanes have played a pretty light schedule thus far.

5. Colin Simmons, Edge, Texas

Height: 6-3 | Weight: 246 | Previous rank: 5

2026 stats over six games: 25 tackles, 10.5 sacks, 16.0 tackles for loss, 25 pressures, two forced fumbles, seven run stops

Did you catch Simmons against Tennessee in September? He had 5.5 sacks in that game alone. The production is off the charts -- he has 31.5 sacks, 44.5 tackles for loss and eight forced fumbles over three seasons. And in 2026, he is leading the nation in sacks (10.5), tackles for loss (16) and pressure rate (22.5%). Simmons is the type of closer most NFL defenses want rushing off the edge.

Simmons -- who has missed some time with an ankle injury -- is explosive out of the blocks with natural bend, and he can beat opponents with outside or inside moves. And he isn't given enough credit for the power element in his game.

6. Xavier Gilliam, DT, Tennessee

Height: 6-2 | Weight: 305 | Previous rank: 6

2026 stats over eight games: 25 tackles, 6.0 sacks, 10.5 tackles for loss, 24 pressures, 10 run stops, two forced fumbles, two pass breakups

No player in college football has improved his draft stock more since the start of the season than Gilliam, starting with a three-sack outing against Furman to begin the campaign. He has been terrific in his first season with the Vols after following defensive coordinator Jim Knowles and transferring from Penn State. He is incredibly quick and explosive at the snap, and he generates a ton of interior pressure as a result. For a defensive tackle to go early in the draft, he must be consistently disruptive. Gilliam checks that box.

7. Charlie Becker, WR, Indiana

Height: 6-4 | Weight: 208 | Previous rank: 8

2026 stats over nine games: 50 catches, 875 receiving yards, nine touchdown catches

I love the way Becker attacks the football. He consistently wins in tight coverage with his big frame, excellent hands and nice adjustments to find the ball in the air. Becker can locate the open spots in the coverage, and he can stretch the field with his speed. He has averaged 17.5 yards per reception this season. I'll be watching him at the combine; he is going to test really well and should post a pretty fast 40-yard dash time.

8. CJ Carr, QB, Notre Dame

Height: 6-2 | Weight: 215 | Previous rank: 10

2026 stats over eight games: 66.7% completion rate, 1,849 passing yards, 18 touchdown passes, one interception; 95 rushing yards, three rushing touchdowns

There's a lot to like in Carr's game. He's smart and processes quickly before and after the snap, which is part of the reason he has taken just two sacks all season. He's accurate to all levels and throws with anticipation. And while his arm strength is good but not great, he can cause conflict for defenses with his mobility. Carr can throw on the move or pick up a first down on the ground. Nothing fazes him, and he's always in control. In short, Carr is pretty advanced in the key areas of NFL-level quarterback play.

Just as it is for Darian Mensah on the other sideline, Saturday's matchup with Miami will be important.

9. Dylan Stewart, Edge, South Carolina

Height: 6-5 | Weight: 250 | Previous rank: 9

2026 stats over five games: Nine tackles, 2.0 sacks, 3.5 tackles for loss, 14 pressures, three forced fumbles, one run stop

Stewart didn't play much in the early part of the season. He missed the first two games as he recovered from a back injury, and then he was suspended for one game for punching an Alabama player in the helmet and arguing with coaches on the sideline. But when he is playing, you can tell pretty quickly. His traits jump off the tape. It's just a matter of whether the production can catch up; Stewart has 13 career sacks over three seasons despite recording 82 pressures over those 29 games.

Stewart can vary his path to the QB, and he closes quickly with speed to power. He also has the big frame to hold the point and shed blockers against the run. The pass-rush ability is there, but he needs to figure out how to translate his physical traits into stat-sheet production on a more consistent basis.

10. Trinidad Chambliss, QB, Ole Miss

Height: 6-0 | Weight: 205 | Previous rank: 7

2026 stats over eight games: 63.9% completion rate, 2,189 passing yards, 18 touchdown passes, eight interceptions; 241 rushing yards, seven rushing touchdowns

A lot will be made about Chambliss' smaller frame and the fact that he'll be 25 years old before the 2027 NFL season even begins, but he's the ultimate point guard at the quarterback position. I'm really impressed with his pocket presence and mobility, and the mechanics are sound. Chambliss puts zip on his passes with a nice tight spiral and avoids turnovers (11 career picks). And he's a playmaker who sees the field well, often relying on his legs to pick up first downs -- or score. Chambliss has 15 rushing TDs over the past two seasons.

Since transferring in from Ferris State and taking over for Austin Simmons early last season, Chambliss has played his best on the brightest stages. He always seems to respond when he's challenged. He's a real leader on offense.

11. Chris Cole, LB, Georgia

Height: 6-3 | Weight: 235 | Previous rank: 11

2026 stats over eight games: 49 tackles, 3.5 sacks, 9.5 tackles for loss, 17 pressures, 10 run stops, three pass breakups, 2 touchdowns

Cole is all over the field every Saturday. He's 235 pounds but looks like a safety at the second level. Cole is quick to diagnose thanks to his football IQ and then flies to the ball, especially in lateral pursuit. He is going to be a combine standout with that tremendous speed.

He is versatile, too. Cole can line up off the ball on the inside or on the outside, and he will consistently make plays against the run, in coverage and as an occasional pass rusher -- I see solid bend and burst off the edge. Cole is an outstanding player and is perfect for the way NFL football is played today.

12. Austin Simmons, QB, Missouri

Height: 6-4 | Weight: 220 | Previous rank: 12

2026 stats over eight games: 63.3% completion rate, 1,952 passing yards, 16 touchdown passes, two interceptions; 57 rushing yards

This might be a little bit of a surprise to some folks, but go watch the tape. There is no better thrower of the football in the collegiate ranks right now than this young lefty -- he's a pure passer. Simmons can sling it with the best of them -- the ball explodes out of his hands. But he's also very accurate and mixes in good touch with all that velocity. Simmons transferred from Ole Miss after a 2025 season in which he was hurt early and lost his job to Trinidad Chambliss, and his electric arm has allowed Missouri to hit big plays down the field in 2026. Simmons is 14th in the nation with 10.4 air yards per attempt.

What's holding him back? Simmons has started just 10 career games. His experience is still going to be pretty light by the end of the season, and that might scare some NFL teams. There's a chance Simmons returns to school for another year, but he deserves to be here on the Big Board because of his outstanding skill set and high ceiling.

13. Ashton Hampton, CB, Clemson

Height: 6-2 | Weight: 205 | Previous rank: 13

2026 stats over eight games: 27 tackles, one interception, nine pass breakups, 3.0 tackles for loss

Hampton's confidence shows in his play. You can tell he loves matching up with the opposition's No. 1 receiver and going to battle. And more often than not, Hampton wins. He has allowed just 2.7 yards per pass attempt in his direction this season, which ranks seventh in the nation.

He plays an aggressive style, crowding receivers at the line of scrimmage, getting in his hip pocket and disrupting routes right away. Hampton can plant and drive on the ball (though his ball production is only moderate, with four career picks), and he has the recovery speed to make plays with his back to the QB when necessary.

14. Trevor Lauck, OT, Iowa

Height: 6-5 | Weight: 314 | Previous rank: 15

2026 stats over eight games: Eight starts, zero sacks allowed, five pressures allowed

Lauck has been a mainstay at left tackle since the beginning of last season, starting 21 games there over that time (one sack allowed in 2025, none this season). His pass protection traits have stood out in particular this season, as he's technically sound. I see good footwork and balance on the tape, and he sustains well and finishes his blocks.

15. Nick Marsh, WR, Indiana

Height: 6-3 | Weight: 210 | Previous rank: 16

2026 stats over nine games: 38 catches, 669 receiving yards, eight touchdown catches

The Michigan State transfer mixes physicality with athleticism. He has speed, and we see that in after-the-catch opportunities. But he also makes tough tight-window catches and fights for the ball. Marsh has improved there this season, winning in tight coverage more and more (11 contested catches). He has sure hands and can haul in off-target passes. Marsh just turned 20 years old, and the arrow is pointing up.

16. Jordan Seaton, OT, LSU

Height: 6-5 | Weight: 307 | Previous rank: 20

2026 stats over eight games: Eight starts, zero sacks allowed, three pressures allowed

Seaton has started 30 games at left tackle, including 22 at Colorado before transferring to LSU before the 2026 season. And he has not allowed a sack since 2024. He can push blockers past the QB and has improved as a run blocker, showing the ability to pull there. Seaton is in great shape this season, and he looks the part. He just needs to be coached up a little to realize his full potential as an elite left tackle.

17. Will Echoles, DT, Ole Miss

Height: 6-3 | Weight: 315 | Previous rank: 14

2026 stats over eight games: 21 tackles, 1.5 sacks, 4.0 tackles for loss, 15 pressures, six run stops, three pass breakups

NFL teams love penetrating, disruptive interior defensive linemen, and Echoles gets into opponents' backfields on a consistent basis. He had 11.5 tackles for loss and five sacks in 2025, and while the sacks haven't really come yet in 2026, he's causing headaches for QBs with pressure. Echoles is explosive and can beat double-teams with his high effort level. He's also very effective in lateral pursuit. And I like his professional approach to the game.

18. KJ Duff, WR, Rutgers

Height: 6-6 | Weight: 225 | Previous rank: 17

2026 stats over eight games: 45 catches, 774 receiving yards, nine touchdown catches

You just aren't going to find wideouts with his skill set very often. Duff is a matchup nightmare at 6-foot-6, and offensive coordinators can line him up as a wideout, "move" tight end or even H-back because of that frame. Duff routinely uses his size to box out defenders. He attacks the ball in the air, and I see outstanding hands and body control. He adjusts well to off-target throws. Over his career, Duff has averaged 17.2 yards per catch, presenting his big-play potential.

19. Kelley Jones, CB, Mississippi State

Height: 6-4 | Weight: 205 | Previous rank: 18

2026 stats over eight games: 27 tackles, seven pass breakups, 1.5 tackles for loss

I had an eye on Jones last season for the 2026 class before he went back to school, and his consistency over these past two seasons is impressive. He anticipates well in coverage, and he uses his huge 6-foot-4 frame and long arms to attack receivers in press and make plays on the ball. Jones has only two interceptions (both last season), but he has broken up 18 passes since the start of 2025.

Jones can fly, too. He could put up a really good 40 time at the combine in March. He's comfortable with his back to the QB and is disruptive at the catch point. And he's a willing tackler in run defense.

20. Greg Johnson, G/C, Minnesota

Height: 6-6 | Weight: 325 | Previous rank: 21

2026 stats over eight games: Eight starts, zero sacks allowed, one pressure allowed

Johnson has played significant snaps at left guard and center this season, and he's a high-level blocker at both spots. Versatility is one of his best traits; he had 50-plus snaps at both tackle spots last season in addition to his work on the interior. Johnson is a strong run blocker, with an aggressive, nasty edge to his game. He's powerful and can sustain well. But he also anchors well in pass protection, and he has never allowed a sack across 45 career games (36 starts).

21. Kade Pieper, G, Iowa

Height: 6-3 | Weight: 298 | Previous rank: 22

2026 stats over eight games: Eight starts, zero sacks allowed, two pressures allowed

Pieper has played primarily right guard, but he's versatile, and some scouts might see him as a center in the pros. He's an athletic blocker who can pull and get to the second level to help spring big runs. He's also effective driving defenders off the ball. Over 34 career games (21 starts), Pieper has not allowed any sacks.

22. Jadan Baugh, RB, Florida

Height: 6-1 | Weight: 225 | Previous rank: 19

2026 stats over eight games: 152 carries, 801 rushing yards, 13 rushing touchdowns; nine catches, 59 receiving yards

Baugh is tied for fourth in the FBS in rushing touchdowns (13). He has it all, including really good field vision, breakaway speed and shiftiness. Baugh can cut back to make defenders miss, and he has the power to break tackles. He's a handful to bring down, and he almost never puts the football on the ground -- he hasn't fumbled since 2024, and that was his only career fumble across 1,162 offensive snaps. Baugh is also dependable as a receiver out of the backfield when called upon.

23. Trey'Dez Green, TE, LSU

Height: 6-7 | Weight: 237 | Previous rank: 23

2026 stats over four games: 19 catches, 272 receiving yards, two touchdown catches

Green missed three games with a leg injury, but he got into the end zone in his return against Auburn and made it 4-for-4 on hitting 50 receiving yards on the season. The physical and athletic traits are outstanding, and opponent defenses are going to have issues game planning around him -- he's 6-foot-7 with quicks and hands! But what really jumps out to me about his tape is his after-the-catch ability. Of his 272 receiving yards this season, 152 have come after the ball is in his hands.

24. Arch Manning, QB, Texas

Height: 6-4 | Weight: 222 | Previous rank: 24

2026 stats over eight games: 64.8% completion rate, 1,727 passing yards, 15 touchdown passes, seven interceptions; 279 rushing yards, two rushing touchdowns

Manning is QB6 on my board -- but he's still a top-25 player because of the skill set. I see the size, mobility and arm strength that NFL teams look for in a franchise quarterback. He can make throws rolling out, and he is dangerous as a runner (10 rushing touchdowns last season).

But Manning is too inconsistent, especially when it comes to accuracy and decision-making. He's going to be a tough evaluation. Watch just about any game he plays, and you'll ride the roller coaster of getting excited about his NFL ceiling and then wondering whether he's ever going to truly put it all together. Manning doesn't see the field as well as other quarterbacks on this list, and he occasionally throws off balance. And while the accuracy is better this season than it was in 2025, it still has to improve. I'm very curious to see how the rest of this season plays out.

25. Dante Moore, QB, Oregon

Height: 6-3 | Weight: 220 | Previous rank: 25

2026 stats over four games: 69.7% completion rate, 926 passing yards, nine touchdown passes, zero interceptions; 22 rushing yards

Moore's season is likely over after taking a hit against USC and suffering a concussion. Scouts will want to see him healthy in the predraft process, but there will also be questions about whether Moore could return to school because he played only four games in 2026.

When Moore is at the top of his game, he's an impressive passer. He changes arm angles, he's mechanically sound, he displays precise ball placement, and there's good touch on his deep ball. Throws look effortless because of his arm strength, and he can deliver strikes while rolling out. There's even some scramble ability there. The toolbox is full.

But can he take over games against top-tier competition? His performance against Penn State in 2025 (at a time when the Nittany Lions were the No. 3 team in the country) was exceptional. I thought he was going to build on that and enter the 2026 draft as one of the top QBs on the board. But he couldn't bottle that performance and repeat it against other top teams over the rest of that 2025 season. And it doesn't seem like he will get the chance in 2026.

Position rankings

Quarterbacks

1. Drew Mestemaker, Oklahoma State
2. Darian Mensah, Miami (Fla.)
3. CJ Carr, Notre Dame
4. Trinidad Chambliss, Ole Miss
5. Austin Simmons, Missouri

Just missed: Arch Manning, Texas; Dante Moore, Oregon

Running backs

1. Jadan Baugh, Florida
2. Mark Fletcher Jr., Miami (Fla.)
3. Nate Frazier, Georgia
4. LJ Martin, BYU
5. Kewan Lacy, Ole Miss

Wide receivers

1. Jeremiah Smith, Ohio State
2. Charlie Becker, Indiana
3. Nick Marsh, Indiana
4. KJ Duff, Rutgers
5. Jackson Harris, LSU

Just missed: Cam Coleman, Texas; Ryan Coleman-Williams, Alabama; Deuce Alexander, Ole Miss

Tight ends

1. Trey'Dez Green, LSU
2. Jamari Johnson, Oregon
3. Luke Reynolds, Virginia Tech
4. Jelani Thurman, North Carolina
5. Andrew Rappleyea, Penn State

Just missed: DJ Vonnahme, Iowa; Peter Clarke, Temple

Offensive tackles

1. Trevor Lauck, Iowa
2. Jordan Seaton, LSU
3. Trevor Goosby, Texas
4. Carter Smith, Indiana
5. Lance Heard, Kentucky

Just missed: Elijah Paige, USC

Interior offensive linemen

1. Greg Johnson, Minnesota

headlines.story:
The Jacksonville Jaguars rolled past the Indianapolis Colts last Sunday and are comfortably atop the AFC South. The Baltimore Ravens, on the other hand, have lost three straight and will start undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano on Thursday with Lamar Jackson (thumb) and Tyler Huntley (toe) both out. Fagnano completed 10 of 21 passes for 91 yards and an interception in relief last week against the Buffalo Bills, and his first start comes on a short week against a Jaguars defense that allows 15.9 points per game (second fewest in the league) and generates pressure on 39% of dropbacks. It could be a long night for the Ravens if they fall behind.

Baltimore needs Derrick Henry to carry the offense. Jacksonville leads the league in run defense at 77.4 yards allowed per game but will be without DT DaVon Hamilton. On the offensive side for the Jaguars, running back Chris Rodriguez Jr. would have a larger role if Bhayshul Tuten is unable to go because of an ankle/foot injury. Trevor Lawrence threw three touchdown passes on only 14 attempts last week, and this is another game where he might not need to throw much.

Betting outlook

Jacksonville is favored by 10. Before Baltimore's quarterback injuries, the early market had the Ravens favored by three. That's a 13-point swing, and the over/under on the game total has dipped to 40.5. The market has already made a major adjustment, so I'm not rushing to lay double digits with the Jaguars on the road.

The Jaguars average only 59.1 plays per game (26th in the league) and run the ball on 48.3% of their snaps. That could help the Ravens stay within the number if Henry can keep the chains moving. The other possibility is Fagnano turns it over and gives Lawrence short fields. The Jaguars have scored 55 points off takeaways this season.

The player prop market may offer better value in this matchup. Lawrence averages a league-low 5.1 fourth-quarter dropbacks per game, and he could have another light workload if Jacksonville builds a lead. Henry has rushed for 58, 45 and 53 yards in his last three games, and the Jaguars have been stout against running backs.

Notable player props, bets

Note: Odds by DraftKings  and subject to change.

Trevor Lawrence passing yards UNDER 235.5 (-112)

Moody: Lawrence is playing some of the best football of his career, but the Jaguars haven't needed him to throw often. He has gone under this line in four of seven games this season. If the Jaguars build an early lead against a Baltimore team starting an undrafted rookie quarterback, Lawrence may not have enough passing volume to clear this line. The biggest concern is Baltimore allowing a few explosive passing plays.

Trevor Lawrence rushing attempts OVER 3.5 (+101)

Matt Bowen: Lawrence has three rushing attempts in four straight games, but I think he will be forced to move outside of the pocket versus the Ravens defense on Thursday night. And let's remember that end-of-game kneel downs count here, too.

Zay Flowers receiving yards OVER 46.5 (-113)

Moody: Flowers has cleared this line in six of seven games this season. Baltimore's quarterback situation is the big reason the number is so low. Flowers went without a catch on five targets against Buffalo, but he also was playing with a quarterback who was abruptly called into action. This time, Fagnano has had a few days to prepare. Baltimore enters this game as a double-digit underdog against a tough Jaguars run defense, so the Ravens could find themselves throwing quite a bit. Fagnano's accuracy is a concern, but Flowers should see enough targets to clear this line.

headlines.story:
Quarterback Justin Herbert's struggles in offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel's offense have gotten to the point where an opposing player compared his passes to "throwing deli meat." Los Angeles Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh does not agree, however.

Los Angeles Rams safety Quentin Lake couldn't hold back his laughter when discussing what it was like facing Herbert in Week 8 on the latest episode of the "St. Brown Podcast," co-hosted by Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown and his brother Equanimeous St. Brown, which was published Wednesday.

"I mean he was throwing deli meat out there. He's seeing ghosts," Lake said. "I don't know what's going on but like, we knew we were going to get a couple. At least one."

Herbert did in fact throw two interceptions against the Rams, one to Lake, as the Rams defeated the Chargers 24-9 in the matchup of Los Angeles teams. The Chargers fell to 0-7 on the season as they failed to score a touchdown for the second straight game.

Herbert, a former Offensive Rookie of the Year and two-time Pro Bowler, leads the NFL with 10 interceptions in those seven games and is ranked last with a QBR of 32.6.

Harbaugh was asked about Lake's comments Wednesday afternoon.

"As far as anybody else's opinion, I don't see that. Everybody's entitled to their opinion," he said. "It's not what I see."

Harbaugh added that he thought Herbert "did his job exceptionally well" against the Rams but conceded there were "two throws he would have liked to have back."

Herbert also was asked about Lake's comments and said, "I haven't looked into it. I haven't heard anything about it, so I can't make a comment about it."

Harbaugh has continually defended McDaniel and stood by his offensive coordinator, who joined the club after he was fired by the Miami Dolphins. The Chargers are ranked last in the NFL with an average of 14.1 points per game and second to last in the league with 2,018 total yards.

headlines.story:
Tramell Jones Jr. is expected to make his second career start for Florida when the No. 24 Gators host Oklahoma on Saturday night, a source confirmed to ESPN.

Coach Jon Sumrall declined to name a starter Monday but tweaked his depth chart to add "or" between quarterbacks Jones and Aaron Philo and said he had "a plan that is already kind of in motion and in place."

Sumrall benched Philo after he threw two interceptions during a 27-8 loss to Georgia on Saturday. Jones replaced Philo in the second quarter, committed two more turnovers and had a third one negated by a penalty.

The toughest part of the quarterback evaluation, Sumrall said, is that Florida's offensive line has been so porous that it's difficult to tell which guy really gives the Gators (5-3, 3-3 SEC) a better chance against the Sooners (4-4, 2-3) in the Swamp.

"I don't know if Tom Brady was our quarterback on Saturday if it would have helped us," Sumrall said. "And I'm not trying to be a smart aleck. He would have been under too much duress and pressure to operate."

CBS Sports first reported the move from Philo to Jones against the Sooners.

Jones has completed 70.8% of his passes for 579 yards with four touchdowns and three interceptions. He has rushed for 77 yards and a score. He won his previous start, at Texas last month, while filling in for Philo when he had a shoulder injury.

Jones became the first Florida quarterback since Jesse Palmer in 1997 to win his first career start on the road against a top-10 team. Jones completed 22 of 35 passes for 155 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions against the Longhorns. Days later, Sumrall said he was dealing with an injury that might require offseason surgery.

Philo has completed 70.5% of his passes for 1,367 yards with nine touchdowns and five interceptions. He has 104 yards and three touchdowns on the ground.

Philo's first pick against the Bulldogs was one that Sumrall said he had never seen before. Philo stumbled trying to avoid a sack on the team's opening series and threw an underhand pass toward the sideline. His attempt to throw the ball away landed in the hands of Georgia cornerback Ellis Robinson IV. He was benched after throwing another interception two drives later.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

headlines.story:
It's Week 10 of the college football season and some offenses are treating the end zone like it requires a reservation. That's good news for our under wagers, less convenient for anyone expecting a shootout.

Kentucky heads to Knoxville with upset potential, UCLA gets a chilly road test in Minnesota, and Oregon-Ohio State could deliver more tension than touchdowns.

We break down where we're backing underdogs, fading offenses and finding reasons to enjoy a punt this November.

Here are the bets Mark Zinno and I like for this week. 

Odds by DraftKings and subject to change.

Kentucky +6.5 at Tennessee

Kentucky has enough offense to make Tennessee attempt to do something it hasn't consistently done against SEC opponents: score touchdowns. 

The Volunteers have just 13 scores across five conference games. More than half came against Furman, Georgia Tech and Kennesaw. Vols RB DeSean Bishop can get his yards without Tennessee putting this game away.

The Wildcats backfield -- CJ Baxter and Jason Patterson -- give Kentucky a way to attack Tennessee's less imposing run defense rather than repeatedly testing its coverage. If those carries force Tennessee to commit more defenders to the run, QB Kenny Minchey can look for receivers Kenny Darby and Willie Rodriguez.

Minchey has thrown just one interception all season. Ball protection helps against a Tennessee team that leans heavily on its defense. If Kentucky avoids giving the Volunteers short fields, Tennessee has to create its own offense. Bishop can carry the running game, but QB George MacIntyre hasn't supplied the passing production to turn that into a comfortable win.

I like Kentucky +6.5, with a smaller play on the +195 moneyline. Kentucky has already won three SEC road games; this is another upset within its reach.

Fresno State at Utah State UNDER 42.5

Utah State's offense is the reason to like the under. The Aggies can hit a big pass, but that hasn't translated into an offense that goes anywhere or finishes drives. They've allowed 23 sacks, so even when they get something going, one bad snap can leave them punting.

Fresno State also isn't walking into an easy matchup. Utah State's defense is the better part of this team. It can make running difficult, keeping QB Jayden Mandal from getting easy yards downfield. Fresno converts fewer than 37% of its third downs so asking it to keep putting together scoring possessions is a lot.

I expect stretches where somebody moves the ball, looks like they might score and then the possession goes nowhere. The Bulldogs are top-20 in the FBS for field goal attempts, while the Aggies are bottom 10 in field goals made (only 58%). Add in that both teams are also comfortable taking their time -- especially with a lead -- and this could be a snail-pace game.

Oregon at Ohio State UNDER 46.5

I trust these defenses more than either offense's ability to put up scores. Ohio State has allowed only four touchdowns at home. Oregon doesn't have the run game to make QB Dylan Raiola's job easier. The Buckeyes can limit those handoffs without giving him easy completions, which puts more of the scoring on his ability to beat them through the air.

Buckeyes QB Luke Fahey is making his second start against an Oregon defense allowing a 36% rushing success rate, which is top 25 in the country. With that, Ohio State can't assume RB Bo Jackson will handle everything while Fahey continues to settle in. WR Jeremiah Smith can always turn one catch into a touchdown -- and he'll certainly try after his stats have slipped for a Heisman campaign -- but he can get his numbers and this total can still be too high. Ohio State can control the game while the total stays under. -- Maldonado

Mark Zinno's plays

Virginia Tech at SMU First Half UNDER 27.5

I played the same bet two weeks ago when the Hokies went to Clemson and it cashed easily. I like this one just as much, as this features two teams with defenses that are in the top 30 in total defense. 

The Hokies will face a much tougher quarterback in Kevin Jennings, but they are coming off a bye and have had two weeks to prepare for an SMU passing attack that is seventh in FBS. However, SMU's best offensive performance in conference games were against Florida State, Louisville and California. Those are three teams in the bottom five in the ACC in total defense and points per game allowed. The Hokies allow just 20.5 points per game in ACC play and are third in total defense.

James Franklin teams continue to struggle to score on the road in conference play, and Virginia Tech is averaging just 25.6 points in the ACC. The Mustangs are allowing just 331.5 yards per game. The loser of this game likely has no chance at the College Football Playoff, so this will be treated like a playoff game with a slow start.

Minnesota +5.5 vs. UCLA

If there was ever a spot to fade an undefeated team in the Big Ten, this is it. You've got UCLA cracking the top 5 in the AP poll for the first time in a quarter-century and having to leave the cozy confines of warm Southern California for the sub 50-degree temperatures of Minneapolis in the first week of November.

UCLA is also starting its backup QB Ty Dieffenbach, who has only completed 57.7% with two touchdowns and one interception in three games as a starter. He benefitted from facing three weak teams since taking over.

It's a good bounce-back spot too for the Gophers after a tough OT loss to Indiana last week, giving them confidence they can play with anyone. They will need another top effort from their defense because the Minnesota offense (130th in FBS in total offense) leaves a lot to be desired. 

Taking care of the ball will be at a premium because the Bruins are second in the nation in turnover differential at plus-15. My guess is that their turnover luck runs out here. Add in the early 11 a.m. local start time and the Gophers can start faster than expected. Sprinkle a little on the moneyline for the Gophers as well.


Utah -5.5 vs BYU

A lot of people are staying away from the "Holy War" because in the previous 97 meetings, both teams have never been ranked inside the top 10. Well, I'm not. The better team here is the Utes. 

This is one of these games where oddsmakers are telling me what I need to know. The fact that this game has a spread near a touchdown indicates the sizable gap between the two teams. I'd be less confident if it were a field goal or less. The BYU offense is really missing LJ Martin. They've reached more than 380 yards in total offense in only one Big 12 game and it was against Iowa State, which has the second-worst defense in the conference.

The Utes have gained more than 400 yards in every game this season and are one of 10 teams in FBS to average at least 200 rushing yards and 200 passing yards per game. Utah's run game is the biggest advantage it has, which is why it is seventh in the FBS in time of possession. 

He's less heralded, but Utes QB Devon Dampier is the better quarterback in this game, leading a passing offense that averages 258.5 passing yards per game. Utah outgained BYU last year by over 100 yards in a three-point loss in Provo. The Utes get revenge this time around.

Kentucky at Tennessee UNDER 51.5 (-136)

I'm betting a Tennessee under again. I've moved the line over 51 here after getting burned last time with South Carolina scoring a miraculous 10 points in the final 67 seconds in a 27-24 final.

I'm still backing a Volunteers defense that hasn't allowed more than 345 yards to an opponent in SEC play and is averaging just 17.6 points per game allowed. I'm still fading a Tennessee offense that hasn't scored more than 26 points with George MacIntyre at quarterback.

I agree with my colleague Pam Maldonado that Kentucky will need to run the ball more because the Vols' pass defense is too good, and the Tennessee offense has struggled to find the end zone. All of this continues to point to an under and it's hard to envision Tennessee winning a game that goes over.

Delaware team total OVER 29.5 at Kennesaw State

If I asked you who has the best offense in Conference USA prior to reading this, you would have never guessed Delaware, but QB Nick Minicucci and the Blue Hens are tops in CUSA in total offense and own the 13th best passing attack in all FBS at 286.3 yards per game. 

They get to face a Kennesaw State defense that is second-to-last in conference ahead of only, you guessed it, Delaware. The Owls are also 133rd in time of possession meaning that the Blue Hens should have ample opportunities to score here against a KSU defense that is allowing 30.6 points per game at home this season against FBS opponents. The Blue Hens should be flying high here. (OK, I'll show myself out!)

headlines.story:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- The New England Patriots' injury bug has reached the highest levels of the franchise.

Owner Robert Kraft is recovering from back surgery, which he said will keep him "on injured reserve" and force him to miss Rob Gronkowski's Patriots Hall of Fame induction on Saturday afternoon.

"As much pain as I was in before having surgery, it pains me even more to miss the ceremony," Kraft told ESPN on Thursday.

Kraft added that doctors have instructed him to stay off his feet, which means he will also miss Sunday's home game against the Green Bay Packers, as well as the Patriots' trip to Munich to face the Detroit Lions the following week.

Kraft, 85, shared the news with Gronkowski, who underwent multiple back surgeries during a playing career that included three Super Bowl championships with the Patriots, with a touch of humor.

"I always told Gronk that in my next life, I wanted to come back as him because I had never seen him have a bad day. But after a couple of back surgeries, I take that back. I never want to experience that again," he cracked.

Gronkowski was voted into the Patriots Hall of Fame by fans in April in his first year of eligibility.

Because Gronkowski is part of Fox's pregame show on Sundays, Kraft had hoped to have the induction paired with the show being aired at Gillette Stadium early in the season.

But when the Patriots' schedule was announced in May, there was only one Fox game -- the Nov. 8 contest against the Packers -- and that was also the date the network was committed to its Salute to Service coverage.

So the Patriots have worked with Fox to coordinate Gronkowski's schedule, allowing the four-time All-Pro tight end to be present for his induction Saturday and also to be honored at halftime Sunday, while also fulfilling his broadcasting obligations.

Kraft reminisced about Gronkowski's impact after joining the Patriots as a second-round draft choice out of the University of Arizona in 2010.

"I just love Gronk. One of my greatest moments of love and affection for him was draft day, celebrating on the stage with his dad and brothers. It personified who he is," Kraft said. "He became a fan favorite almost immediately and remained the standard at tight end for nearly a decade."

The Patriots (5-3) have been plagued by injuries throughout the season, especially to key offensive players. New England defeated the Miami Dolphins in Week 8 without star wide receiver A.J. Brown, running back TreVeyon Henderson, wide receivers Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs, and starting guards Mike Onwenu and Alijah Vera-Tucker. Tight end Hunter Henry also left the game because of a foot injury.

Gronkowski played nine seasons in New England, was part of Patriots teams that won nine AFC East championships, appeared in the AFC Championship Game eight times, and made it to the Super Bowl four times.

With New England, he totaled 521 receptions for 7,861 yards and 79 touchdown receptions in the regular season and posted 81 receptions for 1,163 yards and 12 touchdowns in the postseason. Gronkowski also played two seasons with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Kraft noted how his thunderous touchdown spikes were felt across the region, as was his infectious energy and philanthropic work that contributed to him being named the franchise's Ron Burton Community Service Award recipient in 2016.

Kraft said Gronkowski's one-handed catch against the Denver Broncos in 2014, which set up his 50th career touchdown, was one of the best he's ever seen.

headlines.story:
THE SOCKS WERE a small thing. But for Jay'shawn McCloud, they were a necessity he did not have. In middle school, his football coaches made sure he had a pair for a game. 

Football had begun to offer McCloud a glimpse of a future, a different, more optimistic one than initially considered. His father had been incarcerated since McCloud was a toddler and wasn't a part of his life. His mother was raising five children and was stretched to the breaking point. Before McCloud reached his teens, they had been forced out of their apartment. The siblings were separated, and McCloud and his mother ended up in a cramped room at an extended-stay hotel on a busy state road outside Jacksonville, Florida. 

Extended-stay hotels exist as an option of last resort for families who have nowhere else to go. They are not homeless shelters per se, but are populated by the same desperate demographic and the facilities suffer from similar structural indignities. 

McCloud, 18, said he lived with his mother in the hotel for three months. After he left, she remained for three months more. 

All the while, football offered something more than a place to play. His middle school coaches occasionally bought him meals and helped provide necessities. Later, his high school head coach became an advocate and a steady presence in his life, monitoring his grades, intervening with school counselors and giving him reasons to stay on the team. 

For years, McCloud's living arrangements were in flux. In eighth grade, he moved in with the family of a teammate, Landon Martin, and stayed with them until his sophomore year of high school, when he left Florida to live with his grandmother in Gary, Indiana. A year later, he returned to Florida and moved in with an aunt. When she fell ill months later, he went back to the Martins. Through the upheaval, McCloud and Martin remained teammates on the Clay High School Blue Devils, where both have emerged as standouts.

"So many people have helped me," says McCloud who plays on the defensive line. "My coach is 100% the reason I got recruited from the start. He's such a great person to talk to. He just helps me out a lot." 

Buying socks was never part of a coach's job description. Under the rules governing scholastic athletics, some of the modest financial assistance McCloud's coaches provided, including money for rides, meals and even socks were, strictly speaking, against the rules. But coaches often find themselves doing far more than teaching X's and O's. 

Players have always needed this kind of help and the coaches who intervened risked their livelihoods. A practice of goodwill was essentially criminalized. 

But there seems to be a change in the thinking regarding coaches and the ways they are allowed to assist underresourced kids. Florida has eased some of the restrictions that once limited how coaches in all high school and middle school sports can help players. 

In May, Gov. Ron DeSantis signed the "Teddy Bridgewater Act," named after the former NFL quarterback and Miami high school football coach. The law allows head coaches to spend up to $15,000 of their own money, per team, annually on certain forms of assistance. This includes rehabilitation services, physical therapy, food and transportation.

Beyond meals, Clay head coach Jeff Gierke arranged meetings with school counselors, connected him with tutors, oversaw his recruitment, which also included offers from Temple and Wake Forest, and made sure McCloud kept showing up. The help he received from his coaches was essentially a bridge, a way for McCloud to stay afloat until his relationship with the Martin family became something resembling a family. The support paid off. McCloud is on track to graduate high school after the current semester and enroll in college early, where he plans to study psychology. 

For athletes facing instability at home, this help can mean the difference between staying connected to a team and walking away. But for coaches, there has always been an inherent risk. Many of these gifts fall under the impermissible benefits umbrella, where a coach risks suspension or termination. 

Gierke says he has never been sanctioned and now spends very little of his own money. Before he had a family he says he was more generous about taking kids out, sometimes spending a few hundred bucks out of his pocket. 

In recent years, high school and middle school coaches across all sports often find themselves responding to needs that address an athlete's broader welfare. It's a long simmering issue, especially now against the backdrop of a shrinking social safety net. 

FOR PARENTS PRESSED up against the sharp edge of financial ruin, navigating the never-ending 20 dollars here, or 50 dollars there requests from young athletes can tip the scales. 

Those working class, and often poverty class, families are sometimes forced to rely on federal and state safety net programs to keep the proverbial lights on. Over the last several years, these programs have been gutted across the nation, especially so in red-leaning states.  

The federal H.R. 1 Bill, signed into law in 2025, is the latest uppercut to these programs. In the last year, Louisiana has seen a 19% drop in the number of people eligible for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. Arizona has seen a 7% enrollment decrease -- approximately 136,000 people -- in the state's Medicaid program. 

Florida has some of the nation's most restrictive unemployment assistance rules, with lower benefit limits and shorter durations than almost anywhere else in the country. The state's longstanding refusal to fully expand Medicaid has also left many low-income families without access to affordable health care. 

Recent federal cuts to SNAP have further weakened the safety net. The new rules make SNAP a benefit people must continually demonstrate they deserve. Many adults must now prove they do 80 hours a month of work, volunteering or job training to continue receiving benefits. Those who fail to meet the requirement can receive benefits for only three months in a three-year period before losing them. 

Recipients must provide pay stubs or a letter from an employer documenting their work hours and income, a relatively simple task for someone with a steady paycheck. But the verification process can be much more difficult for self-employed workers and those juggling multiple jobs or irregular hours. 

For kids such as McCloud, these policy changes can rupture their lives. Behind the mundane statistics and election season talking points are the lives of actual people being thrown into the balance. 

"We will likely see a rise in food insecurity, more Floridians without health coverage, and more families being pushed below the poverty line as a result of the 2025 law," said Sadaf Knight, CEO of the Florida Policy Institute, a nonpartisan research and advocacy organization.

In the five months after new federal restrictions on SNAP took effect last year, the number of Floridians receiving benefits fell by more than 277,000, or nearly 10%, according to the Florida Policy Institute. 

Similar declines were reported across the country, with some of the deepest drops in the Deep South. The Southern Poverty Law Center reported that between last July and February of this year, SNAP enrollment fell 5.5% in Alabama, 6%  in Georgia and 9.5% in Mississippi. 

Tuesday's election results may lead to a reversal of some of the more stringent policies, but in the meantime, the pressure on the safety net is likely to grow. Beginning in October, states now have to shoulder a larger share of the administrative costs of running SNAP, adding to the financial strain on programs serving low-income families. 

The effects of a fraying safety net extend even to Clay County, a fast-growing and relatively prosperous suburb of Jacksonville. Large subdivisions of single-family homes now sprout from former timber forests, bringing new money and development to the once rural community. The county's median household income of nearly $88,000 is well above the statewide median of $74 568, and its 9.1% poverty rate is well below the state's 12.6%. 

But those figures obscure the financial strain facing many families. Beyond those officially counted as living in poverty, 29% of U.S. households earn more than the poverty threshold of about $31,000 for a family of four but still do not earn enough to cover the basic costs of living, according to United Way research. The organization calls these households ALICE, an acronym for Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. 

Bill Bland, managing director of The Food Pantry of Green Cove Springs, about two miles from Clay High School, said the number of people seeking help has crept up recently. The pantry typically provides a monthly allotment of four bags of groceries, supplemented with seasonal produce and sometimes meat and eggs. But demand has surged 30% in the past three months, he said. 

"Everything costs more right now, and people are having to make choices between maybe making a car payment or buying food," Bland says. "We're kind of an emergency stopgap. Everybody's got their own story. Somebody may have lost a job in the family. Somebody may have gotten sick. It runs the gamut." 

For coaches, that need can show up in their players in ways that others do not see.

"I've coached at affluent schools. I've been at inner-city schools. I've been in private schools," Gierke says, who is active in the Florida Coaches Coalition, which advocates on behalf of high school coaches. "And you know what? There are always a couple kids who need help." 

According to Gierke some players just come out and ask for help. "It's like, 'Coach, can I get a shirt?' Or 'Coach, can I wash my clothes here?'" he says. "They'll do it discreetly. They'll just bring you a backpack, and you do it for them in the morning." 

Other times, coaches recognize the need without being asked. Many students are embarrassed by their circumstances, and over time, coaches learn to spot the signs and offer help quietly. 

Early in his coaching career at another school, Gierke had a star running back who he learned was sleeping in a shed behind a relative's house. "His mom couldn't take care of him anymore, and he went to go live with an uncle," Gierke recalls. "Uncle's like, yeah, you can sleep in the shed." 

Once the coaches learned of the boy's living situation, they arranged for him to stay with the family of a teammate. He went on to play football at the University of Tennessee. 

"He's doing really good now," Gierke says. 

For many coaches, helping a player in need means providing a meal, a ride or, in especially difficult circumstances, a place to live. But Bridgewater's efforts to support players at his alma mater took on a far greater scale, raising questions about where help ended and competitive advantage began. 

IN 2024, BRIDGEWATER became head coach at Miami Northwestern Senior High School, a storied Liberty City institution that has produced generations of athletic stars and prominent figures in entertainment and politics. He led the team to a state championship in his first season. The following summer, he disclosed the extent of his spending on the team, bringing his efforts into conflict with the rules governing high school and middle school sports in Florida. 

Before the start of the season, Bridgewater posted a fundraising appeal on social media, saying he had spent several thousand dollars of his own money on the team. He said he spent $700 on Uber rides for players. He also spent $14,000 on a four-night preseason training camp, $9,500 on team-branded clothing, $2,200 a week on pregame meals, $1,300 a week on physical therapy services and $300 a week to line the football field. 

"Help me carry the load so I no longer have to take from my personal funds to keep smiles on these young [men's faces] and remind them that they matter," Bridgewater wrote on Facebook. 

The post raised questions about whether he had violated the rules. 

Bridgewater, who threw for 75 TDs and over 15,000 yards for six teams, earned an estimated $66 million over his 12-year career. He was spending a substantial sum of his own money on a team fresh off a state championship at one of Florida's most storied programs. 

His generosity raised a difficult question for the officials who regulate high school football in Florida. When does helping players become an advantage that can attract top talent? 

"What Teddy Bridgewater was doing led some people to say he was recruiting because kids were taking Ubers from 45 minutes away and all this other stuff," Gierke says. "But at the same time, he had the means to do that because of what he has achieved in his career. And he was looking out for his kids."

Bridgewater did not respond to several requests for comment. 

After returning to the NFL with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers for the 2025 season, he defended his actions to reporters, saying he knew from experience what it was like to at times be hungry, or need a ride. He said he was simply giving his players what they needed. 

"When I decided to coach, those players became my sons, and I wanted to make sure I just protect them in the best way that I can. Miami Northwestern is in a tough neighborhood, and sometimes things can happen when kids are walking home," he told reporters. "I was just trying to protect them, give them a ride home instead of them having to take those dangerous walks... I can't change who I am because of the rules." 

But the rules did not make an exception for good intentions. After an investigation, the Florida High School Athletic Association allowed Miami to keep its championship even as it determined that Bridgewater had violated its rules on benefits. In the wake of the association's findings, Miami Northwestern suspended him from coaching. 

The sanctions ignited a furor among supporters of the school and left other coaches confused. 

"Let's be honest. How many coaches can give $15,000 to their teams?" says Rodney DuBose, athletic director and assistant football coach at Oakleaf High School outside Jacksonville. "Still, I stand on the table and applaud what that man did. We all do what we can for our athletes. In my mind, it becomes an impermissible benefit when you do things only to win ball games, or to get players to come to your school. When that's your motivation, impermissible benefits follow." 

DuBose knows first-hand how much a coach's help can mean. Growing up in a rough section of Bridgeport, Connecticut, he was a star wide receiver when his high school coach offered him a glimpse of a different life. Each summer, when the coach went on vacation, he paid DuBose to house-sit and care for his three dogs. 

"He would say I'm going to give you this amount of money and I will see you in a week," recalls DuBose, who went on to play college football at Sacred Heart University. "I was in a neighborhood where I was hearing pop, pop, pop. But when I got to my coach's house, he had a pool. He had a big screen TV. I saw a whole new world." 

DuBose's experience helps shape how the coaches look after players at Oakleaf High. When a player is invited on an informal college visit, but his parents cannot go along, DuBose or head coach Christopher Foy makes sure he gets there. If an athlete cannot afford sweats or other team gear, the coaches find a way to provide it. 

"We have one kid that if we can get them to college, his NIL is going to be more than we're going to make for the next 10 years," Foy says. "So, [if] we have to drive him to a visit, we do it." 

Sometimes, the help has nothing to do with money. Last season, the father of an Oakleaf player had his work visa abruptly revoked. Facing possible deportation, he went into hiding. The player began arriving late for school because each morning he had to drive his mother to her custodial job at another school across the county. Oakleaf officials were on the verge of removing him from the rolls when he explained his circumstances to his coaches. DuBose and Foy intervened, persuading school officials to adjust his schedule and move his free period to the first period of the day, giving him more time to get to school. The student graduated last spring. 

"That's the kind of thing we do all the time," DuBose says.

Luther Campbell, the Miami music impresario who helped make the rap group 2 Live Crew a national phenomenon in the late '80s, had spent more than two decades mentoring and coaching young football players in South Florida before resigning from coaching earlier this year to launch an ultimately unsuccessful bid for Congress. He considered the rules that led to Bridgewater's removal unfair and set out to change them. 

During his coaching career, Campbell said he paid mandatory insurance premiums for some athletes, bought others meals and sometimes paid for players to get taxi and Uber rides home from games and practices. Such assistance, he said, was common among coaches. 

The alternative, Campbell says, was sometimes leaving players stranded in dark parking lots in dangerous neighborhoods. Coaches faced a choice between finding a way to get their players home safely and leaving them to fend for themselves. 

"Say we have a night game in Homestead, which is an hour and a half away, and the game is over at 10 p.m. We get back home about 1 a.m. and the parents don't come to pick a kid up. What are we supposed to do?" Campbell says. "It's technically illegal for us to give the kid a ride. Are we supposed to leave him standing outside in the dark in a blighted neighborhood? This situation with Teddy was a widespread problem. And we needed to address it." 

Campbell took his concerns to State Sen. Shevrin D. Jones, who introduced legislation to establish rules governing the help coaches have long provided their players. 

"Firing someone for doing something that could change a child's life is a reach," Jones says. "I felt like we had to do something about that." As the bill moved through the legislature, State Sen. Corey Simon, a former Florida State football star who played eight years in the NFL, offered his own example of the kind of help his high school coach once gave him. 

"I learned how to drive a manual transmission because my coach back in high school let me borrow his Nissan," Simon says. "He said, 'well, it's a stick.' And I said, 'Well, coach I don't know how to drive a stick.' And he says, '...I need to teach you how to drive my car.'" 

The legislation passed with overwhelming bipartisan support. It stipulates that help to athletes must be provided in "good faith," parents must give written consent, and the spending must be reported to the Florida High School Athletic Association. 

"In Florida, we want to encourage mentorship -- not punish it," DeSantis wrote on X. "This legislation creates a structured and transparent way for coaches to provide assistance using personal funds." 

Craig Damon, executive director of the state athletic association charged with enforcing the new law, says the measure largely codifies an approach the association had followed for years. 

"My first reaction was that this is not necessary," Damon says. "We went back and looked over the past 15 years, and I think we've had like four cases where the coach received a sanction for something like providing a ride to a kid. And in those situations, there was evidence through text messages or some other written communication showing the kids were promised a ride if they would switch schools." 

The association will presume that reported assistance was provided in good faith unless evidence suggests otherwise. If questions arise about a coach's spending, the association's compliance unit steps in. 

Appeals are handled by the association's Sectional Appeals Committee, and finally, the association board. The guidelines limit assistance to emergency and nonrecurring needs, and require school administrators to authorize it and coaches to report each instance. Those restrictions, Damon says, are intended to help distinguish legitimate assistance from benefits that could be used to recruit players. 

Damon, who coached football at Central Florida's North Marion High School for 13 years before joining the association in 2013, said he understood the circumstances that could lead a coach to step in. 

If a team stops at a fast food restaurant and a few players have no money to pay for a meal, Damon said, a coach is likely to pick up the tab. To him, that is part of the responsibility that comes with looking after a team, not an effort to gain a competitive edge. 

"We didn't sanction anybody for that because that's basically taking care of that kid while you are with him," he says. "We completely understand that there are situations that come up as a coach where just as a human being you need to do what is considered to be in the best welfare of a student athlete." 

Schools have been slow to use the law's reporting mechanism, and so far, the association has received no reports on what is being spent on athletes, Damon says. "It has been very quiet," he says. 

The association said it had not yet heard from counterparts in other states expressing interest in the law. 

"In the simplest sense, the law just allows you the freedom to help take care of a kid who needs it," says Bobby Ramsay, head coach at Jacksonville's Andrew Jackson High School, located less than a 10-minute drive north of the city's downtown core. "It just makes it legal to help a kid out and do what you feel is right for him." 

Ramsay has coached high school football for 25 years, and his former players include Baltimore Ravens running back Derrick Henry and Arizona Cardinals backup quarterback Carson Beck. 

Sitting on the metal bleachers overlooking the school's football field, Ramsay thought back on the various teams he has had through the years. Each one, he said, had players who needed help. He has paid for a cast for a player who broke his thumb, purchased a plane ticket for a former player pursuing a college career, and provided countless cleats to players who could not afford them. 

"You're always trying to do the right thing for your players," Ramsay says. "In some ways, they are like your own kids." 

FOR MCCLOUD, BEING on the team changed his life, allowing him to build a relationship with Martin. When he met Landon, who turns 18 next week and is now the quarterback at Clay High School, they were middle school wrestlers. Their relationship began with a joke. 

"I went up to him and made a remark," Martin says. "I was like, 'You have kids at home or something?' He was so much bigger physically. And he just laughed." As the two grew closer through wrestling and football, the Martins learned more about McCloud's living situation. Eventually, they invited him to move in. 

In some ways, theirs is an unlikely bond. Martin is white and grew up in a more stable home. McCloud is Black and has spent much of his life navigating poverty and instability. But as their friendship grew, the differences became immaterial. 

"My parents were like he needs help. So, my mom and dad were all in for it," Martin says. "And then we kind of became best friends. Now, he's my brother." 

McCloud's mother signed a notarized in loco parentis document formalizing the arrangement. Since then, he has lived with the Martins on and off. Staci Martin, Landon's mother, said the family is far from wealthy. She works part-time as a cosmetologist, and her husband, Nathaniel, is a security analyst for a bank. Their four-bedroom, three-bathroom house in the largely working-class city of Green Cove Springs is a fixer-upper they have spent years renovating. 

But the Martins see opening their home to young people who need help as an expression of their Christian faith, not a question of how much they have to give.  "We bought the house with shag carpet and paneling," she says, of the home they purchased in 2015. "We bought it to renovate it. We've been fixing it up this whole time. We just recently took out a loan to finish it." 

When they learned McCloud was living in a hotel, the Martins offered him a place in their home, hoping to give him some of the stability other children take for granted. 

"When we found out he was living in a hotel, we just asked him if he want to have a better opportunity and stay with us to give him some normalcy," Staci Martin says. "Scripture says we should feed and clothe people who need it. Kids shouldn't have to experience that." 

The Martins have welcomed other members of the Clay football team into their home. With their two oldest children away at college, they have room for two more players. Senior wide receiver and defensive back Mi'keise Battle, whose mother has cancer, has moved in with the family. Sophomore running back Kamari Davis also spends most nights there, making it easier for him to get to school and football practice. 

"We're always together," Landon Martin says. "You never see us without each other." 

For all that has gone right, though, one painful reality remains. McCloud's mother does not attend his games. She has not been there to witness the success he has found in football, or the future that is beginning to take shape beyond it. Asked about what others describe as a strained relationship, McCloud offered little explanation. 

"Family matters," he said. 

"It's been pretty hard, but I've learned to adapt. I come from nothing, but people around football have helped me a lot," McCloud said, flashing a smile beneath a navy Liberty University beanie after a team pregame meal in the Clay High School cafeteria. He is committed to play football there next year.

Nobody at Clay High School needed a law to know what a pair of socks, a ride home, or a seat at the dinner table could mean to a kid like McCloud. Coaches had been doing that math for years, mostly out of sight. Friends did it too. But the Teddy Bridgewater Act takes the quiet part out of it.

McCloud, who plays on the defensive line for the Blue Devils -- who are enjoying their first winning season since 2021 -- knows what that freedom looks like from the other side. "So many people have helped me," he says.

The help is the same as ever. Now nobody has to hide it.

headlines.story:
Everyone has some level of trust issues with their fantasy football roster.

Maybe it's that flex spot in your lineup, the one you flip on a weekly basis, rotating between a big play wide receiver or a running back who can give you some passing-game upside. The quarterbacks? I'm there right now in one of my leagues, arguing (with myself) on which fringe QB1 I'm going to start this week. Just give me the 16-18 points I need to win.

So, that got me thinking about the players we can trust, and those we can't, both heading into the Week 9 slate of games and for the rest of the season.

In doing this exercise, we are focused on each player individually, based off their current situation. I'm not comparing running backs to other running backs in this piece, for example. Instead, I'm telling you what I am trusting -- based on game tape, numbers, usage -- and vice versa. There are some bigger-name players in here, and others you might want to put on the fantasy radar.

Players to trust

Jameson Williams, WR, Detroit Lions

Williams is playing his best football of the season, scoring 19.5 fantasy PPG over his past four, plus he's finding the end zone (at least one touchdown in three straight). Yes, Williams has always been a boom/bust option in the lineup, but he's an electric mover -- with big-play ability -- in one of the league's most explosive offenses. And he can deliver numbers without high-end target volume. Managers should view Williams as a WR2/flex who can produce breakout weeks (26.1 points in Week 7).

Jonah Coleman, RB, Denver Broncos

I think we have to go with Coleman as the Broncos' top option at this point. Coleman had a season-best 20.4 points in the Week 8 win over Kansas City, finishing with 104 total yards and a touchdown on a team-high 15 touches. While J.K. Dobbins will still see carries, Coleman has more value as a dual-threat back, and I don't see that changing when RJ Harvey (knee) returns. I'd play Coleman as an RB2 for the positive Week 9 matchup versus the Panthers, and he's likely to stay in that range moving forward.

Ryan Flournoy, WR, Dallas Cowboys

Flournoy has emerged as Dak Prescott's No.3 target behind CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, providing a stable floor as a deeper-league WR3. Flournoy is scoring 13.3 fantasy PPG over his last four, with a touchdown catch in two. Available in more than 75% of ESPN leagues, Flournoy can also be viewed as a bye-week fill-in for managers in shallower formats. I'll take 5.3 targets per game in my lineup -- and double-digit production --  with the Colts' defense up next.

Braelon Allen, RB, New York Jets

Allen has looked really good on the tape in relief of an injured Breece Hall (quad). Decisive and powerful with the ball, Allen has scored 18.4 fantasy PPG over his last four -- with 100-plus total yards in each. Now, if Hall returns for the Week 9 matchup with Kansas City, Allen's overall value will take a hit. However, even in a shared backfield, I'd still start Allen as a flex. And with the NFL trade deadline looming, the Jets could potentially move Hall. Stay tuned on that.

Malik Washington, WR, Miami Dolphins

I've written about Washington multiple times this season as a streaming pickup, but aren't we at the point where he should be added to more rosters? Sure, this is a low-volume passing offense in Miami, but Washington is the No. 1 target, and his versatility in the offense creates more value. Washington has at least 11 points in four of his past five games, and will see the ball on backfield alignments, fly sweeps and screens. There is some Deebo Samuel Sr. to his game. It's a good matchup this Sunday versus the Lions' defense, too.

Antonio Williams, WR, Washington Commanders

I really liked Williams' college tape at Clemson. It's the route running and coverage awareness, plus Williams is slippery after the catch. And Williams can now play a larger role as a rookie for the Commanders with Terry McLaurin (knee) down for the season. In the Week 8 win over the Eagles, Williams caught a season-high five passes (on seven targets) for 54 yards (10.4 points). Available in more than 80% of ESPN leagues, Williams should be on the fantasy radar.

Players not to trust

Matthew Stafford, QB, Los Angeles Rams

Stafford still has value in superflex formats, but in 10-12 team leagues? He should be played only as a matchup-based starter. In his past two games, both without Davante Adams (IR, hamstring), Stafford has failed to top the 200-yard passing mark, so he is very touchdown-dependent as a thrower. Plus, he provides absolutely no upside as a runner (minus-3 yards rushing over his last four). And without a receiver to step into Adams' role, the Rams will lean on more multiple-TE sets and the run game.

DK Metcalf, WR, Pittsburgh Steelers

Metcalf has only three games of double-digit fantasy production this season. And where are the big plays? The fade ball throws from Aaron Rodgers? The explosive catch-and-run targets? Metcalf has just four receptions of 20 or more yards, despite seeing 8.1 targets per game. In a Pittsburgh offense that can't generate explosive plays in the pass game, I don't see how managers can trust Metcalf (9.7 fantasy PPG). The Steelers return from the bye to play Cincinnati in Week 10.

Dalton Kincaid, TE, Buffalo Bills

Kincaid scored 18.6 fantasy points in the Week 8 win over Baltimore, his second straight game with double-digit points, plus he has the tools to stretch the seams or flex outside as a target for Josh Allen. But will Kincaid see enough weekly volume to be played as a TE1? Kincaid now has four games with 10 or more points (all with six or more targets), and three with fewer than four points (all with three or fewer targets). To me, the inconsistent numbers keep Kincaid down as a matchup-based tight end, and the Week 9 game versus the vaunted Minnesota defense is one I'd stay away from.

Bryce Young, QB, Carolina Panthers

After a hot start (19 or more fantasy points in four of his first five games), Young has scored just 15.78 total points in his past two starts combined, throwing at least one interception in each. Yes, Young has been playing with a banged-up knee, which has limited his pocket mobility. However, this Panthers offensive line is going through multiple injuries and not protecting on the edges, as Young has been sacked 11 times over the last two games. With some tough upcoming matchups (DEN, @NO, BAL, @TB, @MIN), Young should be viewed as a QB2.
