headlines.story:
The Playbook is your one-stop shop for all your fantasy football decisions for Week 9, which kicks off Thursday night with a game between the Jaguars and Ravens.

This column features score projections, over/unders, win probabilities, and of course, easily digestible fantasy advice for seasonlong leagues and DFS. This guide should help you with all sorts of decision-making, including sit/start advice, last-minute waiver adds and lineup choices.

Additionally, we have folded our Shadow Reports into the game-by-game breakdowns here. Using our play-by-play data, we're able to identify defensive schemes and where each wide receiver and cornerback lines up on each play. By tracking these WR/CB matchups, including potential shadow situations, we can offer the best fantasy guidance each week.

  • If you want a more detailed look at some of this data, be sure to check out the weekly Shadow Reports: WR vs. CB Cheat Sheet. You can also take a look at the analysis of each team's strength of schedule for the remainder of the season.

All of this advice is centered on 12-team PPR leagues with relatively standard scoring and lineup settings (1 QB, 2 RB, 3 WR, 1 Flex, 1 K, 1 D/ST), although I'll often mention "shallow" or "deep" leagues for some starters. The charts show all players who have been projected for at least 6.0 fantasy points this week, as well as all D/STs. "Matchup" is automatically determined using a proprietary metric that factors in raw and volume-adjusted fantasy points allowed to each position by the opposing defense.

  • DFS values in the charts below (and their relative quality) are provided only for Sunday's main slate, which is why there are no values for games scheduled on days other than Sunday after 1 p.m. ET.

(Editor's note: Projections and rankings will align almost perfectly, but sometimes when a projection is close, a player might be ranked slightly higher or lower because of other factors, including upside or risk. This column is subject to updates during the weekend, although at the very minimum, rankings will be updated on the site and projections will always be updated inside the game leading up to kickoff.)

 JAX-BAL | CIN-ATL | DAL-IND | NYJ-KC | DET-MIA | CLE-NO | NYG-PHI | LAR-WAS
DEN-CAR | HOU-LAC | GB-NE | LV-SF | ARI-SEA | TB-CHI | BUF-MIN

Jacksonville Jaguars @ Baltimore Ravens

Projected score: Jaguars 28, Ravens 14

Lineup locks: Trevor Lawrence, Derrick Henry, Bhayshul Tuten, Zay Flowers, Parker Washington

Fantasy Scoop: Washington is hanging onto lineup lock status, but it's in jeopardy after a boom/bust first half of the season. Washington opened the season with a pair of top-12 fantasy outings but has followed with just one top-25 in his past five games. The concern with Washington was that there would be too many mouths to feed in Jacksonville, and that seems to be rearing its head, as he's seen nine-plus targets in three games but six or fewer in the other five outings. The latter includes Sunday's season-low two targets. Washington's 24.5% target share on the season remains strong, and he's set up with a good Week 9 matchup against a Baltimore defense that sits in top 10 in catches, yards and fantasy points allowed to wide receivers. Leave him in your lineup.

Over/under: 41.9 (14th highest)
Win probability: Jaguars 92% (highest)

Cincinnati Bengals @ Atlanta Falcons

Projected score: Bengals 27, Falcons 21

Lineup locks: Joe Burrow, Bijan Robinson, Chase Brown, Ja'Marr Chase, Drake London, Tee Higgins

Fantasy Scoop: Mike Gesicki continues to break math, having scored exactly one touchdown in six of seven games, including one in each of his past five outings. After totaling exactly two touchdowns in each of the past three seasons, Gesicki has six scores on 24 targets in 2026. Allow me to state the obvious: Gesicki's scoring streak is unsustainable. He has seen a respectable four end zone targets, but his 3.1 expected TD total (xTD) is still well below his actual output. Gesicki sports a 9.2% target share (same as in 2025), which isn't nearly high enough to allow consistent fantasy TE1 production. That was evident in his two games before Sunday, when he totaled 10 yards on three targets. He shouldn't be near lineups against Atlanta.

Shadow Alert: London can expect shadow coverage from DJ Turner (assuming he's healthy enough to play) when aligned on the perimeter (62% of his routes) this week. Expectations should be lowered slightly.

Over/under: 48.7 (7th highest)
Win probability: Bengals 70% (10th highest)

Dallas Cowboys @ Indianapolis Colts

Projected score: Cowboys 31, Colts 25

Lineup locks: Jonathan Taylor, Javonte Williams, CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, Tyler Warren

Fantasy Scoop: Warren returned from a two-game injury absence Sunday and was limited to 18 yards on four receptions. It was his worst fantasy outing of the season despite the fact that he matched a career high with 10 targets. Warren has now seen nine or more targets in three of his past four games, and his 23.5% target share (when active) ranks fourth among all tight ends. That usage has helped him to three touchdowns and 12.6 fantasy PPG, which ranks fifth at the position. Yardage has been an issue due to Warren's short area role (4.3 aDOT), but he has proved to be a viable PPR merchant who also gets run near the goal line. Though the Cowboys have been serviceable against tight ends, they still sport the league's worst defensive EPA, which positions Warren for a bounce-back game in Week 9. He remains a solid TE1 option.

Over/under: 55.8 (2nd highest)
Win probability: Cowboys 71% (8th highest)

New York Jets @ Kansas City Chiefs

Projected score: Chiefs 28, Jets 19

Lineup locks: Kenneth Walker III, Rashee Rice, Garrett Wilson

Fantasy Scoop: Adonai Mitchell exploded for a 7-142-1 receiving line on nine targets Sunday. His 27.2 fantasy points were a career high and more than double his total (21.3) for his first four games of the season. Mitchell has now played three full games (he was limited in his return from injury in Week 7) and has registered at least 60 yards in all three. Mitchell clearly has a solid connection with Geno Smith, but there are a lot of mouths to feed in a Jets offense that also includes Wilson, Omar Cooper Jr., Mason Taylor and Kenyon Sadiq (not to mention the team's running backs). Boom/bust production is likely from Mitchell, as we've seen from Wilson (under 9.0 fantasy points in three games, but 13.9-plus points in the other five) and Cooper (22-plus fantasy points in Weeks 6 and 7, but zero targets in Week 8). After consecutive good matchups, the New York offense will now need to deal with a Kansas City defense that has allowed only two TDs and the second-fewest fantasy points to WRs. Only one receiver (Jaxon Smith-Njigba) has reached 15.0 fantasy points against the Chiefs. As with Cooper, Mitchell is a risky flex option.

Over/under: 46.9 (9th highest)
Win probability: Chiefs 79% (5th highest)

Detroit Lions @ Miami Dolphins

Projected score: Lions 31, Dolphins 25

Lineup locks: Jared Goff, Jahmyr Gibbs, Ollie Gordon II, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Sam LaPorta

Fantasy Scoop: Malik Willis is on the streaming radar this week. The dual-threat quarterback has dealt with one of the league's hardest schedules this season, having faced only one defense that sits worse than 15th in fantasy points allowed to the position (Raiders, Week 1). He was serviceable in that game (16.7 fantasy points) and was even better in his only other two games against defenses in the upper half in fantasy points allowed to QBs (18.9 points vs. the Bengals in Week 5 and 26.0 points vs. the Jets in Week 7). This week, Willis draws his easiest matchup of the season, a Lions defense that has surrendered the most completions, yards, TDs and fantasy points to the position. Every QB Detroit has faced has scored 17-plus fantasy points. Willis, who has two pass TDs in two straight and sits top five among QBs in carries, rushing yards and rushing TDs, should be viewed as a fringe QB1.

Over/under: 56.3 (highest)
Win probability: Lions 70% (9th highest)

Cleveland Browns @ New Orleans Saints

Projected score: Browns 21, Saints 21

Lineup lock: Chris Olave

Fantasy Scoop: Harold Fannin Jr. put up career-high marks in catches (10) and yardage (154) on a season-high 12 targets Sunday. It wasn't even Fannin's best fantasy outing of the season (24.1 points in Week 3), but it is another boom in what has been a painfully boom/bust season. The second-year tight end has reached 23 fantasy points twice but has fallen short of 5.0 points three times. The good news is that his usage has been way up the past two weeks (28% target share, after 17% during Weeks 1 through 6), which has helped him to 245 receiving yards during the span. Fannin's volatility makes him a bit risky, but he's set up with a good Week 9 matchup against a New Orleans defense that has allowed the sixth-most catches, yards and fantasy points to tight ends. Fannin is a back end TE1.

Over/under: 41.7 (15th highest)
Win probability: Browns 51% (15th highest)

New York Giants @ Philadelphia Eagles

Projected score: Giants 28, Eagles 19

Lineup locks: Malik Nabers, Isaiah Likely

Fantasy Scoop: When we last saw the Giants (Week 7), Cam Skattebo resumed duties as the team's lead back. After essentially being benched in Week 6 (zero touches), Skattebo rebounded with 121 yards and one TD on 18 touches. With Tyrone Tracy Jr. on injured reserve, Skattebo will work as the team's clear lead rusher, though he hasn't been much of a factor in the passing game (11-76-0 on 13 targets) and figures to defer most of that work to Devin Singletary, who also found the end zone in Week 7. Skattebo's role is enough to place him back in the RB2/flex mix, but keep in mind that he was limited to 10.8 fantasy PPG during Weeks 1 through 5 despite averaging a hefty 18.2 touches. The Eagles have been solid against running backs this season despite having faced the most RB touches.

Over/under: 47.1 (8th highest)
Win probability: Giants 82% (4th highest)

Los Angeles Rams @ Washington Commanders

Projected score: Rams 28, Commanders 22

Lineup locks: Jayden Daniels, Kyren Williams, Puka Nacua

Fantasy Scoop: Blake Corum has produced one touchdown, 60-plus yards and 13-plus fantasy points in four consecutive games. Despite the success, he remains no more than a borderline flex option. Still second in line behind Williams, Corum is averaging 10.6 touches and has cleared 11 touches only twice. His usage hasn't changed much between the first four weeks of the season (zero TDs, 5.6 fantasy PPG) and the most recent four weeks (four TDs, 15.2 PPG). Corum's recent scoring run is unsustainable, and, while he's pacing for slightly more touches this year (27 more, to be exact), we saw something similar in 2025. Corum had a four-week run in which he produced one-plus TD, 60-plus yards and 13-plus fantasy points in each game but averaged 4.3 fantasy PPG with a total of one TD in his other 13 outings. This season, Corum is well over his head in the TD department (1.6 xTD, two carries inside the 5) and is not seeing enough volume as a rusher (29th among RBs) or receiver (31st in targets). Corum is a TD-dependent flex against a Commanders defense that has allowed 3.6 yards per carry to running backs this season (seventh lowest).

Over/under: 49.8 (5th highest)
Win probability: Rams 69% (11th highest)

Denver Broncos @ Carolina Panthers

Projected score: Broncos 25, Panthers 21

Lineup locks: Chuba Hubbard, Jonah Coleman, Tetairoa McMillan

Fantasy Scoop: Week 8 presented us with our first look at the Coleman/J.K. Dobbins backfield, and it was the former who took control as the lead back. Coleman held a clear edge over Dobbins in snaps (38 to 12), carries (11 to seven), routes (16 to two) and targets (5 to zero). The rookie turned 15 touches into 104 yards and one touchdown. There's certainly a risk that Dobbins could earn back a larger share of the carries, and RJ Harvey (currently on IR) will have a substantial role as a pass catcher once healthy, but Coleman's Week 8 usage and strong overall play suggests he's safely atop the depth chart for now. This week, he'll face a Panthers defense that has allowed the second-most touchdowns (11) and fantasy points to RBs. Coleman is a viable fantasy RB2, whereas Dobbins belongs on benches/waivers.

Shadow Alert: McMillian has added bust risk this week, as he's a good bet to be shadowed by Pat Surtain II when aligned on the perimeter (69% of his routes).

Over/under: 46.1 (11th highest)
Win probability: Broncos 62% (13th highest)

Houston Texans @ Los Angeles Chargers

Projected score: Texans 24, Chargers 18

Lineup locks: Woody Marks, Nico Collins

Fantasy Scoop: After opening the season with a 14-193-3 receiving line on 18 targets in his first two games (21-plus fantasy points in both), Collins has slumped to 10-136-0 on 17 targets during his past three contests (under 11.0 fantasy points in all three, the first time that's happened since Weeks 1 through 3 of the 2022 season). Despite the slump, Collins should remain in lineups. He's playing well overall (his 71% catch rate and 9.7 YPT are both up from 2025) and remains C.J. Stroud's top target. He's set up with a solid matchup against a Chargers defense that hasn't faced much pass volume (second-fewest attempts) but has allowed a 69% catch rate to receivers (third highest) and surrendered an 11-80-1 receiving line to Puka Nacua in Week 8.

Over/under: 42.3 (13th highest)
Win probability: Texans 71% (7th highest)

Las Vegas Raiders @ San Francisco 49ers

Projected score: 49ers 33, Raiders 22

Lineup locks: Brock Purdy, Christian McCaffrey, Ashton Jeanty, Mike Evans, Brock Bowers, George Kittle

Fantasy Scoop: Do the Raiders have a new lead back? They certainly did in Week 8, as rookie Mike Washington Jr. handled 25 carries on 38 snaps, whereas Jeanty was limited to two rushing attempts on 22 snaps. Jeanty (four targets on 13 routes, compared to zero targets on four routes for Washington) remained the team's primary receiving back, but the massive shift in early-down usage was a significant -- albeit not totally surprising -- development. Since totaling 23 carries in Week 1, Jeanty's rushing attempt total has dipped or stayed the same every week of the season, which has been at least somewhat related to a lack of efficiency (3.1 YPC). Washington, meanwhile, sits at 4.3 yards per carry on the season, though he wasn't quite as effective in a larger role Sunday (83 yards on 25 carries). The carries figure to even out a bit moving forward, and Jeanty holds a massive role in the passing game (he paces all backs in targets, catches, receiving yards and receiving TDs), so there's still enough here to allow him fringe RB1 fantasy production. You were hoping for more from your Round 1/2 pick, but the bottom line is that, even with fewer carries, he should remain in lineups, especially this week against a 49ers defense that has surrendered the most catches and receiving yards to running backs this season.

Over/under: 55.4 (3rd highest)
Win probability: 49ers 85% (3rd highest)

Green Bay Packers @ New England Patriots

Projected score: Patriots 26, Packers 23

Lineup locks: Drake Maye, Josh Jacobs, Matthew Golden, Christian Watson, A.J. Brown, Tucker Kraft

Fantasy Scoop: Jordan Love has had quite the high-floor/low-ceiling start to 2026. Love has delivered at least 13 fantasy points in all eight games but has reached 22 points just once. He's finished between QB7 and QB20 in fantasy points in all eight weeks. Love's passing output has been good (he leads the NFL in attempts and yardage), but he's also thrown an interception in six games and remains a nonfactor as a rusher (11-10-1 rushing line on the season). As long as Green Bay remains a pass-heavy offense (very possible, barring a trade for a running back or improved play from Jacobs), Love will provide a solid fantasy floor, but he's likely to max out as a fringe QB1 most weeks. That's exactly how he should be valued this week in a neutral matchup against New England.

Over/under: 48.8 (6th highest)
Win probability: Patriots 62% (14th highest)

Arizona Cardinals @ Seattle Seahawks

Projected score: Seahawks 29, Cardinals 18

Lineup locks: Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Michael Wilson, Trey McBride

Fantasy Scoop: Tyler Allgeier took advantage of injuries to Jeremiyah Love and Bam Knight en route to delivering 191 yards and two TDs on 16 touches against Dallas on Sunday. Allgeier was playing clear second fiddle to Love early in the game, but the injuries led to an every down role and a 36.1-point effort that nearly equaled his total for his first seven games of the season (48.0). Love has been placed on injured reserve, so Allgeier's Week 9 value will depend on the status of Knight. If he's sidelined, Allgeier will have a clear path to a featured role and will launch into the RB2 mix. Should Knight play, an Allgeier-led committee will be likely, similar to Weeks 6 and 7, when Allgeier handled 26 carries and five targets on 74 snaps, compared to Knight's 22 carries and seven targets on 71 snaps. In that scenario, both would be underwhelming flex options against a Seattle defense allowing 3.3 yards per carry (second lowest) to RBs. On Monday night, D'Andre Swift became the first RB to reach 17.5 fantasy points against Seattle this season and only the third since the start of 2025, and he needed three touchdowns to do it as he was limited to just 2.7 yards per carry for 69 in total, and two catches for 10 yards.

Over/under: 46.6 (10th highest)
Win probability: Seahawks 87% (2nd highest)

Tampa Bay Buccaneers @ Chicago Bears

Projected score: Bears 26, Buccaneers 19

Lineup locks: Bucky Irving, D'Andre Swift, Luther Burden III, Colston Loveland

Fantasy Scoop: Over the past two weeks, the Buccaneers have called 16 pass plays and 104 run plays. You read that correctly. Game scripts were as run-friendly as possible in both games thanks to sizable leads and Sunday's heavy rain. The circumstances have been beneficial for Irving (45.0 fantasy points during the two games) and Rico Dowdle (22.8) but not for the team's wide receivers and tight ends (combined 6-60-1 receiving line and 19.4 fantasy points). This should be obvious, but Tampa Bay's recent stretch is nowhere close to sustainable and is a strong bet to return to normalcy against a much better Chicago team in Week 9. Still, the Bucs pass offense will be tough to trust, and only Emeka Egbuka (if he returns from injury) should be considered for your WR3/Flex slot.

Over/under: 44.7 (12th highest)
Win probability: Bears 75% (6th highest)

Buffalo Bills @ Minnesota Vikings

Projected score: Bills 27, Vikings 23

Lineup locks: Josh Allen, James Cook III, Justin Jefferson, DJ Moore

Fantasy Scoop: The Vikings rolled with a three-headed backfield committee against the Lions in Week 8. Aaron Jones Sr. (19 snaps, five carries, two targets) and Jordan Mason (14 snaps, eight carries, zero targets) handled most of the opportunities, but DeeJay Dallas (17 snaps, one carry, zero targets) was on the field often when the team was passing. So far this season, Jones has yet to clear 10.0 fantasy points in three games with Mason active, Mason has been busy as a rusher but has yet to catch a pass and Dallas has eight touches in seven games. The good news is that this group has a strong Week 9 matchup against a Bills defense that has allowed the third-most TDs (10) and fantasy points to running backs. The bad news is that none can be trusted in lineups, especially considering how little Minnesota finds the end zone.

Shadow Report: Jefferson can expect shadow coverage courtesy of Christian Benford this week. Buffalo has struggled defensively, surrendering the most TDs and fifth-most fantasy points to WRs, so, if anything, Jefferson should be upgraded.

Over/under: 50.3 (4th highest)
Win probability: Bills 62% (12th highest)

headlines.story:
For 19 years, a pocket of college football fans has been desperate to relive 2007. I know this because I'm one of them. Every time we get a huge upset, every time there's a particularly messy Saturday, every time some usurper however briefly (or not so briefly) enters the top five, I tilt my head, stroke my chin and think, "This sure is putting off 2007 vibes."

The 2007 vibes have been pounding us over the head of late. They aren't being subtle. The first two weeks of the season saw wins from underdogs of 29.5 points (UMass over Rutgers) and 24.5 points (Oklahoma State over Oregon), and a top-two team has lost to an unranked foe for four straight weeks -- a streak that will sadly end this Saturday, since No. 1 and No. 2 are playing ranked opponents. Eleven teams have spent at least one appearance in the AP top five, including debutants Utah and UCLA this week. Three teams immediately fell out after appearing on the list.

It's been delightfully messy. But is it 2007?

As a 2007 obsessive -- or shall we say, 2007 connoisseur -- I devised a checklist and a scoring system (50 total points) to see where 2026 is keeping up with the most vaunted of chaos seasons -- and where it still has a ways to go.

Nobody can hold onto the top two spots (10 points)

This was one of 2007's most defining characteristics, and 2026 is absolutely holding its own so far.

The hierarchy was stable at the start of the season, with LSU and USC occupying the top two spots, in some order, into October. But Stanford's monumental upset of USC as a 40.5-point underdog kick-started a run the sport has never matched. In the nine weeks from Week 6-14, 11 top-two teams lost, eight as favorites and six as double-digit favorites.

Score: 10/10 to date

As far as parallelism goes, 2026 has followed along nicely. We saw a bit more September movement this year, with Oregon falling out of the No. 2 spot in Week 1 after a mediocre performance against Boise State (so the Ducks' Week 2 loss to Oklahoma State didn't qualify), and we got a small shake-up when Texas knocked off Ohio State in Week 2. But once again, things really got rolling in Week 6.

That's five losses in the past four weeks, all by favorites of at least 6.5 points (and two by favorites of double digits). Georgia's loss to Auburn as a 19.5-point favorite was the biggest surprise in this batch.

So far, so good!

Some truly mind-blowing upsets (10 points)

We fall off-course a bit here.

While top-two teams didn't start losing until October, September gave us a few monumental upsets to keep energy levels nice and high.

We had five huge upsets in the first six weeks -- including two of the most celebrated on record (App State over Michigan, Stanford over USC) -- and then the stream of top-two losses took over.

Score: 4/10 to date

We got mind-bending upsets in each of the first two weeks, but the tap has been dry since.

We've had some other results that came close to clearing the bar -- Western Michigan's gut-wrenching loss to No. 16 Michigan on a miraculous Hail Mary, Boise State's seven-point loss to No. 2 Oregon and Coastal Carolina's 31-24 loss to West Virginia in Week 1, Utah State's 16-14 loss to No. 19 Washington in Week 2, plus Indiana's near-losses to Northwestern (29-23 as a 20.5-point favorite) and Minnesota (23-16 as a 20.5-point favorite). But the standards are ridiculously high here, and 2026 hasn't quite gotten there.

Unlikely teams taking starring roles (10 points)

This might be the most celebrated aspect of the 2007 season. It's one thing for top teams to lose; it's another for the proverbial unwashed masses to threaten to take over.

In Week 5 of the 2007 season, Rutgers crept into the AP top 10 despite starting the season unranked. Then, before the magical results of Week 6, South Florida, Boston College and Kentucky all showed up at the top-10 party. South Carolina and Oregon joined in Week 7, then came Arizona State in Week 9. Rivals Kansas and Missouri made their debuts in Week 10, followed by Hawaii in Week 15.

All 10 teams began the season unranked and spent at least a small amount of time in the top 10. Some advanced much higher than that. For pretty much any fan of any non-blue-blood school, this felt like a time of infinite possibilities.

Score: 4/10 to date

Thus far, three teams that were unranked in the preseason have stormed the top 10: Florida in Week 5, UCLA in Week 8 and Kentucky in Week 9. The appearance was just a cameo for the Gators, who proceeded to get rocked by Missouri and South Carolina, but UCLA remains unbeaten and Kentucky is a top-10 team in November for the first time in 49 years.

The rise of both the Bruins and Wildcats has been fun and inspiring -- and rather reflective of the current age, where only usurpers from the Big Ten and SEC are allowed to usurp for too long -- but it pales in comparison to the teams that stormed the castle in 2007.

Untimely QB injuries (5 points)

We don't talk about this factor as much because it's not as fun, but it's unquestionable that quarterback injuries significantly impacted how 2007 played out.

Oregon's Dennis Dixon had emerged as a Heisman front-runner for a top-two Ducks team when he tore up his knee against Arizona in mid-November. Sam Bradford suffered a concussion in the first quarter of Oklahoma's late-season loss at Texas Tech. Pat White dislocated a thumb and missed significant time (and finished just 5-for-10 passing) in West Virginia's devastating loss to Pitt. USC's John David Booty fractured a finger on his throwing hand during the Trojans' loss to Stanford.

Not surprisingly, top teams are a bit more beatable when they're playing backup quarterbacks (or their starter is suddenly far less effective).

Score: 4/5 to date

This is certainly an area in which 2026 is keeping up.

Preseason No. 2 Oregon was underachieving even with Dante Moore, but the Ducks are just 2-2 since he suffered a likely season-ending concussion after a dirty hit against USC. Preseason No. 1 Ohio State lost Julian Sayin late in a win over Indiana and lost replacement Luke Fahey's first start (against USC). Big Ten quarterbacks have been dropping like flies all season. Granted, these injuries haven't played roles in as many upsets, but they've been a major subplot of the season.

Cult heroes we can't get enough of (5 points)

Jacob Hester was an unheralded fullback who became team captain and leading rusher for LSU's 2007 title team.

Missouri's Chase Daniel and Kansas' Todd Reesing were Texas products who weren't recruited by the home-state heavyweights but became all-time greats for all-time favorite teams elsewhere in the Big 12.

Pat White was a 180-pound, low-three-star athlete who signed with West Virginia late in the 2004 recruiting cycle but led the Mountaineers to three top-10 finishes and two major bowl wins as quarterback. (He also shared a backfield with another under-recruited, under-sized speedster in Steve Slaton, plus the most fullback fullback of all time, Owen Schmitt.)

The late Colt Brennan was an impossibly Californian former Colorado walk-on and juco transfer who landed in June Jones' Hawaii offense in 2005 and proceeded to throw for 14,193 yards in three seasons -- it felt as if all of those yards came in late-night games on ESPN -- powering the Rainbow Warriors to a Sugar Bowl bid after an unbeaten 2007 regular season.

The underdog stories overflowed in 2007, but the list of cult heroes didn't stop there. From Heisman winner Tim Tebow (maybe you've heard of him?) to the guys who bought those "Tide Rolled!" billboards after UL Monroe upset Nick Saban's Alabama, there were heroes aplenty.

God, 2007 was amazing.

Score: 3/5 to date

Granted, November and beyond is when heroes define themselves -- Indiana's Fernando Mendoza, after all, didn't lead that amazing late comeback against Penn State and become last year's Heisman favorite until Nov. 8. But the growing mythology around Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith, and perhaps Miami's Malachi Toney to a lesser extent, is noteworthy.

Meanwhile, another receiver, Oregon State's Jesse Legree, has emerged as one of the fastest and most impressive "overlooked recruit makes it big" stories in quite a while. Throw in a dash of wacky Jason Eck, and you can certainly make the case that 2026's cult hero score is coming along nicely. We'll see what the rest of the season brings.

A Les Miles figure (5 points)

For those of us old enough to have lived through 2007 in real time, it's impossible to properly describe the on-field nonsense that Les Miles seemed to get away with on a weekly basis at LSU.

Granted, his messiest moment wouldn't come until 2010, when he somehow baited Tennessee into having 13 defenders on the field for what seemed like the final play of the game, but 2007 was a Miles masterpiece. He called a preposterous fake field goal flip in a win over Steve Spurrier's South Carolina. He went for it on fourth down five times against Tebow and Urban Meyer's Florida ... and went 5-for-5 in a 28-24 win. And in the closing stages at Auburn, he seemed completely oblivious to the fact that the clock was running out, then watched Matt Flynn find Demetrius Byrd for a game-winning 22-yard touchdown with one second left.

Despite all this chaos -- and despite fielding a ridiculously talented team -- LSU still managed to lose twice in 2007, falling to both Kentucky and Arkansas in overtime. And yet, because of all the other chaos, the Tigers still not only reached the BCS championship game, but won it.

Score: 4/5 to date

I didn't connect all the dots until recently, but Indiana's Curt Cignetti is the most Milesian coach we've seen in the 2020s. He doesn't eat grass (as far as we know), and he's not quite as chaotic, but his sideline demeanor and eccentric interviews make him the most unique character in the sport, and he somehow created an all-time catchphrase in his first day on the job at Indiana.

Last Saturday clinched it for me, however. Cignetti openly mismanaged the clock on two separate occasions in the final minute against Minnesota, costing his team around 40-50 seconds as they first fell behind by three points and then tried to work their way into field goal range. But then Paddy McAteer calmly bombed in a 60-yard field goal to force overtime, and the Hoosiers won.

Not sure I've yelled "WHAT ARE YOU DOING" that loudly at my television since 2007 LSU-Auburn.

A unique ending that somehow disappoints. Granted, LSU's endless chaos made the Tigers worthy champions, but there's no question that the 2007 title game felt like an epic letdown. After all the madness -- upsets, rises from South Florida, Boston College, Kansas, etc., Missouri and West Virginia occupying the top two spots in the BCS rankings heading into Championship Week -- we ended up with preseason No. 1 LSU facing an Ohio State team that had been to the national title game the year before. Blue blood vs. blue blood.

Honestly, 2007 might have been the most perfect year imaginable for a 12-team playoff. While it would have allowed cream to rise to the top in its own way, the number of glorious matchups we'd have seen would have been worth it.

Hypothetical 2007 CFP (based on final BCS rankings):

  • No. 9 West Virginia (10-2) at No. 8 Kansas (11-1) -- winner plays No. 1 Ohio State (11-1)
  • No. 12 Florida (9-3) at No. 5 Georgia (10-2) -- winner plays No. 4 Oklahoma (11-2)
  • No. 11 Arizona State (10-2) at No. 6 Missouri (11-2) -- winner plays No. 3 Virginia Tech (11-2)
  • No. 10 Hawaii (12-0) at No. 7 USC (10-2) -- winner plays No. 2 LSU (11-2)

My SP+ ratings did rank LSU a healthy No. 1 that season with a 31.2 rating -- for reference, Georgia is the current No. 1 with a 28.1, three points worse -- but while there are currently only two teams with an SP+ rating of 26 or higher in 2026, seven teams cleared that bar that season: LSU, Oklahoma, West Virginia, Kansas, Florida and Missouri. Two of them would have played in an epic first-round matchup in Lawrence, and all of them would have had a puncher's chance at a title run. So, too, would Georgia, who might have finished the season as the hottest team in the country.

Alas, in 2007 we were still seven years from a four-team CFP and 17 years from a 12-teamer (and 20 years from a 24-teamer, but don't get me started on that). Only LSU and Ohio State got a crack at the title, and the Tigers unleashed a 31-0 midgame run to cruise, 38-24.

Score: TBD (but I'm going to say a tentative 4/5 here).

Among the current top 12 in the CFP rankings are nine teams that finished last year in the top 12 of the year-end polls. We've enjoyed solid chaos levels, and we do have upstarts like UCLA and Kentucky -- plus an unbeaten Utah -- near the top. But even with the baked-in randomness of a four-round CFP, I'm not thinking the odds are great that we're going to end up with some wild, unexpected semifinalists or finalists. Hopefully I'm wrong.

Hopefully the recent upsets continue and I have a reason to revisit this piece after the season. But for now, we're only looking at a score of about 33 out of 50 on the 2007 scale. Granted, that might be as close as virtually any season of the last nearly two decades has come, but if nothing else, this exercise should have reminded us just how wacky 2007 really was. If all you got out of this exercise was a reminder of Les Miles' ridiculousness and a search of "Pat White highlights" on YouTube, it was worth it.

headlines.story:
Heavy is the head that wears the crown.

It has been true from Henry IV to anyone who has gotten one of those paper ones from Burger King, and it's certainly an accurate depiction of life at the top of the college football landscape this season.

Indiana, the defending national champion, lost at home and, amid offensive woes, has narrowly escaped disaster against unranked foes the past two weeks.

Ohio State, the preseason No. 1, has already racked up a pair of losses, came within inches of a third against Indiana and will likely play the rest of the season without its starting quarterback.

Texas, which beat the Buckeyes to take over the No. 1 spot, proceeded to lose back-to-back games to unranked opponents (though Florida has since climbed back into the Top 25 on the strength of the edible arrangements the SEC sent to every CFP committee member).

Georgia followed, but even the mighty Dawgs were no match for the curse of No. 1. They lost between the hedges to unranked Auburn.

That left Miami, which went to overtime against a team that fired its coach a week later (Florida State), then escaped Bill Belichick's unranked North Carolina by the skin of its teeth a week later.

From 2014 through 2025, teams ranked 1 or 2 in the AP poll had an .888 winning percentage in the regular season, and last year, they lost a grand total of two games.

With four weeks left to play in this regular season, Nos. 1 and 2 have already lost six times.

There's less turnover at the average Wendy's drive-thru than at the top of the college football rankings this year.

All of which brings us to Week 10, which could be either another bloodbath for the sport's top teams or the moment in which the cream rises to the top.

Current No. 1 Miami heads to South Bend for a showdown with Notre Dame. The rivalry is one of the most significant of the past half-century in college football, dating to the Catholics vs. Convicts, but this year's game comes with some fresh wounds. A year ago, Miami knocked off Notre Dame in the opener, and though the Irish spent all of November ranked well ahead of the Canes and in line for a playoff berth, the committee bumped up Miami and dropped the Domers in its final rankings despite neither team playing a game.

That set off a series of emotional reactions, as Notre Dame blew off a bowl game, unfollowed Jim Phillips on Instagram and asked to speak to the manager several times.

Notre Dame spent plenty of time this offseason hyping the game, promising revenge, but it was the committee once again that saw a simmering fire and opened up a fire hose worth of new fuel, putting the Irish at No. 11 in its first set of rankings. The baffling decision -- Notre Dame is No. 1 in ESPN's FPI metric and No. 4 in the AP poll -- means that a loss by the Irish would be a potentially fatal blow for a playoff bid this year, too.

Meanwhile, Miami has a lot to prove, too. Its best win came vs. Wake Forest, and last week Billy Edwards Jr. -- the unseasoned oatmeal of college QBs -- carved up the Canes' secondary like a Thanksgiving turkey. In the aftermath, Mario Cristobal admitted there is a lot of work to be done but given the myriad injuries Miami has suffered in the back end of its defense, there are big questions as to how much this unit can improve.

But if the current No. 1 is in jeopardy in South Bend, the line of teams waiting to wear the crown faces its own do-or-die moments in Week 10.

No. 2 Georgia travels to Oxford, Mississippi, for a rematch of last year's Sugar Bowl vs. Ole Miss, hoping Glenn Schumann's defense can finally figure out how to contain Trinidad Chambliss. The Rebels are coming off a dominant win over Auburn, but it has been a bit of a roller coaster for the Rebels, who have alternated impressive wins with frustrating losses. Georgia, meanwhile, has been held to less than 28 points in three straight games for the first time since 2019, just in time for fans to perform their annual ritual of taking down their Halloween decorations and putting up their "Fire Mike Bobo" season decorations.

No. 3 Utah hosts No. 9 BYU for an early brunch in Salt Lake City. The 10 a.m. local kickoff time is an especially egregious slap in the face for two fanbases primarily made up of folks whose religion forbids coffee, but the stakes couldn't be higher. Utah's résumé largely comes down to an ugly home win over Houston and a bunch of snoozers. BYU has one of the biggest victories of the season against Notre Dame but has struggled mightily the past two weeks against lackluster opponents UCF (a 39-31 loss) and Arizona State (a 27-20 win). And all of that comes against the backdrop of the Big 12's continuing circus of officiating in every Cougars game. This week, all video reviews will be accompanied by the theme song from "Benny Hill."

Alabama was gifted the No. 5 ranking by the committee based on a little-known codicil in the College Football Playoff constitution known as the "But Paaaawwwwwlllll" Principle, in which the Tide always get the benefit of the doubt in all debates over rankings or who gets the fries at the bottom of a Five Guys bag. Bama faces Lane Kiffin and No. 14 LSU, whom the committee seemed to view with as much enthusiasm as Sankey views a new Kiffin social media post. A home loss for the Bayou Bengals will probably be the end of their playoff hopes, while a third loss for Alabama could knock the Tide all the way down to No. 7 in the rankings next week.

The SEC's biggest surprise, No. 6 Kentucky, gets another shot to burnish its résumé, too. While the rest of the SEC was rewarded for big wins, the committee slotted UK behind UGA and Bama despite a superior strength of record. Given Alabama's emphatic second half in a win over Kentucky, there's at least some rationale for the ranking, but if the Wildcats can go on the road and topple a team that beat the Tide head-to-head, that would be a huge résumé booster and add another stop on the SEC's "wheel of destiny" standings.

No. 7 Texas goes to No. 16 Missouri in another matchup of two-loss SEC teams, too, giving Arch Manning another chance to convince the country he's terrible only to engineer a 97-yard game-winning drive that undermines 57 minutes of hot takes.

Add it all up and Week 10 has the makings of the most pivotal action of the season. It could be the Saturday in which the true powers announce their presence with authority, stake out the high ground in the race for a national title and finally add a semblance of stability to the top of the standings. Or it could follow the season's trend of chaos and controversy and provide us with the most nonsensical shifts in power since the final season of "Game of Thrones."

Either way, when the dust settles, the college football landscape is going to look a lot different.

The best of the rest of Week 10

Oregon at Ohio State

The preseason No. 1 and No. 2 teams will face off in Columbus this week, but it won't be with the same cache most pundits envisioned in August.

Ohio State blew a big lead to Texas, narrowly escaped Indiana, lost its QB (likely for the year) and then lost by two scores to a reeling USC.

Oregon nearly lost to Boise State, got thumped by Oklahoma State and Illinois (both unranked now) and lost a heartbreaker to UCLA.

So now, we get what might have been the marquee matchup of 2026 happening as an undercard between two teams with five combined losses and flickering playoff hopes, both without their star quarterbacks.

Indeed, Dan Lanning surely had to pick up his phone sometime Tuesday evening to see his Ducks had been ranked in the committee's top 25 and assumed it was a prank. Losing twice to unranked teams, starting three QBs and firing your offensive coordinator isn't a typical top-25 résumé.

Still, there's ample talent remaining on both sidelines and plenty at stake. A loss for either will likely be the nail in their playoff coffin, but a win could help shift the narratives that have soured dramatically since September.

The key to the game might be Dylan Raiola, who finally seems to be living up to the promise of his recruiting profile. After being benched following a brutal performance against UCLA, Raiola has been solid the past three games, including throwing for 336 yards and three touchdowns in a win over Northwestern last week. Ohio State will need to lean on its run game as a counter. Bo Jackson ran for a season-high 121 yards in the loss to USC in Week 9.

Virginia Tech at SMU

Two of the ACC's three unranked 6-2 teams face off in Dallas. This is a critical stretch for SMU, which hosts No. 16 Wake Forest next week. The Mustangs still have a shot at making the ACC title game if they win out, but last week's late loss to Syracuse stings. Still, it's not exactly a surprise. SMU has been tied or ahead in the fourth quarter of eight of its past nine losses.

Michigan State at Michigan

Fun fact: There are four power-conference teams that have not trailed by more than one score all season. No. 1 Miami, No. 8 UCLA, No. 9 BYU (combined 23-1) and ... Michigan! The Wolverines are either 5-3 or 4-4 (depending on how many seconds you think are in a regulation football game), and all but a 52-17 blowout of UTEP have been decided by a touchdown or less, including last week's 28-21 victory over Rutgers. Michigan State hasn't shown much more life offensively, so this one could look much the same, but the good news for Wolverines fans is this: A woeful offense and a mediocre season are exactly the ingredients necessary to deliver a particularly painful loss to Ohio State to end the regular season.

Under-the-radar games

Duke at NC State

Here's the list of all the players over the past 20 years who have racked up 900 rushing yards, 300 receiving yards and scored 19 or more touchdowns in their first eight games of a season:

Duke's Nate Sheppard.

That's the whole list.

Sheppard was amazing last week against Boston College with 129 yards of offense and five rushing scores. Defenses have tried to stop him by any means necessary, but it's hard to find answers for a player who can do just about anything. In fact, here's another stat: Sheppard is the only power-conference player since 2011 (Wisconsin's Montee Ball) with 14 rushing touchdowns, four receiving touchdowns and a passing touchdown in a season -- and he has done it in just eight games.

Penn State at Washington

Penn State opened the season at No. 18 in the country. Washington was No. 17. They're a combined 3-7 vs. Power 4 opponents this year, with two of those wins coming against Purdue. So, the voters might have gotten that one wrong. The Huskies are 2-0 with Elijah Brown at QB, despite their offensive averaging almost exactly the same yards per play, success rate and explosive rates as it did under Demond Williams Jr. Washington's offense has been one long rom-com: Team finds star QB. Star QB tries to leave for a richer team. Team woos star QB back by standing outside his window holding up a boom box playing Peter Gabriel (and also offering a boatload of NIL money). Team realizes it doesn't actually need the star QB after all. Backup QB takes off glasses and suddenly the team realizes its true love has been right there all along.

Clemson at Syracuse

Clemson finally figured out the key to getting its offense going last week: Play against Florida State's defense. Sadly, Dabo Swinney's request to do that every week was denied by the ACC, forcing Clemson to file another lawsuit against the league. Regardless, the Tigers now turn their attention to a resurgent Syracuse, which has found life after a 2-4 start with a healthy Steve Angeli at QB and freshman Calvin Russell III (17 catches, two TDs and a game-winning 2-point conversion in the past three weeks) at receiver. After taking Louisville to the wire three weeks ago, the Orange have knocked off North Carolina and SMU in back-to-back weeks. Syracuse has played seven FBS games and all but one were decided by a touchdown or less (a 27-13 loss to Pitt).

Upset alert

UCLA (at Minnesota)

Despite its 8-0 record, UCLA was ranked eighth in the committee's first top 25. Why? Well, look at who the Bruins have played. A two-point win over Oregon in the Ducks' first game after Dante Moore's injury and a 17-7 win over a Wisconsin team that looks like it just ate a wheel of cheese before each offensive drive are the only two games UCLA has played against a top-75 team by FPI. Moreover, UCLA's seven passing touchdowns this year are the fewest by an 8-0 power-conference team since 2012 Notre Dame. That's either a recipe for disaster against a more explosive opponent or UCLA will end up playing for a national championship and honoring Wayne Knight's fake girlfriend he met on MySpace.

Florida (vs. Oklahoma)

Perhaps the biggest shocker of this season is that somehow Oklahoma's offense wouldn't be the unit that provided the Sooners' most embarrassing play of the year.

After the blowout loss to South Carolina, Brent Venables fired offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle in hopes of sparking something for the Sooners. Venables weighed his options between handing the offense over to Jason Witten or putting a chef's hat on one of his other assistants and hoping a super smart rodent will call plays in some sort of "Ratatouille" situation, allowing the Sooners to suddenly become a scoring machine. He opted for the more ridiculous option and turned to Witten.

UTSA (at FAU)

UTSA couldn't crack the committee's top 25, but its No. 22 strength of record should have it well within striking distance of a playoff spot should Boise State slip again this season. But that requires UTSA to keep winning, too, and this week's trip to FAU will be no easy task. The Owls are 4-0 at home this year, and QB Caden Veltkamp is fifth nationally with 23 touchdown passes and fourth with 2,536 passing yards.

Heisman five

With just over a month to go before we officially hand out the hardware, these are the players making the strongest push for the 2026 Heisman Trophy.

1. Miami QB Darian Mensah

The Canes got just seven possessions last week against North Carolina, but Mensah made the most of them, throwing for 274 yards and three touchdowns. What was most impressive, however, was Mensah's patience against the Heels, who bracketed Malachi Toney with double coverage for most of the game. Mensah never put the ball in harm's way but rather chiseled away at the UNC defense in a methodical, "death by 1,000 cuts" march. For the season, he has taken 471 snaps and turned the ball over once. He's the first QB since 2018 Tua Tagovailoa with 25 passing touchdowns and one or fewer interceptions through eight games, which would seem impressive anywhere except Miami, where the fans have seen too many Tagovailoa Miami Dolphins games to appreciate the comparison.

2. Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith

The Julian Sayin injury was clearly a problem for Ohio State in its loss to USC, but no one can say Smith didn't do his part to help. He finished with 10 catches for 83 yards and a touchdown -- his third double-digit catch game of the season.

3. Miami WR Malachi Toney

Toney had seven catches for 75 yards and two touchdowns in the win over North Carolina, and he had two more astonishing near catches, including one along the sideline that was ruled incomplete after the ball shifted in his hands as he hit the ground out of bounds. At some point, Miami needs to assemble a highlight reel of all Toney's ridiculous catches that were either overturned on review or called back because of penalties in a "director's cut" version of a Heisman season. It's like Zach Snyder's "Justice League" except with quality action sequences.

4. Notre Dame QB CJ Carr

Carr threw for 210 yards and a pair of touchdowns against Navy last week, but it'll be his performance Saturday against Miami that's likely to determine whether he's a real threat to win the Heisman or just a periphery candidate stacking his numbers against mediocre competition. Carr has played just four ranked Power 4 opponents in his career. His numbers in those games: 50.8 QBR, 60% completions, four TD passes, three picks.

5. Wake Forest QB Gio Lopez

Like Mensah, Lopez is off to a nearly mistake-free start to the season. But here's the wild thing: In the past 20 seasons, only 15 FBS quarterbacks have opened a season with at least 17 total touchdowns and one or zero turnovers through eight games. Only one has done it twice -- Lopez. In 2024, he had 17 TDs and one interception at South Alabama. This year, he has 24 touchdowns and one pick at Wake Forest. In between, he spent a year at North Carolina. Lopez's career is basically the same as if Al Pacino had made "Jack and Jill" in between "Godfather" and "Godfather II."

Post-week 9 power rankings

1. College kickers
2. Utah
3. Feisty South Carolina

4. Bill Belichick channeling his emotions after a bad breakup into beating Miami
5. Ole Miss
6. Extensions for coaches rumored to be interested in the Florida State job
7. Wake Forest again
8. Internal joy
9. An extra hour of sleep following great Pac-12 After Dark games
10. Indoor cocktail parties

Unranked: External applause; correctly spelling coaches' names; American Conference officials' tackling technique; healthy Big Ten QBs; the AP poll; Oklahoma

Two-minute drill

Nebraska at Illinois

The thing about college football is, with just 12 games in a season, a lot of quirky things can happen as a result of a ridiculously small sample size. Play enough games, though, and eventually the cream rises to the top, the flukes even out and the near misses get offset by the victory-from-the-jaws-of-defeat wins. Unless, of course, you're Nebraska.

This season, the Huskers have lost three games by a grand total of 13 points. Less than two touchdowns is the difference between a near certain playoff team with wins over Indiana and Oregon and ... this. And even that doesn't really capture how close the Huskers have come. In those three losses, they've trailed for an average of 2 minutes, 53 seconds.

But fluky things happen in a small sample size, right?

Unfortunately for Nebraska, the misery is no fluke. Go back a full decade to the 2017 season, and Nebraska is 16-43 in one-score games. Those 43 losses are nine more than any other FBS team -- and that next-closest team is Arkansas, a football program whose fans have used the phrase, "In the good old days under Houston Nutt." Nebraska's luck isn't just bad -- it's impossible.

There are theories, of course. Subpar coaching has cost the team valuable points in crucial moments. QB play has been below average. Tom Osborne met the devil at a crossroads outside Omaha and sold the program's soul in exchange for Tommy Frazier. But none quite explain how these losses keep happening, year after year, coach after coach.

There is only this: All things must pass, and Nebraska, too, will one day escape from this wicked curse. Perhaps it will be against Illinois this week. Perhaps not until Scott Frost is thrown into the abyss. But someday, the football gods will smile on Nebraska, and its wish will be granted: no more close losses. Only 20-point blowouts.

Florida State at Boston College

Last week, fans fundraised to have a plane fly over Doak Campbell Stadium with a sign imploring the school to fire Mike Norvell. Only, they spelled Norvell's name wrong. And that about sums up the state of FSU football.

How did we get here?

Well, perhaps "here" is actually the norm, not the aberration. Since 2001, Florida State has had 13 seasons with five or more losses and 12 seasons with nine or more wins.

What if Norvell's fate was always going to look like this, and the surprise was the 19-game winning streak he had in the middle of a tenure in which he was otherwise 22-39. Set aside that stretch from the midpoint of 2022 through the now infamous viewing of FSU's playoff snub in 2023, the Seminoles are 25-53 over the past decade against Power 4/5 opponents under three different head coaches. That's a .321 winning percentage. That's worse than Syracuse, Purdue or this week's opponent, Boston College, in the same span. In fact, only Arkansas, Vanderbilt, Rutgers, Kansas, Colorado and Maryland have worse marks among teams which have been in power leagues since 2017.

It would be easy enough to blame Norvell for the current status of FSU. Perhaps instead he ought to be credited for dragging the Seminoles from a decade-long mess just long enough to see daylight before the playoff committee slammed the door in his face.

Iowa at Northwestern

In this week's Anger Index, we might have overlooked one team that certainly should be plenty outraged about the committee's rankings: Northwestern. There are four power-conference teams 6-2 or better that were left out of the committee's top 25. Three are in the ACC, making them the football equivalent to the sound of a dog whistle -- technically there, but imperceptible to committee members. The other? Northwestern. Moreover, the Wildcats' two losses are both on the road by a combined 14 points to two ranked teams -- Indiana and Oregon. This week's opponent, Iowa, is also 6-2 -- but it was blown out by Ohio State and lost to unranked Minnesota. Iowa's résumé seems to be based mostly off beating then-No. 18 Michigan on a last-second touchdown. Yet, the Hawkeyes came in at No. 19. Northwestern gets a chance to correct the record this week as it hosts Iowa, testing Chip Kelly's offensive proficiency against the Hawkeyes' ability to play such a plodding, monotonous brand of offense that pediatricians recommend it to help soothe teething babies.

North Carolina at UConn

Bill Belichick returns to New England, where his Tar Heels -- fresh off a near-upset of No. 1 Miami -- can take another step toward bowl eligibility by beating UConn. More importantly for Belichick, this road trip significantly shortens his daily commute to toilet paper Robert Kraft's house.

Texas A&M at South Carolina

Mike Elko has to be furious with the playoff committee right now. Texas A&M is 4-4, sure. And yes, its offense is the equivalent of a newborn deer learning to walk but look at those quality losses! A&M lost by 10 to No. 6 Kentucky. It lost on the road to No. 14 LSU and No. 18 Missouri. It hung tough in an 11-point defeat against No. 5 Alabama. No other team in the country can claim a résumé with so many elite losses. Not even this week's opponent, No. 21 South Carolina, comes close. A&M's strength of schedule is a robust 16th nationally, according to ESPN, ahead of Tennessee, Indiana and Georgia. If that's not enough to get the Aggies into playoff contention, then maybe a 24-team playoff isn't big enough.

West Virginia at Texas Tech

The difference for Texas Tech between last week's win over No. 22 Arizona and the prior week's loss to unranked Cincinnati was the run defense. Against the Bearcats, Texas Tech allowed 255 yards on the ground. Last week, Arizona tallied ... 12. This week, the Red Raiders will face their biggest rushing challenge to date against West Virginia, where QB Michael Hawkins Jr. is tied for the Power 4 lead in total touchdowns with 27 and rushing touchdowns with 16.

Delaware at Kennesaw State

Since returning from injury two weeks ago, Delaware QB Nick Minicucci has thrown for 639 yards and nine touchdowns. For reference, that's more TD throws in two games than Arkansas, Boston College, Michigan State, UCLA, Michigan, Clemson or 17 other FBS programs have managed all year. Interestingly, only five FBS defenses have allowed fewer passing TDs this year than Kennesaw State (six).

Rice at North Texas

Barring an epic meltdown at home against Rice this week, North Texas is looking at a 7-2 start with a massive showdown at UTSA on the horizon that could determine the favorite in the American. How impressive is that for coach Neal Brown? When Eric Morris left for Oklahoma State, he took just shy of two dozen players, a handful of coaches and, we assume, the good coffee maker with him. UNT opened the season with just 32% of its production returning, according to ESPN's Bill Connelly -- the seventh-lowest tally in FBS. Despite the massive makeover, the Mean Green are right back in the hunt for a conference title.

headlines.story:
Florida State president Richard McCullough put it bluntly when he explained why he made the decision to fire Mike Norvell in the middle of another losing season.

"This is a big business decision," he said. "It's the future, the fate of Florida State football."

That might sound trite, like something any administrator would say during a moment of change, but McCullough was not just speaking in canned phrases. It's always a schoolwide problem when a major football program takes a turn for the worse. But right now, the failures of Florida State's football team are bad for business on a much larger scale.

Universities outside the Big Ten and SEC are constantly jockeying for position to make sure they have the proper landing spot the next time there is a shift in the collegiate landscape, and Florida State has been among the most vocal. But now, there is no guarantee that another conference, even with room, would want the Seminoles. Once the ACC's marquee program, Florida State has become the league's worst team.

The fall has been staggering. In 2023, nearly three weeks after winning the ACC title, Florida State sued the league to challenge the grant of rights and its $130 million withdrawal fee as a way to test the waters on the potential for future conference prospects. Being the top dog gave Florida State the confidence that it could speak boldly and take bold action, too. Though the two sides eventually settled, Florida State officials have continued to look toward the future and have joined Clemson, North Carolina and Miami in pushing against Section 205 of the Protect College Sports Act, which would cap the number of teams in a Power 4 conference and require independence for three years to move from one of the four leagues to another.

But since the start of 2024, the Seminoles have the worst record in ACC play, 4-17, the worst conference stretch over such a span in school history. In conversations with 16 people familiar with Florida State, "misalignment" and "dysfunction" were described as major problems inside the football building. One staffer familiar with the inner workings of the football office said there were "snakes in the grass, and no synergy" as Norvell tried to navigate an increasingly difficult work environment knowing his job was on the line.

Multiple football and athletic department sources pointed to the aftermath following a snub from the College Football Playoff in 2023 as a dark cloud that never vanished. From there, seemingly everything went wrong. Transfer portal misevaluations. Poor high school recruiting and development. Being slow to increase its football spending. An inability to sign a game changer at quarterback. A vacuum in player leadership. Coaching staff hires that never meshed. Terrible injury luck.

It all adds up to three straight losing seasons and a precipitous fall nobody at Florida State saw coming the night they held up the ACC championship trophy in Charlotte, North Carolina, nearly three years ago.

"They're the headline story for what college football is right now," another source familiar with the football office said. "Indiana is the other one. It just goes to show you how quickly things can change."

Seminoles' abrupt fall

In January 2024, Norvell interviewed for the Alabama job to replace Nick Saban, and Florida State officials grew nervous that their head coach would leave. Hours passed without hearing from Norvell, and in that time, Florida State got a plane ready to pick up his potential successor, Lane Kiffin, so that he could come and interview for the job.

Norvell was torn but ultimately decided to stay because he believed he had an opportunity to build on what he saw as a solid foundation. The 2023 season, despite how it ended, showed that Florida State was on the right path. The CFP snub led to more than 20 players opting out of the postseason or entering the transfer portal, leaving the Seminoles significantly outmanned in an embarrassing 63-3 loss to Georgia in the Capital One Orange Bowl. Norvell figured that result was just a blip, and with a newly expanded 12-team playoff debuting in 2024, there was no way the Seminoles would ever be left out as a conference champion again.

Florida State officials gave him an eight-year contract that would pay him more than $10 million annually that also included a buyout that would pay Norvell 85% of his remaining salary if he was fired. Also included in the deal: more resources for football, including a bigger recruiting budget. Everybody, seemingly, thought the future in Tallahassee was bright.

Then came the 2024 season. Norvell faced a major decision: picking the right quarterback to replace Jordan Travis in the transfer portal. DJ Uiagalelei and Cam Ward had both visited Florida State. Norvell wanted Ward, but he declared for the draft on Jan. 1, 2024.

Norvell was put in a bind. If he waited and Ward stayed in the draft, he would be left with no transfer quarterback and Brock Glenn -- who led the Seminoles to 19 total points in the ACC title game and the Orange Bowl -- as QB1. But multiple football staff sources also indicated the price Ward demanded was $1 million more than Florida State had offered. So Norvell opted for Uiagalelei. The coach believed he could help the onetime No. 1 quarterback recruit in the country finally live up to his full potential. It's still not clear if Ward was truly gettable.

Miami put the full-court press on Ward, and ultimately he withdrew from the 2024 NFL draft, signed with the Hurricanes and became the No. 1 pick in 2025. Uiagalelei, on the other hand, struggled in his five starts, throwing four touchdown passes and six interceptions before a finger injury ended his college career. Florida State played three quarterbacks that year and, decimated by injury, finished an unthinkable 2-10.

Norvell has acknowledged that he shifted his philosophy on the transfer portal after the 2023 season. Rather than going after players who had proven production at smaller schools, the way he did on the way to the league title, he sought unproven players from big-time programs he had relationships with from high school recruiting. The result was a team lacking not only on the field, but off it, as the locker room went from unified to "a bunch of guys who pocket watched," more interested in what they were earning than what was best for the team, one source familiar with the football office said.

Florida State had been ahead of the curve with NIL in 2023 as one of the top-spending teams in the country. That was thanks to one family that funded the collective for 18 months. But that commitment ended after the 2023 season. Multiple football and athletic department sources said Florida State struggled to get buy-in from its collective and Seminole Boosters, the fundraising arm for athletics, to help keep pace with where the market was headed.

In the minds of the football staff, that left Florida State behind the top spenders. Norvell declined to be interviewed when reached this week, but in an interview with ESPN this April, he described the impact the rapidly changing landscape had on the program.

"It was definitely a big factor," Norvell said at the time. "The NIL world really exploded at that moment. There are a lot of guys that we weren't in the price range for. It was a struggle to get kids on campus. We made a choice to go after more potential. For what we needed in the moment, it was tough."

Multiple football sources said Norvell had $10 million to work with for the season. Florida State sources say the number was $15 million total for the entire calendar year. Either way, it was more than the amount spent by the bulk of Florida State's opponents -- but the Seminoles won only two games. "That was not a 2-10 roster," one former staffer said. "If you had said that team was an eight-win team, I would've taken that as probably about where it was."

After the House settlement, allowing schools to spend up to $20.5 million to pay players through revenue sharing, Florida State front-loaded its contracts and spent about $25 million on its roster in 2025. Joining forces with other public schools, Florida State lobbied the state's board of governors to temporarily provide relief to existing rules requiring athletic programs to remain self-sufficient, allowing universities to spend up to $22.5 million in auxiliary funds annually on athletics.

But others, including rival Miami, were far more aggressive. Last season, the Hurricanes had a roster that reportedly cost around $35 million. One source pointed out high school recruits would come to campus and say Miami offered them double or triple what Florida State had.

"What happened is bigger than just one person, but they're trying to paint the picture that Mike had all the resources to be competitive, and that is the furthest thing from the truth," a source familiar with the football office said. "It's hard to go into a gunfight when you're walking in with a butter knife."

Those same sources point to what Miami has done, particularly at quarterback, over the past three seasons. Ward, Carson Beck and Darian Mensah have elevated Miami from midtier to national championship contender. Meanwhile, Florida State signed Uiagalelei, Tommy Castellanos and Ashton Daniels.

"Miami needed a quarterback, so they went and got a quarterback from another roster regardless of money," another source familiar with the football office said. "Look what that attitude did for them. We have been told, 'This is how much we can do, make it work or find someone else.' That's what you got. A team of good bargain players."

To that point, one agent said that he sent a defensive transfer on an official visit to Florida State this past January and that the offer the school made was more than $200,000 less than what the player is earning at his new school this year. The agent believes the offer was made to save money, adding that his communication with Florida State raised concerns about a lack of alignment inside the front office. Those in the football office counter that at that time, general manager John Garrett and his staff had just been hired and were acclimating to their new environment.

"You never know who you're talking to over there," the agent said. "They'll get on the phone and say they're the GM, and they're really not the GM. They weren't very honest about how they run things over there, even with the money part. It wasn't trustworthy."

Failed fixes in Tallahassee

A new-look front office was put in place to help Norvell following the team's 5-7 record in 2025, a season that nearly cost him his job. Florida State opened the 2025 season with a 31-17 win over Alabama, but it was all downhill once ACC play began. The low point was a 20-13 loss at Stanford, a team that would finish the season 4-8.

The loss was so humiliating that university leadership and athletic director Michael Alford met to discuss whether to fire Norvell immediately. McCullough still believed in Norvell and wanted to help him succeed, so he decided to give him one more year. The administration had calculated it would cost about $170 million to make a coaching change, including the cost of the new hire, Norvell's $50-plus million buyout, turning over the entire coaching staff and spending more on the roster.

Instead of eating that cost, the school increased its investment in the roster and bolstered the personnel department. In came Garrett, who had been at Florida State as director of scouting in 2022 and 2023, the two best years Norvell had with the Seminoles. When he arrived, a front office source at another school said Garrett was surprised to find how much the roster had deteriorated since his previous time there.

Beyond the portal misses, Norvell had never been able to land a top-10 recruiting class, nor develop the high school players he did sign consistently enough. Of the 13 Florida State players to earn first-team All-ACC honors since 2020, only one signed with Norvell -- punter Alex Mastromanno. Of the six quarterbacks Norvell signed between 2020 and 2025, five transferred.

Football staffers put their roster budget at $24 million for 2026. The university said they were given a total roster spend of $31 million, placing the program in the top 30 in the country and among the top three in the ACC but not close to the national championship contenders, who are spending in the realm of $40 million to $50 million.

Still, sources within the university contend that a $30 million roster should be enough to beat ACC schools spending far less. It is one thing to lose to Alabama or even Clemson. But losing to Georgia Tech, Boston College, Stanford, Pitt and NC State is different. Of its 17 ACC losses since the start of 2024, eight were by one score -- three on replay review and one when the ball took an awkward bounce off helmets on two separate punts and cost the Seminoles the game.

That begs the ultimate question: Does Florida State not have enough money to win, or was the money spent unwisely?

"We're putting in a lot of money into our roster," one university source said. "We're not Ohio State or Miami, but we are spending a lot of money, and the fact of the matter is there were decisions that were made that were not good."

Still, the administration hoped Norvell, who was well-liked and respected among university leaders, would win as the season opened. One influential Florida State booster said before the season opener against SMU, "Mike didn't forget how to coach."

Maybe not, but the losses started to build again, and fan frustration boiled over before the Clemson game. Before kickoff, a plane flew above Doak Campbell Stadium, with the (misspelled) message: "FSU: FIRE NOVELL." Florida State lost as a home favorite to fall to 3-5, playing the fourth quarter to a nearly empty stadium. McCullough called the loss a "defining moment" and the catalyst for his decision to fire Norvell.

"We're at the point now like, 'How can we afford not to do this?'" McCullough said Sunday during his news conference.

That brings us back to what is at stake. Florida State fired Alford in September and will run the coaching and athletic director searches simultaneously. Multiple sources within the university said the school will spend what it takes to make sure that football is in a much better position moving forward. McCullough previously said administrators needed to do an entire in-house restructuring inside athletics to create better alignment with the university, its board and Seminole Boosters, its fundraising arm.

The first sign of change came Tuesday night, when Seminole Boosters announced a partnership with their collective, The Battle's End. Ingram Smith, the CEO of TBE, said on social media, "The work ahead for everyone associated with Florida State football is significant. Meeting that challenge will require a unified vision, collective commitment and alignment across all facets of the program.

"The Battle's End and Seminole Boosters have joined forces in a coordinated effort to build the future of Florida State football. Together, we are immediately beginning the work of assembling a competitive roster, with The Battle's End leading NIL efforts as part of a shared commitment to restoring sustained success at Florida State."

Getting that alignment right will be essential after years when different power brokers tried to protect their own interests at the expense of the program as a whole. Even interim coach Rick Stockstill alluded to that in his news conference Monday, saying, "I really truly believe Florida State is close. But it's going to take everybody pulling the rope in the same direction."

The pressure to get things right has never been higher. Whoever takes the reins next in Tallahassee will need to get the program back to the top of the ACC quickly. Florida State remains one of the biggest brands nationally, leading the ACC with 19.92 million total viewers in Nielsen-rated games through Week 8. Viewers still tune in to watch the Seminoles, but now the product needs to match the brand.

Max Olson contributed to this report.
