headlines.story:
Should your favorite team be going all-in at the NFL trade deadline, which hits at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday? Should it be realistic about its strengths and weaknesses and stay put over the next week? Or is the best plan something in between?

Today, I'm going to answer those questions for the 18 teams that reached Week 9 at .500 or better. Given their roster and play this season, I believe that four teams should stand down at the deadline and avoid sacrificing serious draft capital for any moves. Nobody is going to turn down a steal of a deal if one is available, but those four franchises shouldn't be prioritizing major additions.

Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show'

But as for the rest, I've split the other 14 teams into several tiers, ranging from organizations that should be extremely active at the deadline to ones that should be very selective and careful about making the right move for a very particular sort of player. I'll lay out each team's needs and current situation.

I'll also name two possible trade candidates for each team. One will be a luxury trade addition, where the team would be adding a starter or even a borderline star to the roster and paying accordingly for the privilege. The other is a bargain deal, where the team would instead be looking for a rotational player or depth for the back of its roster. (Teams are listed alphabetically within each tier.)

Jump to:
BAL | BUF | CHI | CIN | CLE | DEN
DET | GB | JAX | KC | LV | LAR
MIN | NE | NYG | PIT | SF | SEA

Should be aggressively adding

Let's start with the teams that should be most aggressive in seeking out talent before the deadline and work our way down to the ones that should put their phone on airplane mode.

Buffalo Bills (6-1)

Positions of need: OL, LB, S

Was Buffalo's 36-10 victory over the Ravens a sign that defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard was able to find the right mix of players and pressures during the bye week or a product of the Ravens being stuck playing Joe Fagnano at quarterback for most of the game? I'd lean more toward the latter than the former, but I also wouldn't be shocked if Leonhard's defense took a step forward after having a week to rest and reflect on what went wrong early in the season. Playing an early-season schedule that included the Lions, Patriots and Rams also didn't help matters for Buffalo, who will now get the Vikings, Jets and Dolphins over the next three weeks.

That self-scouting might determine how aggressive general manager Brandon Beane wants to be at the deadline. The Bills believe in linebackers Dorian Williams and Terrel Bernard, but adding a cover linebacker to rotate in wouldn't hurt. The Bills also just cut C.J. Gardner-Johnson, who started six games for them earlier this season, so landing a safety who can hold up in coverage would be a helpful move.

Luxury target: I loved the idea of the Bills going after guard Quenton Nelson, which would have given them a difference-maker at their weakest spot up front, but that's no longer an option. Would the Cardinals ever be willing to trade safety Budda Baker, who has made eight Pro Bowls and continues to make an impact as a disruptive force in center field and along the line of scrimmage in his age-30 season? Baker is due more than $8 million over the remainder of this season and $17.8 million in 2027, which is the final year of his existing deal.

Bargain target: If the Chargers are unloading, the Bills might call about cornerback Elijah Molden, who is due $3.3 million over the remainder of the season. The Colts could also be interested in moving 28-year-old Cam Bynum, a move that would save Indy nearly $6 million in cash. Buffalo doesn't have a ton of cap space, but it could restructure Greg Rousseau's contract or ask the Cardinals or Colts to retain some money by sending a better pick as part of either deal.

Detroit Lions (5-2)

Positions of need: DL, LB, CB

The Lions have seen their rivals in Chicago make a huge move in trading two first-round picks for Jeffery Simmons, and the Packers are also going to get Micah Parsons back from a torn ACL. Yes, the Lions have welcomed Brian Branch back into the lineup and will hope to get Kerby Joseph on the field in the weeks to come, but even with those two safeties in the lineup, the Lions have real questions about their defense.

Those issues were sadly exacerbated by the neck injury suffered by star linebacker Jack Campbell in the win over the Vikings on Sunday. Campbell's health is more important than any football situation, and it seems callous to talk about replacing him in the lineup. But because Campbell is one of the better linebackers in the league, the Lions will have to adjust without one of their best players on the field.

Detroit is fielding the league's fourth-best offense by points allowed per possession, so anything general manager Brad Holmes can do to help the defense would go a long way to getting the Lions to the top of the NFC North. The good news is virtually anything would be of use. A rotational edge rusher to work in with DJ Wonnum across from Aidan Hutchinson? A cover linebacker to help fill in for Campbell? A cornerback -- or even two -- to push Roger McCreary, Rock Ya-Sin and Ennis Rakestraw Jr., none of whom have looked like they are ready to start for a playoff team this season? The Lions don't want to mortgage their future, but finding the right trade would go a long way toward topping their rivals in the division.

Luxury target: In my column suggesting trades a few weeks ago, I argued for the Lions to swoop in on Khalil Mack and Donte Jackson in a deal with the Chargers to address both edge and cornerback. That would cost Detroit nearly $8 million over the remainder of the season, a not insignificant amount for any team to take on in the middle of the season. The Lions could trade more draft capital to get the Chargers to pay that total down, but the picks should be more important to Holmes than the cash at the moment.

Bargain target: Veteran cornerback Mike Hughes was with a very different version of this Lions team in 2022 before leaving for the Falcons in free agency. He has started most of his time there, but after A.J. Terrell Jr. returned from injured reserve, Hughes has been in a reserve role, including a season-low eight defensive snaps during last week's loss to the Buccaneers. He wouldn't be an obvious upgrade on any of the options in Detroit, but the 29-year-old has been a reliable low-end starter at corner for most of his time in Atlanta.

Jacksonville Jaguars (5-2)

Positions of need: OT, DT, CB, S

The Jaguars could be one of the few competitive teams to deal players at the deadline if they decide to move on from wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. But most of their calls should be about adding talent to the roster. A swing tackle would be helpful with Anton Harrison expected to miss the remainder of the season and Patrick Mekari -- who can play either guard or tackle -- on injured reserve after undergoing back surgery before the season.

General manager James Gladstone might also have to address the defense, which lost defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton and safety Eric Murray to season-ending injuries last week against the Colts. Cornerback might also be a concern, given that Travis Hunter's offensive role has expanded, which could lead to some series off on defense. Montaric Brown was having a rough season before suffering a hamstring injury, too. The Jags don't need to add a star on defense, but another solid contributor or two would be big as they enjoy a three-game lead atop the AFC South.

Luxury target: Eagles defensive tackle Moro Ojomo could be set to follow Milton Williams' path toward a big contract in free agency. Ojomo's path to the starting lineup in Philadelphia has been buried by the presence of Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis, both of whom are on long-term contracts for significant money. But in 740 snaps last season, Ojomo managed six sacks and 12 knockdowns, although he hasn't been quite as productive as a pass rusher this season.

Ojomo is a free agent after the season, so the Jaguars would need to sign the 25-year-old to an extension if they want to make this something more than a short-term option. With Arik Armstead's contract expiring after the season, though, Ojomo could take the role as the lead interior disruptor for Jacksonville in the long term. He also makes just $2 million over the rest of the season.

Bargain target: Commanders utility lineman Andrew Wylie can credibly play both guard and tackle and has 17 playoff starts on his résumé. The 32-year-old hasn't been needed in Washington this season, even after Laremy Tunsil's preseason injury, with Wylie playing just 17 offensive snaps so far. Given that Walker Little and Cole Van Lanen have played left tackle for the Jags over the past 12 months, Wylie could be a backup at guard and a potential replacement at right tackle if one of those two goes down.

Los Angeles Rams (4-4)

Positions of need: K, WR, LB

The Rams were all-in to win a title while Matthew Stafford was still playing at an MVP level. But Stafford hasn't hit those heights this season and made too many mistakes early in Sunday's game against the Chargers. Both he and the rest of the Rams' offense settled down as the game went along, scoring touchdowns on either side of halftime and turning two short fields from Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert into 10 points. It wasn't the prettiest victory, but the Rams won't care.

The kicker issues that have plagued the Rams led coach Sean McVay to carry two of them on the roster Sunday. Brandon McManus was needed for only a chip-shot field goal, but returning to the roster, Joshua Karty was used as a kickoff specialist and flagged twice for placing his kickoffs short of the landing zone. Nobody wants to trade for a kicker, but general manager Les Snead should be trying to find a player who can fill both roles, which would open up a spot on the bottom of the roster for a player who can help on special teams coverage.

With Davante Adams (hamstring) sidelined for at least another month and Puka Nacua playing at less than 100%, adding another wideout would also be logical for the Rams. Konata Mumpfield has caught 43% of the passes thrown in his direction this season, Jordan Whittington has just four targets all year, and Tutu Atwell hasn't been able to command more than the occasional target during his time as a pro, even if he had 52 receiving yards against the Chargers.

There's no like-for-like replacement for Adams or Nacua available on the trade market, so the Rams will have to decide whether they want to add a player who could identify as another WR2/WR3-caliber option to run ahead of the guys they already have. Trading for someone such as the Colts' Keenan Allen might be useful, but the Rams need backups who can also contribute on special teams.

Luxury target: The exciting trade would be for Brian Thomas Jr., who would be a major short-term upgrade on Atwell as the downfield threat and the potential replacement for Adams as the X receiver after the veteran's contract expires this season. We know James Gladstone has Snead's number, given that Jacksonville hired its general manager out of the Rams organization, but the Jags also might not want to enrich a potential Super Bowl opponent.

Bargain target: Jets wide receiver Isaiah Williams isn't going to be the focal point of the offense, but the 5-foot-10 player out of Illinois  did manage 34- and 73-receiving yard games for the Jets earlier this season. Perhaps more importantly, he's a capable return man who can contribute for the Rams on special teams, meaning he can be active on game days when Adams and Nacua are in the lineup.

The Rams could also look at Joey Slye of the Titans as a veteran kicker who has missed just one of his 25 attempts this season.

Minnesota Vikings (6-1)

Positions of need: QB, RB, IOL, P

Would the Vikings really make a midseason move to replace quarterback Kyler Murray, who has struggled as their starter? Murray's 44.9 QBR through Week 8 is 26th, with his raw numbers adjusting for what has been a remarkably easy slate of opponents. Murray threw an interception before being knocked out of the game against the Packers to start the season and had a tough matchup against the Bucs in his return in Week 3, but his past four starts were against the Dolphins, Saints, Colts and Lions, all of whom rank 22nd or worse in EPA per dropback so far this season.

Bringing back Daniel Jones might appeal after he failed to take a single snap during his brief time with the Vikings in 2024, but Jones has actually been worse than Murray this season, ranking 29th in QBR. And while Murray is making the veterans minimum this season, the Vikings would be on the hook for at least $3.3 million in 2026 and a potential $10 million in injury guarantees in 2027 if Jones gets hurt down the stretch. That's a lot for a player who hasn't looked effective since returning from a torn Achilles.

It might be more realistic to upgrade the infrastructure around Murray. Upgrading at running back would be a logical place for the Vikings to go, given that their rushing attack led by Aaron Jones Sr. and Jordan Mason ranks 27th in success rate (33.7%), 28th in EPA per rush (minus-0.27) and 30th in yards after initial contact per attempt (2.5) on designed runs this season.

A more subtle move might be upgrading the interior of the offensive line, where left guard Donovan Jackson is out for the season and right guard Will Fries has been a disappointment since joining the team on a five-year, $87.7 million deal in 2025 free agency. Adding a guard who can step in on the left side this season and take over on the right side for Fries if he's a cap casualty after 2026 would make sense. Even adding a depth option would work.

Luxury target: You can probably guess that the big addition would be acquiring Jonathan Taylor from the Colts, a move that would get the Vikings the sort of explosive, versatile running back they don't currently have. Taylor is owed $4.4 million this season and $16 million next season, so getting a year and a half of Taylor at something close to $13 million per campaign would be in line with what solid backs are earning in free agency.

Signing Taylor would take some of the load off the passing game, too, and Murray's legs could help create running lanes for Taylor. The Colts back is also a very viable receiver out of the backfield, which would offer Murray an easy checkdown option when he is under pressure and/or wants to get the ball out quickly.

Bargain target: Jackson Powers-Johnson hasn't had a great pro career with the Raiders, who benched the 2024 second-round pick earlier this season. Powers-Johnson has spent most of his time as a pro at guard, a curious choice for a player who was so good as a college center. Trading for Powers-Johnson would get the Vikings some depth on the interior, and if Minnesota likes him as a center long term, it could move Blake Brandel to guard next offseason.

Should be selectively adding

These teams have multiple needs and a path to making a deep run through the postseason, so they should be making calls to try to add players at the deadline. For various reasons, though, they shouldn't be quite as desperate as the teams in the tier above. Is this a young team that needs to evaluate its own talent? Is it unlikely to find a difference-maker at its biggest position of need? Has it already dealt away significant draft capital or recently acquired a standout player? These teams shouldn't be all-in, but they shouldn't be folding, either.

Chicago Bears (6-2)

Positions of need: CB, OT, TE

The Bears made a big swing for a defensive tackle last week, trading two first-round picks to the Titans for Jeffery Simmons. And just like their move for Khalil Mack in 2018, the initial returns are spectacular. Simmons excelled against the interior of the Seahawks' line in a 34-17 victory, picking up a sack and helping to create pass-rush opportunities for Montez Sweat and Austin Booker.

General manager Ryan Poles is unlikely to sacrifice significantly more draft capital after sending so much to the Titans in the Simmons trade, but if the Bears see themselves as Super Bowl contenders this season, it's reasonable to try to plug other holes on their roster. Cornerback continues to be an obvious liability, with Tyrique Stevenson Sr. allowing two touchdown catches against the Seahawks. Coach Ben Johnson would also love to add an inline tight end after Cole Kmet suffered a season-ending knee injury against the Patriots.

Luxury target: There's a way the Bears could add without needing to give up much draft capital. Alontae Taylor played under Dennis Allen with the Saints, and while he struggled during Allen's final half-year as head coach in 2024, he generally looked like an above-average cornerback for much of his time with New Orleans. The Titans agreed, signing Taylor to a three-year, $58 million deal this offseason.

That relationship has quickly grown sour. The Titans made Taylor a healthy scratch after five games, then sat him for the entirety of another game despite activating him the following week. Taylor returned to the lineup as a nickel cornerback last week against the Bengals, but the Titans very clearly have buyer's remorse. You can also imagine that Taylor might prefer to be somewhere else, too.

Taylor is guaranteed $5.5 million over the remainder of 2026 and $21 million in 2027. It's fair to say the Titans would prefer to have someone else pay out that deal. Taylor might be best in the slot, where Kyler Gordon plays for Chicago when healthy, but he would be better on the outside than Stevenson or Malik Muhammad II. If the Bears are willing to pay what Taylor is owed, the Titans should be happy and willing to trade him to Chicago for a swap of late-round picks, which would satisfy Chicago's need for a corner without having to give up much draft capital at all.

Bargain target: What about a different sort of reunion? Nahshon Wright was a surprise starter for the Bears a year ago owing to injuries ahead of him on the depth chart, and while the 2021 third-round pick took some risks in coverage, the good outweighed the bad. Wright picked off five passes and earned a Pro Bowl nod before signing a one-year, $3.5 million deal with the Jets.

New York hasn't been as impressed with Wright, who has been limited to special teams duties without playing a single defensive snap. There's no sense in leaving Wright on the bottom of the roster for the remainder of the season, given that he'll be a free agent in 2027. The Bears didn't seem too committed to the idea of keeping Wright as a long-term option on the outside themselves, but he might be better than Stevenson or Muhammad.

Cincinnati Bengals (5-2)

Positions of need: TE, LB, CB

The Bengals would mostly be looking to replace injured players throughout the roster. They're down two tight ends after Erick All Jr. and Tanner Hudson hit injured reserve, so any replacement they add would be rotating in alongside Drew Sample and Mike Gesicki. Cornerback Jalen Davis is on injured reserve, so while DJ Turner II's heel injury thankfully appears to be relatively minor, the Bengals could look for more options at cornerback.

Linebacker remains a weak spot for Cincinnati, where second-year starters Demetrius Knight Jr. and Barrett Carter have flashed but also struggled for consistency. Knight's missed tackle rate has improved dramatically, but a pass defense that's eighth against standard dropbacks by QBR drops to 19th with play-action. The Bengals are also 31st in yards allowed per carry (5.1) on the ground since Week 3. Upgrading at linebacker could address both weaknesses.

Luxury target: The Eagles might not be dealing all of their veterans, but I wonder if Howie Roseman could be talked into a move for Zack Baun, who has been one of the league's best linebackers since moving to the position on a full-time basis in Philadelphia. Baun is coming off back-to-back Pro Bowl seasons and has allowed a 72.8 passer rating in coverage this season, but he's also about to turn 30, and the Eagles might need to devote resources toward positions Roseman values more consistently.

Baun would cost the Bengals only $607,500 over the rest of 2026 before $17 million in salary in 2027, which is the final year of his current contract. The Eagles might also be interested in supplementing their defensive line depth by taking a shot on 2025 first-round pick Shemar Stewart, which would reduce the amount of draft capital the Bengals need to send to get a deal done.

Bargain target: Panthers tight end Ja'Tavion Sanders got off to a promising start as a rookie, but he managed just 190 receiving yards over 13 games in 2025 and has been a healthy scratch for the entirety of the 2026 season so far. He needs a change of scenery, and while the Panthers have clearly soured on him, Sanders' athleticism and ability after the catch played up in 2024. He would be an interesting receiving tight end option for the Bengals as a replacement for Hudson.

Kansas City Chiefs (5-2)

Positions of need: WR, CB

General manager Brett Veach will be looking to address the passing game on both sides of the ball at the deadline. Rashee Rice has returned from his hamstring injury, but the fourth-year wideout has struggled to stay on the field during his Chiefs career, and his availability for the remainder of the season can't be treated as a guarantee. Tyquan Thornton will likely miss the rest of the season after dislocating an ankle, and Xavier Worthy is averaging 33 receiving yards per game. Unless running back Emmett Johnson is the second coming of Ricky Watters, the Chiefs need at least one more threat in their passing game for Patrick Mahomes.

Kansas City is also thin at cornerback. Mansoor Delane has missed time because of an ongoing shoulder issue. L'Jarius Sneed is on injured reserve because of a knee injury, and given how often teams were picking on him in coverage out of the slot before he left the field, I'm not sure the Chiefs want to count on Sneed in that role even after he's healthy enough to return. Finding a cornerback with inside-outside versatility would be a plus for Veach.

Luxury target: Brian Thomas Jr. would be the dream addition for the Chiefs at wide receiver, but the Jaguars won't (and shouldn't) trade a potential long-term No. 1 receiver to their rivals in the AFC. Would the 3-5 Cowboys consider trading George Pickens, who is a free agent after the season and unlikely to be back on a long-term deal? Pickens would probably be a short-term fix for Kansas City, but it doesn't have anyone who can win on the outside like him. Dallas might be willing to move forward with CeeDee Lamb and Ryan Flournoy at wide receiver and play more 12 or 21 personnel. If the Chiefs play free agency right, they should be able to land a fourth- or fifth-round pick for Pickens as a compensatory selection next offseason.

Bargain target: Veach has preferred to take low-cost shots on young cornerbacks from other organizations in years past, trusting defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo to develop them into useful contributors. Struggling Commanders cornerback Mike Sainristil would qualify as an opportunity to land a young contributor on the cheap. He was very good as a rookie before taking a step back in 2025 and another in 2026. Sainristil originally came into the league as a slot option before earning a starting role on the outside; could the Chiefs move Sainristil back inside and get more out of the 2024 second-round pick?

New England Patriots (5-3)

Positions of need: DT, OL, CB

The Patriots have a pair of great pass-rushing defensive tackles in Christian Barmore and Milton Williams, but they could stand to add a nose tackle to their rotation alongside Cory Durden, who is playing the largest snap share (49%) of his pro career. The Patriots have done a solid job against the run, ranking 11th in success rate on the ground, but you have to go back to only last season's Super Bowl to recall a scenario in which struggles against the run made the difference in a key spot for the Pats.

Injuries at cornerback have also exposed New England to more Charles Woods than it would care to see, which could lead the team to target a corner who can play in man coverage behind Carlton Davis III and Christian Gonzalez or fill in if one of those two is injured. Davis is also a potential offseason cap casualty, so Eliot Wolf could look to add a corner who could step in as a replacement for the veteran after the season if there's a higher-end option available.

Luxury target: I'm not sure the Patriots will be in the luxury market, having already traded their 2028 first-round pick to the Eagles in the A.J. Brown deal.

Bargain target: I pitched the Colts' Grover Stewart as a logical fit for the 49ers last month, but the Niners understandably made a splashier choice in reuniting with DeForest Buckner. Stewart is still a solid nose tackle in his early 30s, and the Colts will understandably want to get off the nearly $7 million Stewart is owed between now and the end of the season, which is also his final year under contract. Indy could eat some of that money to make a deal more palatable for the Pats.

The Patriots could also look into reuniting with a longtime member of the organization in Jonathan Jones, who has allowed a 78.3 passer rating against while playing limited snaps as a backup cornerback in Philadelphia. Jones isn't the biggest cornerback on the planet, but he's a capable man coverage guy who can hold up outside in a pinch. He would be an upgrade on Woods as New England's fourth corner.

New York Giants (4-2-1)

Positions of need: RB, DT, LB

John Harbaugh wants to do something. The Giants were reportedly in on Jeffery Simmons before the Bears completed a trade for the Titans star and have been linked to a trade for running back Jonathan Taylor. Of course, Big Blue already made an early-season move for quarterback J.J. McCarthy, who surprisingly beat the Texans in his first start for the organization. With the Ravens struggling, it wouldn't be a surprise to see Harbaugh give his old bosses a call to see whether there are any potential cap casualties or free agents who might shake loose before the end of the season, too.

Part of the calculus has to involve self-scouting and goal setting. The Giants would love to win the NFC East for the first time since 2011, and at 4-2-1, they're well ahead of what appears to be an underwhelming pack of opponents. Is that worth possibly trading away future picks to shore up a team that's leaning on McCarthy and Jameis Winston at quarterback the rest of the way? Are Harbaugh and general manager Joe Schoen on the same page, given that they have very different levels of job security?

Luxury target: Taylor might cost too much for a New York squad that's already down its fourth- and fifth-round picks in the 2027 draft, but what about Derrick Henry? If the Ravens decide their season is up without Lamar Jackson on the field, Henry could be a potential trade candidate. He's owed only $650,000 over the rest of 2026 and $12 million in 2027. And while the future Hall of Famer has struggled for most of the season, playing with a more mobile quarterback in McCarthy might help create some running lanes.

Bargain target: With the Chargers still winless, Harbaugh could call up former Ravens executive Joe Hortiz (and brother Jim Harbaugh) and attempt to make a move for Dalvin Tomlinson. The well-traveled defensive tackle has slipped as a pass rusher from his 2020-24 peak, but Tomlinson would be a rotational player for a Giants team that's barely getting by on the interior.

San Francisco 49ers (6-1)

Positions of need: Edge, WR, DT

General manager John Lynch made his big move last week in trading a middle-round pick for DeForest Buckner, who offers the Niners a second disruptive pass rusher on the interior alongside Osa Odighizuwa. San Francisco also reportedly attempted to reacquire Jauan Jennings, only for the little-used Vikings wideout to prefer spending the winter in Minnesota. The 49ers could dip back into the wide receiver sweepstakes, given how many injuries they have at the position, but I also think they could stand pat. Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel Sr. and De'Zhaun Stribling all return from their respective injuries in the coming weeks.

The Niners still have one of the league's worst run defenses, so while Buckner is a very good two-way player, adding defenders who can help on early downs would go a long way. So much for this team relies on its stars staying healthy, and if any of them go down, there aren't many like-for-like replacements who would be able to play the same role in the same way and would be available on the open market.

Luxury target: Let me go off the board for a spot that isn't an obvious need. San Francisco has intercepted just three passes this season, all of which have come from cornerback Renardo Green. We know this organization has no qualms about targeting high-end talent and what it perceives to be special football players without worrying too much about positional scarcity or even age. Finding one player who might be able to swing a playoff game with a big play could be a logical target for Lynch.

The 3-5 Falcons are still in the thick of the NFC South race, but they can't have serious aspirations about making a deep playoff run. Jessie Bates III is a free agent after the season, and the 29-year-old safety has at least three interceptions in seven of his eight completed campaigns as a pro. He just made one of the plays of the season last week against the Buccaneers, forcing a Bucky Irving fumble on an impromptu speed option for a touchback. Bates is also familiar with Raheem Morris' defense, having played under the 49ers' defensive coordinator in Atlanta during the 2024 and 2025 seasons.

If the Falcons aren't re-signing Bates, moving him at the deadline would net them draft capital. And while the 49ers would need to boot a safety out of the starting lineup, Bates' résumé earns him instant credibility as one of the league's best.

Bargain target: It's unclear whether either the player or team would be willing to break up one of the longest-lasting partnerships in the NFL, but the Saints are unlikely to make it to the playoffs in what is likely to be Cameron Jordan's final season as a pro. Jordan is right on the precipice of the Hall of Fame, and after 16 seasons, the only thing left for him to do is win a Super Bowl. Jordan hasn't had much of an impact this season, but he did manage 10.5 sacks for New Orleans a year ago.

Should only be adding the right player

These teams have to be careful. They should be looking for a very particular sort of player, in terms of position or age range. Landing the right player could make these teams better, but they shouldn't be paying over the odds to improve their 2026 roster.

Green Bay Packers (5-3)

Positions of need: RB, OL, LB

The Packers are already down draft capital as part of the Micah Parsons trade, and as he approaches a return to the field, the star edge rusher might instead be considered Green Bay's biggest "deadline acquisition." General manager Brian Gutekunst already imported a bunch of veterans to shore up the offensive line, the most expensive of whom (Kevin Zeitler) hasn't played a single offensive snap.

Gutekunst might be willing to drop into the trade market, but given his extreme focus on adding young talent, the Packers would be more likely to add a player who would help in the long term.

Luxury target: Leaning into the idea of trading for young players on rookie deals, would the Packers consider trading for ... Ashton Jeanty? They've gone after Raiders players quite often over the past few offseasons, and Jeanty would be an opportunity to acquire a running back who had excellent pedigree coming out of college at a relatively low cost. Jeanty has struggled so far as a pro, but his pass-catching ability gives him a solid floor, and he would find it easier to access his explosiveness in a better offense. Jeanty could be part of a rotation alongside Josh Jacobs before taking over once Green Bay decides to move on from its current starter.

Bargain target: There has been a lot of chatter around Cardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat, but a more realistic trade option might be Zaven Collins, who is a free agent after the season. Originally drafted as a linebacker, Collins has settled in as a rotational player on the edge for Arizona, where his athleticism and bend have played up over the past few years. He's just 27 years old, and his ability to rotate in and get pressure could appeal to a Packers team that will want to ease Parsons into the lineup.

Las Vegas Raiders (4-4)

Positions of need: WR, OL, DT

While the Raiders have plausible playoff aspirations, their real goal for this season is building the best possible team around first pick Fernando Mendoza, who remains waiting in the wings behind quarterback Kirk Cousins. We know that the Raiders will add some playmakers between now and the start of the 2027 season, so if there's a logical move to be made at the trade deadline, it would be for players who can help them both now and in the years to come.

There are also young players the organization could trade whom I've mentioned for possible deals elsewhere in this column. Up front, Jackson Powers-Johnson hasn't been able to hold on to a starting job, and the Tom Telesco regime that initially drafted the college center is no longer in the building. And would Las Vegas consider trading running back Ashton Jeanty, who was benched last week for Mike Washington Jr.? It would seem too soon to trade a recent top-10 pick, but the Browns traded Trent Richardson midway through his second pro season, so there's some precedent here.

Luxury target: This would be the ideal, logical landing spot for Brian Thomas Jr. Getting a downfield threat with No. 1 receiver upside would be an upgrade on Tre Tucker, who is admittedly having the best season of his career in advance of free agency. Thomas' ability to run away from coverage would play up in Klint Kubiak's offense, and the Raiders would get the 2024 first-round pick for three seasons before free agency.

Bargain target: The Texans dealt for receiver Kayshon Boutte before the season, but after the return of Tank Dell and the trade for Marvin Harrison Jr., Boutte's already-limited snap share is going to be squeezed. Boutte is a free agent after the season, so Las Vegas would essentially be getting a trial run with a potential starting wide receiver before deciding whether it wants to bring him back in 2027.

Seattle Seahawks (4-4)

Positions of need: QB, WR, CB, TE

The Seahawks already made a surprising and potentially significant move last week when they traded third- and fifth-round picks to the Colts for guard Quenton Nelson, who should massively boost what has been a moribund Seattle run game. The return of running backs Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price should also be an upgrade on Emanuel Wilson and George Holani in the backfield.

The problem in projecting more trades for the Seahawks is that they're already mostly locked into 2026 solutions at their biggest positions of need. Quarterback Sam Darnold hasn't been good enough when healthy, but the Seahawks aren't going to find a better answer on the market. Seattle's non-Jaxon Smith-Njigba receivers have collectively struggled to get open and make big plays, but the team is financially committed to Cooper Kupp and Rashid Shaheed and wants to evaluate Tory Horton. The Seahawks could use depth at linebacker and cornerback, but the move for Nelson is likely to be general manager John Schneider's biggest swing before the offseason.

Luxury target: Adding another tight end to replace injured Elijah Arroyo and give Darnold (or Drew Lock) another reliable pass catcher would be one way to improve the offense. An Eagles team in a soft rebuild could move on from Dallas Goedert, who is on a one-year deal and due only $650,000 over the remainder of 2026. Goedert is one year removed from an 11-touchdown season, so having a second option near the goal line and in the red zone beyond Smith-Njigba would be enough to justify Goedert's salary.

Bargain target: The Jets have phased out well-traveled wideout Tim Patrick, who played just seven snaps against the Dolphins in Week 7 before sitting out as a healthy scratch against the Raiders in Week 8. Patrick appears on special teams only occasionally, which hurts his chances as a fourth or fifth wideout, but he's a crack blocker and had a 78-yard game as a receiver for the Jaguars last December. If the goal is to make life easier for the run game, Patrick can help.

Shouldn't be adding

There are four competitive teams that should stay quiet at the deadline ...

Baltimore Ravens (4-4)

With QB Lamar Jackson out indefinitely because of a thumb injury and backup Tyler Huntley done for the season because of turf toe, the Ravens aren't in position to contend in 2026. It wouldn't be a surprise if the defense took a turn for the better in the second half as Jesse Minter's unit coalesces, but the only move the Ravens could make was the one they did Wednesday, trading for quarterback Jacoby Brissett, who was the most qualified short-term solution likely to move at the trade deadline.

If anything, the bigger question might be whether Baltimore should be moving on from talent and adding draft capital. While some of its veterans are struggling, I believe there would be a market for potential 2027 cap casualties Calais Campbell, Derrick Henry and Marlon Humphrey, especially if the Ravens are willing to eat money on the latter. General manager Eric DeCosta might prefer to try to stay afloat with Brissett, but the Ravens shouldn't be actively targeting more additions to try to salvage their 2026 team.

Cleveland Browns (5-3)

At 5-3, the Browns are ahead of schedule. It seemed realistic after a Week 1 blowout by the Jaguars to believe that Cleveland could be considering deals for veterans such as Denzel Ward and Jerry Jeudy at the deadline, but Todd Monken's team responded by winning five of its next six games. The Browns could plausibly be looking to add talent to a young team in the hopes of chasing down a wild-card spot, and it would be a major surprise if GM Andrew Berry decided to trade any key contributors from a team with a winning record after eight weeks.

At the same time, the Browns might want to be realistic about their ceiling or true talent level. ESPN's Football Power Index ranks Cleveland as the league's second-worst team, while DVOA has it up at 22nd. Its five wins have all come by four or fewer points. Two of those wins were against NFC South teams (Tampa Bay and Carolina), and a third was against the Titans. The Browns beat a Ravens team without Lamar Jackson, and while they topped the Steelers in primetime last month, Pittsburgh responded with a 27-6 win in last week's rematch.

There are plenty of reasons to be excited about what the Browns are building with their past two drafts, and with nine picks in the first five rounds of the 2027 draft, Berry has plenty of draft capital if he does want to make a move. I would argue that any sort of move should be for a player who would make an impact in 2027 and beyond, though.

Denver Broncos (6-2)

The Broncos have their full complement of picks and should net a fourth-round compensatory selection in next year's draft for losing defensive end John Franklin-Myers, which could give Sean Payton some extra ammunition as Denver tries to make it back to the AFC title game. You could make a case that the Broncos are in win-now mode, given that they field the league's oldest roster and sent a first-round pick to the Dolphins in the offseason to acquire Jaylen Waddle.

At the same time, you could argue that the Broncos should hold on to their picks to help refresh their roster with young talent next season. The biggest issue has been their quarterback play, and as Bo Nix has shown some signs of improvement in recent weeks, nobody Denver could add at the deadline is likely to be an upgrade on its existing signal-caller. An explosive tight end would be a worthwhile addition, but there's not really a realistic trade candidate on the market.

Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2)

The Steelers are already fully formed, for better or worse. Aaron Rodgers is going to get the ball out quickly, although he's throwing deep more often than he did a season ago. Receiver DK Metcalf is struggling, and offensive tackle Troy Fautanu hasn't been as good on the left side as he was at right tackle in 2025, but the rest of the Pittsburgh offense is playing at a high level. A good, sometimes great, front seven is doing its best to cover up the secondary. The Steelers are 6-2, but the only one of those wins that has come against a likely contender was against the Bengals in Week 3.

You could make the case that the Steelers should consider adding a defensive back for depth purposes, but most of the places where Pittsburgh would want to upgrade are already occupied by veterans who aren't going to be moving out of the lineup, such as Rodgers, Metcalf and Jalen Ramsey. The guys who are going to get the Steelers out of the wild-card round, if they exist, are already on the roster.

headlines.story:
The 2026 NFL offseason featured 10 head coaching changes, which tied with 1978, 1997, 2006 and 2022 for the most ever in an offseason, per ESPN Research.

The Raiders hired Klint Kubiak after his Super Bowl win as the Seahawks' offensive coordinator. Three AFC North teams -- the Browns (Todd Monken), Steelers (Mike McCarthy) and Ravens (Jesse Minter) -- also changed coaches. Elsewhere in the AFC, the Bills promoted offensive coordinator Joe Brady to head coach, the Dolphins hired former Packers DC Jeff Hafley, and the Titans brought in Robert Saleh. In the NFC, Mike LaFleur, Kevin Stefanski and John Harbaugh were hired by the Cardinals, Falcons and Giants, respectively.

How have these new coaches fared at their new destinations? We called on our NFL Nation reporters to evaluate both the positive and concerning signs from each team so far. Then, we provided a key stat on each team's start.

The 10 teams with new coaches are listed below by ESPN Football Power Index's playoff odds. We'll start in Western New York.

Jump to a team:
ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CLE
LV | MIA | NYG | PIT | TEN

Joe Brady, Buffalo Bills

Record: 6-1
FPI chance to make playoffs: 99.4%

What has gone right this season: Brady's offense, and his partnership with quarterback Josh Allen, is working. The Bills lead the NFL in points per game (33.3) and rank second in both yards per game and yards per play. The trade for wide receiver DJ Moore in the spring has made the Bills' offense more vertical, with Allen leading the NFL in yards per pass attempt (8.7). And their red zone rushing attack, led by Allen and RB James Cook III, has them converting red zone trips into touchdowns at a 70% clip.

What has gone wrong this season: The pass defense has been a mess. The Bills have already moved on from safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson and benched cornerback Maxwell Hairston. Nickelback Dee Alford has been in and out of the lineup with injuries. Now, the Bills are relying on a rookie and a couple of players who started the season on the practice squad to take significant snaps for a unit that ranks 30th in yards allowed per game. -- Nick Suss, Bills reporter

Key stat to know: This is the second time in the past 30 seasons that Buffalo has started 6-1 or better. The last such start was in 2022, when it finished 13-3 and lost to the Bengals in the divisional round of the playoffs. -- ESPN Research

Mike McCarthy, Pittsburgh Steelers

Record: 6-2
FPI chance to make playoffs: 81.0%

What has gone right this season: A Pittsburgh native, McCarthy took the job with a special understanding of the core identity of the team. Halfway through his first season, he has upheld that in a big way. Led by running back Jaylen Warren and a young core of offensive linemen, the Steelers' offense is a physical unit capable of creating explosive plays in the run game. Defensively, McCarthy brought in coordinator Patrick Graham to reinforce those classic principles with his 3-4 front. The Steelers have held opponents to a league-best 51.3 rushing yards per game in the past three games.

What has gone wrong this season: While McCarthy was brought in to maximize quarterback Aaron Rodgers, the passing game still lacks consistency. The Steelers rank 20th in passing yards per game (210.5) and 21st in air yards per attempt (6.5). And it's not all on Rodgers. Top receiver DK Metcalf has been plagued by drops, including one this past Sunday that resulted in an interception. The strong run game has carried the offense in the open field, but the Steelers are scoring touchdowns on only 50% of their red zone trips (tied for 26th in the NFL). Part of the problem is the playcalling. In the past four games, the Steelers utilized designed runs on just 31% of plays in goal-to-go situations. -- Brooke Pryor, Steelers reporter

Key stat to know: The Steelers have a 4-0 record at home in 2026, which is their first such start since going 6-0 at home in 2020. And McCarthy's offense has shown up at Acrisure Stadium, averaging 27.8 points per game there versus 17.3 on the road. -- ESPN Research

John Harbaugh, New York Giants

Record: 4-2-1
FPI chance to make playoffs: 47.0%

What has gone right this season: A lot. The Giants have already matched their win total from 2025. They're clearly a more buttoned-up and fundamentally sound team after repping situational football endlessly in training camp. And they're 3-1-1 in one-score games after finishing 1-7 last season. The biggest gains have been made by their special teams (ranked eighth in EPA) and defense (ninth overall). Hiring defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson has worked out, as Wilson has done a solid job with a group that isn't loaded with talent and lost its best player in edge rusher Brian Burns (torn ACL). They're allowing 46.5 fewer yards per game than last season.

What has gone wrong this season: Injuries have hit the Giants hard. They lost Burns and starting quarterback Jaxson Dart (left knee injury), arguably the two most important players on each side of the ball, for the season. New York spent the spring and summer creating an offense that prioritizes the quarterback's legs and had to pivot. Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy has made it work relatively well with Dart, Jameis Winston and now J.J. McCarthy. But the injuries still have the Giants working with limitations. Their quarterbacks are averaging 13.2 yards rushing per game since Dart's injury. -- Jordan Raanan, Giants reporter

Key stat to know: After their Week 7 win over the Texans, the Giants became the favorites to win the NFC East (-150 on DraftKings), the first time since 2016 that has happened at any point during a season. That year, they finished 11-5 and lost in the wild-card round to the Packers.

Todd Monken, Cleveland Browns

Record: 5-3
FPI chance to make playoffs: 16.8%

What has gone right this season: The Browns are the second-youngest team in the NFL but have taken on a gritty, resilient persona behind Monken to help them dominate late-game situations. All five of Cleveland's wins have been courtesy of game-winning drives. "Coach Monk has put us in these situations in practice time after time ... so whenever we get into the game and whenever we get into these situations, we already have the confidence to go down there and set up a game-winning drive," rookie wide receiver KC Concepcion said.

What has gone wrong this season: The offense -- Monken's area of expertise -- remains a work in progress. Quarterback Deshaun Watson has raised his level of play this season but still ranks 28th out of 30 qualifying players in QBR, and he could miss Week 9 after being put in concussion protocol. Inconsistent play from a new-look offensive line has also contributed to an offense that ranks 29th in points per game (17.4). "It's been a little bit of an up-and-down challenge," Monken said. "But that's part of the NFL, right? That's part of when you play the best in the world as you're trying to find your way, your footing, your players, coaches, schematically, to be consistent." -- Daniel Oyefusi, Browns reporter

Key stat to know: Monken's team has already surpassed the Browns' win total from 2024 (three) and is one win away from beating Cleveland's 2025 total. Before Sunday's loss to the Steelers, Cleveland's four straight wins in division games (dating back to last season) were its longest streak since 1987. -- ESPN Research

Klint Kubiak, Las Vegas Raiders

Record: 4-4
FPI chance to make playoffs: 10.7%

What has gone right this season: Despite the Raiders having an insufficient run game and weak WR room, they rank sixth in points per game (27.6) and 12th in total yards (342.4). That's because the dynamic between Kubiak and veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins has orchestrated one of the league's best passing games. Kubiak has been a good play designer, while Cousins' knowledge of the system has allowed him to execute those calls at a high rate. Cousins is third in passing yards (2,124) and second in touchdowns (19). Cousins' performance under center has led to the Raiders playing well on third down. Las Vegas has the 10th-best third-down conversion rate (41.7%).

What has gone wrong this season: The Raiders cannot run the ball or stop the run. They are 31st in yards per attempt (3.0), 30th in rushing first downs (36) and last in yards before first contact (1.22). Las Vegas has been held to fewer than 100 rushing yards in six of its past seven games. Defensively, the Raiders are allowing opponents to run over them at a high rate. They have given up 146.4 rushing yards per game. Part of that issue is the Raiders' interior defensive line. No one has emerged as a consistent run stopper, as the Raiders are 30th in run stop win rate by interior linemen (24.8%). -- Ryan McFadden, Raiders reporter

Key stat to know: Before defeating the Jets in Week 8, the Raiders were the third team in the past 10 seasons to start 3-0 and lose its next four games. And if the Raiders continue to average 27.6 points per game, it would be their most in a single season since 2002, when they averaged 28.1 and reached Super Bowl XXXVII. -- ESPN Research

Kevin Stefanski, Atlanta Falcons

Record: 3-5
FPI chance to make playoffs: 7.7%

What has gone right this season: The Falcons have been perhaps the league's strangest team. But there have been positives on offense, which is Stefanski's specialty. After quarterback Michael Penix Jr. returned from a torn ACL in Week 3, the Falcons led the NFL in points per game in that span (31.0). Last season, Atlanta was 24th in points per game (20.8). The biggest change Stefanski and offensive coordinator Tommy Rees have made? Getting Penix to play more under center. In 2025, he was under center a league-low 2.7% of the time and in the pistol a league-high 52.1%. This season, he has been under center 49.1% of the time, the fifth-highest rate in the NFL.

What has gone wrong this season: The Falcons followed up beating the previously undefeated 49ers by losing to the Buccaneers despite quarterback Baker Mayfield not completing a single pass. It was the first time since 1974 such a thing had happened. That Week 8 game was played in a driving rain, and the entire thing might have been an anomaly. But Stefanski said in his introductory news conference that he wants Atlanta to run the football effectively and stop the run. The Bucs outrushed the Falcons 324-99 in that matchup. So Atlanta is still struggling with finding its identity. -- Marc Raimondi, Falcons reporter

Key stat to know: The NFC South race is the most wide-open division race this late in the season since 2015 after the Panthers, Falcons and Buccaneers all took turns as favorites during Week 8. Atlanta could emerge from the group if it slows down on turnovers, as its 16 are the second most in the NFL and its most through eight games since 2003. -- ESPN Research

Jesse Minter, Baltimore Ravens

Record: 4-4
FPI chance to make playoffs: 6.4%

What has gone right this season: Not much, quite honestly. When the Ravens started 4-1 -- tying the best start in team history -- Minter had the Ravens looking like a Super Bowl contender and had quarterback Lamar Jackson playing like an MVP again. With the creativity of first-year playcaller Declan Doyle, Baltimore ranked No. 6 in scoring (29.2 points per game) and No. 5 in yards (394.2) after five weeks. But injuries to Jackson caused everything to crumble. "It's definitely my job to make sure that we stay together, that we don't point fingers, that we have each other's back, that we believe in the next-man-up mentality," Minter said. The Ravens are finalizing a trade with the Cardinals for quarterback Jacoby Brissett, so maybe that helps.

What has gone wrong this season: The obvious answer is the loss of Jackson, who has played 14 full quarters this season because of injuries to his ankle and right thumb. But, beyond Jackson's injuries, the biggest disappointment has been the continued second-half collapses. From the time he was hired, Minter's mantra has been: "Be your best when your best is required." But he has failed to get the Ravens to finish games, which was one of the reasons why former coach John Harbaugh was fired. Baltimore held double-digit leads in three of its four losses this season. "There's something there that's missing," linebacker Roquan Smith said of the second-half flops. -- Jamison Hensley, Ravens reporter

Key stat to know: The Ravens have been held to fewer than 14 points in three straight games, which hasn't been done since Weeks 1-4 in 2005. That team went 6-10, allowing them to land defensive tackle Haloti Ngata with the 12th pick of the 2006 draft. -- ESPN Research

Mike LaFleur, Arizona Cardinals

Record: 3-5
FPI chance to make playoffs: 1.1%

What has gone right this season: When the offense works, it really works, showing off LaFleur's offensive ingenuity and playcalling. Granted, that hasn't happened often through eight games. When Arizona's offense gets rolling, it's easy to see the vision LaFleur has for his scheme because it can eat up yards and move downfield in a hurry. And it's clear how LaFleur wants to use his skill players, like wide receiver Michael Wilson and tight end Trey McBride, in those situations. It's just getting the offense to the point where it's rolling that has been an issue.

What has gone wrong this season: The list is long and mighty. Injuries have decimated Arizona's skill positions with RB Jeremiyah Love (high ankle sprain) and WR Kendrick Bourne (tibia) going on IR. The Marvin Harrison Jr. experiment under LaFleur didn't work out, so they traded him to Houston. The red zone offense came to a screeching halt recently. And the Cardinals changed quarterbacks at the end of Sunday's game. More has gone wrong than right this season for LaFleur.

Key stat to know: LaFleur's team is 3-0 this season as an underdog of seven-plus points (7 at Cowboys, 8.5 at Chargers and 13.5 at Rams), which is tied with 11 others for second-most since 1966. The record of 4-0 was set by the 1933 Bears. -- ESPN Research

Jeff Hafley, Miami Dolphins

Record: 1-6
FPI chance to make playoffs: <1%

What has gone right this season: Their rookie class is making an early impact. Linebacker Jacob Rodriguez is a contender for Defensive Rookie of Year, ranking sixth in the NFL in tackles per game. And despite their record, the Dolphins have also shown fight in most games this season -- even after losing running back De'Von Achane, their best player, to an ACL injury in Week 2. This season is more about development than wins and losses, and Miami's young core is starting to take shape. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, rookies have accounted for more than a quarter of the team's defensive snaps this season.

What has gone wrong this season: The aforementioned season-ending injury to Achane left the team without its offensive focal point and one of its captains. The Dolphins also blew a two-score halftime lead to the Patriots and lost winnable games to the Vikings and Chiefs. Quarterback Malik Willis has shown development over the first half of the season, but he has yet to reach the same level of production and efficiency he showed in limited action with Green Bay. Miami's pass rush wasn't expected to be anywhere close to the league's best, but it has been one of the league's worst with an NFL-low nine sacks. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques, Dolphins reporter

Key stat to know: Miami currently has a 29% chance at the No. 1 pick in the 2027 draft, according to ESPN's Football Power Index. That's second behind the Titans (39%) and would increase to 34% with a loss to the Lions in Week 9. -- ESPN Research

Robert Saleh, Tennessee Titans

Record: 1-7
FPI chance to make playoffs: <1%

What has gone right this season: Saleh has done a really good job navigating some adverse situations, which most recently was the trade of franchise cornerstone Jeffery Simmons. Saleh's message to those remaining on the roster was a challenge to take advantage of the opportunity created by the Simmons trade. Despite losing their clear team leader, the Titans took the high-powered Bengals to overtime and forced a season-high four turnovers. It would be easy to point fingers or splinter apart, but Saleh has the Titans fighting every week. "These guys are resilient, man," Saleh said. "They've seen it all. Once the initial shock is over and we get to the grass, the world kind of goes away."

What has gone wrong this season: Tennessee has not figured out how to win close games, with a 1-5 record in games decided by one score (eight points) or less. Quarterback Cam Ward has led multiple drives to take a lead in the fourth quarter, but the defense allowed game-winning drives to the Eagles, Browns and Bengals. Conversely, when the defense set the offense up for a game-winning drive against the Giants, Ward threw a crushing interception in New York's end zone. "I feel like I stand up here every week and say the same thing," Saleh said after the 43-36 loss to the Bengals last Sunday. "We've gotta figure it out, the end-of-game situations." -- Turron Davenport, Titans reporter

Key stat to know: The Titans have trailed at halftime in every game this season, including four matchups where they scored first. They have had consecutive 1-7 or worse starts, which is their worst since three straight from 1982 to 1984. -- ESPN Research

headlines.story:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- For the better part of the past month, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner patiently waited for his phone to ring.

With the Indianapolis Colts struggling and a rebuild underway, Buckner wanted to be traded somewhere he could play meaningful November and December games and pursue Super Bowl championships again. There was only one place he envisioned doing that: San Francisco, the place he began his NFL career.

"I didn't want to go anywhere else," Buckner said. "This is where I wanted to be."

When the San Francisco 49ers and Colts consummated the trade Oct. 27, with the Niners sending a 2027 fourth-round pick to Indianapolis in exchange for Buckner, that call finally came.

Upon getting word from new Colts general manager Ed Dodds that he was, indeed, going back to the team that drafted him No. 7 in 2016, Buckner said he dropped to his knees and began praying.

"It's just crazy the way everything happened," Buckner said. "God, he'll open doors you thought were closed and he was able to open this one back up for me. I'm just trying to make the most of this opportunity."

Buckner's return to the Bay Area isn't just some sentimental reunion. Sure, he joins receiver Deebo Samuel Sr. and linebacker Dre Greenlaw as former 49ers to return in 2026, but there is no hiding from what they hope to get from Buckner -- and what he hopes to get from them -- this time around.

When Buckner last played in a Niners uniform, he was trudging off the field following a devastating loss to the Kansas City Chiefs in Super Bowl LIV. Although that was in February 2020, the 49ers have seven players still on their roster from that game, now including Buckner.

The rest of the list is made up of Greenlaw, Samuel, fullback Kyle Juszczyk, tight end George Kittle, defensive end Nick Bosa and linebacker Fred Warner. It's no coincidence that as Buckner's name picked up steam in trade rumors, that group spearheaded the efforts to bring him back.

Bosa mentioned the idea of trading for Buckner to coach Kyle Shanahan a couple of months ago. Kittle and Juszczyk discussed it with other teammates and personnel types, remaining in contact with Buckner while he was in Indy. Buckner also heard directly from Greenlaw and Samuel at various points. That group holds a bond that Buckner said will "never be broken" from their previous time together.

A common theme in the conversations that group has had over the years? Their shared unfinished business, not just from the Super Bowl loss but in the time that has elapsed since. In some ways, it would make getting over the hump and claiming the franchise's sixth Lombardi Trophy this season even sweeter.

"It would make a good documentary if we did it," Bosa joked. "Obviously having him back ... we want to do it this year."

To be sure, the Niners wouldn't have prioritized bringing Buckner back if they didn't think he could be more than a temporary energy boost. The need for help on the defensive line already existed in the preseason with questions at tackle, and that has only grown after injuries to Alfred Collins (patellar tendon) and C.J. West (knee). Rookie Gracen Halton has emerged as part of the DT rotation, but Buckner's presence should set an example for young players such as Halton and lighten their workload so they can have more success on the field.

Since entering the NFL in 2016, Buckner is one of four players with at least 75 sacks and 25 batted passes, joining Pittsburgh's T.J. Watt, New Orleans' Cameron Jordan and Kansas City's Chris Jones. At 32, Buckner has 4.0 sacks this season, which would already put him atop the 49ers' list.

The team hopes Buckner's addition and the eventual return of Bosa, who is aiming to play Sunday against the Raiders after missing five games because of a calf injury, should generate a more consistent pass rush without having to blitz. Through seven games, the Niners are getting pressure on just 23% of opponent dropbacks when they rush four, the second-lowest mark in the NFL. And though Buckner is more of a classic 3-technique, similar to Osa Odighizuwa and Halton, he still commands -- and beats -- double-teams on a regular basis. That should allow Buckner to play next to Odighizuwa on the interior.

"You start in a spot, but you have to be interchangeable," Shanahan said. "I see it as you've got two inside guys."

At kickoff against the Raiders, Buckner will be in his familiar spot, wearing his usual No. 99 after West offered it up without asking for anything in return -- though Buckner said he will take care of West for the gesture.

Sunday will mark 2,471 days since Buckner last played for the Niners. In some ways, after six-plus seasons in Indianapolis, it will have felt like an eternity. In others, flanked once more by Greenlaw, Bosa and Warner, it will feel like he never left at all.

But for Buckner, it will be the first step toward finishing what he and other foundational 49ers started almost a decade ago.

"Me coming back, it's great," Buckner said. "It's a little nostalgic, but there's still a job to do.

"It's Super Bowl or bust, and you don't want to be anywhere else. And that's why you play the game to form a legacy and to bring the organization back to the top. That's why I came."

headlines.story:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- Last week, Kansas City Chiefs defensive lineman Chris Jones admitted the obvious: Like in each of the past two years, he's off to a slow start.

But even by Jones' usual high standards, his production this season -- or lack of it -- has been more than just slow. It's been snail-like.

Through seven games, Jones, a six-time All-Pro, has generated 13 tackles (tied for 421st among all defenders), three quarterback hits (tied for 134th), two pass deflections (tied for 156th), a fumble recovery (tied for ninth) and half of a sack (tied for 261st).

"I always can be better," Jones said last week. "I'm my biggest critic."

Although Jones is still quick once the ball is snapped, he has been unable to make the splashy, highlight-worthy plays that typically define his game. Too often, the opposing quarterback has been able to evade Jones to either complete a pass or scramble for a positive gain.

Over the past two games -- losses to the Seattle Seahawks and the Denver Broncos -- Jones has failed to record a tackle, a pass deflection or a quarterback hit in his 87 combined snaps.

Jones' play is reflected in the advanced metrics, too. Entering Sunday's game against the New York Jets (1 p.m. ET, CBS), he has produced 14 pressures (tied for 25th) and has a pass rush win rate of 13.1% (ranked 35th) when playing from the interior, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Through seven games last season, Jones had 20 pressures (tied for 11th) and a pass rush win rate of 18.6% when playing from the interior (fifth).

As the Chiefs' oldest and longest-tenured defender, Jones, 32, refused to use his age as a reason for his decline.

"I feel pretty good," he said. "It's all about perspective, again, how you look at it. I've played a lot of games, fortunately. I've been very, very blessed to be successful in this league for a long time. I've seen a lot. I don't think my age right now is playing a factor. We've just got to take advantage of those opportunities when they present themselves."

One issue is the number of double-teams Jones has faced. Against the Seahawks and Broncos, Jones, who has seen the eighth-most double-teams in the league, was regularly double-teamed.

"I mean, that's part of the game," Jones said. "It's expected. For me, it's capitalizing on moments I don't get double-teamed. We can't fight the respect level of being double-teamed. I have to take advantage of those opportunities when they present themselves."

He had limited such opportunities against Denver on Sunday. One came in the first quarter: Jones, who had a one-on-one with right guard Quinn Meinerz, won the battle quickly and forced quarterback Bo Nix into an incompletion on a third-and-2 snap that led to a punt. The matchup between the two occurred again early in the second quarter. This time, Nix negated Jones' beating Meinerz by climbing the pocket and connecting with receiver Jaylen Waddle for a 35-yard gain.

For much of the rest of the game, the Broncos either doubled Jones or had Nix pass from designed rollouts away from wherever Jones lined up.

"Chris is giving it his all," coach Andy Reid said Monday. "He's doing everything he can do. He gets doubled from various angles. He's going to draw a lot of attention. That's an advantage to the other guy to have a chance to get themselves home. As much emphasis is put on Chris, let's take advantage of that and get ourselves on the quarterback. Just not to the quarterback, but on the quarterback."

Compounding the issue is the Chiefs' other pass rushers not named Jones or George Karlaftis -- such as defensive ends Felix Anudike-Uzomah, Ashton Gillotte and rookie R Mason Thomas -- haven't consistently won the one-on-one matchups Jones' presence has been creating for them. On Sunday, the Chiefs pressured Nix on only two of his 34 dropbacks (6%), marking the lowest pressure rate by any team in a game this season.

Jones voiced his frustration after Sunday's game.

"It's only one thing: Rush the passer, get the quarterback down," Jones said. "We blocked a couple of balls, but I don't think we got [Nix] down. I put that on the D-line. We've got to win our one-on-ones. We've got to take advantage of that. We get a one-on-one, we've got to win it."

The Chiefs have collected nine sacks all season, which is tied with the New York Giants and the Miami Dolphins for the fewest in the league. Before the season began, the team was optimistic they had improved their pass rush after recording the fifth-fewest sacks (35) in the league (the D-line recorded 21.5).

There's plenty of season left to play, however, and defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo is hopeful Jones particularly will have a pass-rushing revival, starting with Sunday's game against the Jets.

"We're just going to rely on him to find a way to win," Spagnuolo said of Jones. "Hopefully, at some point, it all falls together."

Last season, Jones played his best in the Chiefs' final 10 games. During that stretch, he recorded five sacks and had a pass rush win rate of 20.5%, the fifth-highest mark in the league. That performance also included successful rushes that led to 16 incompletions, according to NFL Next Gen Stats.

That's why Jones believes he can have another memorable second half in 2026, one that helps the Chiefs return to the postseason.

"I watch a lot of Kobe Bryant, and he [talked] about adversity and how you'll face storms," Jones said last week. "You've got to be ready when a storm passes. Eventually, it's going to pass. I don't waver my faith or my belief in myself or my work ethic that I put in."

headlines.story:
The Carolina Panthers remain an intriguing team just a few days before the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET.

Even at 3-4, the Panthers will be in the mix for a second consecutive NFC South division title, regardless of the results of Week 9's home game against the Denver Broncos (6-2) on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, CBS). That's life in the NFC South, where no team is above .500, and the Panthers, despite their up-and-down start to the season, remain at the top entering the midway point of the campaign.

A plausible case can be made for the Panthers to add reinforcements at the deadline. There's also a reasonable case to trade away an expensive and/or underperforming player, especially if a contender offers a quality draft pick in return. General manager Dan Morgan could also, as he did last year, simply stay put with his roster and hope history repeats itself with the Panthers on top of a forgettable divisional scrum in January.

The Panthers have limited salary cap space ($684,323, as of Wednesday, according to the NFLPA salary cap report). But they have the flexibility -- like all NFL teams -- to maneuver their cap situation with contract restructures that would open up space while pushing current cap charges into the future. Still, it's more likely the Panthers look for a bargain (particularly players on rookie deals) than a big name on the trade market.

Here's a look at three players who could make sense to add before the deadline and two internal players who might garner trade interest with an advantageous exit:

Three players the Panthers could add:

Jackson Powers-Johnson, G/C, Las Vegas Raiders

Age: 23 | Stats: Seven games (four starts) in 2026; 30 games (25 starts) in three seasons.

Why Powers-Johnson makes sense for Panthers: Powers-Johnson, a 2024 second-round pick, probably needs a change of scenery after being benched in Las Vegas. He has guard/center versatility, and while the Panthers just activated Brady Christensen's 21-day practice window on injured reserve, Powers-Johnson is cost-effectively signed through 2027 ($1.6 million base salary in 2026 and just under $2 million next year). The former Oregon standout doesn't have to start immediately to be valuable, but he'd be a clear upgrade as the swing interior backup if Christensen or Sam Hecht gets the call to replace center Luke Fortner.

Why Panthers would pass on Powers-Johnson: The O-lineman hasn't played particularly well under new Raiders coach Klint Kubiak. He is probably a better fit for center, but with Tyler Linderbaum on the roster, he wasn't going to get much of a chance. Powers-Johnson is a better pass blocker than run blocker, and so there might be similar issues with him in Carolina as there have been with Fortner in Brad Idzik's offense. Given their immediate need on the line, the Panthers might not want to give up value for a player who is still finding his place in the NFL.

Will McDonald IV, DE, New York Jets

Age: 27 | Stats: 14 tackles and three sacks in eight games (two starts); 86 tackles and 24.5 sacks in 55 games (31 starts) in four seasons.

Why McDonald makes sense for the Panthers: The previous regime -- which Morgan was a part of -- was quite fond of McDonald as a prospect in 2023, multiple sources with knowledge of that year's Panthers draft plans told ESPN. Before the Jets selected McDonald with the No. 15 overall pick, the then-Panthers' brass had "heavily discussed" him as a potential trade-up target later in the draft, one of the sources said. Four years into his New York tenure, McDonald has been an effective situational pass rusher and not much more. Still, the Panthers could use some help in that regard with a 29th-ranked (4.56%) sack rate.

Why Panthers would pass on McDonald: The Panthers have been terrible against the run for years, and that aspect of their defense is a priority for coach Dave Canales and company down the final stretch of 10 games. McDonald won't offer a whole lot in that regard, and it could be argued he is somewhat redundant with Princely Umanmielen already on the roster. McDonald, while he would come cheap this year ($1.66 million base salary), is set to play on a guaranteed $13.7 million fifth-year option in 2027. And because of McDonald's cost-effectiveness, as well as his pass-rushing success, the Jets aren't likely to part ways with him without a substantial return.

Kimani Vidal, RB, Los Angeles Chargers

Age: 25 | Stats: 29 carries for 132 yards (4.6 YPC) and a touchdown and nine catches for 50 yards and a touchdown in seven games (one start) in 2026; 227 carries for 930 yards (4.1 YPC) and four touchdowns and 30 catches for 248 yards and three touchdowns in 30 games (11 starts) in three seasons.

Why Vidal makes sense for the Panthers: Chuba Hubbard has taken on a ton of work in the first seven games and already has more rushing yards (540) and total touchdowns (7) than he did in 15 appearances in 2025. The Panthers have playoff aspirations but Jonathon Brooks and Trevor Etienne have yet to prove they can be reliable cogs. Vidal has experience as a starter and a rotational player -- who can be effective as a runner and receiver -- and he would be coming from a Mike McDaniel offense that has influenced Idzik's playcalling.

Why Panthers would pass on Vidal: A late-round pick swap for a running back on an expiring contract might not interest Morgan, who has invested notable draft capital in Brooks and Etienne. The Panthers plan to have Brooks back in the lineup (he's on IR for a core muscle/groin injury) eventually, and after dedicating a lot of development time to him and Etienne, the Panthers will probably want to see that through this season. Carolina might just want to be patient in the backfield despite the optics of an underwhelming rotation (with a 22nd-ranked rushing attack).

Two players the Panthers could trade away:

Robert Hunt, RG, Panthers

Age: 30 | Stats: Seven games (seven starts) in 2026; 86 games (80 starts) in seven seasons. Voted to Pro Bowl in 2024.

Why trading Hunt makes sense for the Panthers: Hunt has struggled this season between Fortner and rookie right tackle Monroe Freeling. With Christensen on the mend, perhaps the Panthers could make Hunt available for a notable return.

Christensen had the best stretch of his career at right guard, while filling in for Hunt, in the middle of last season, and with the interior line trade market fielding high demands -- Cam Jurgens and Quenton Nelson both warranted historic hauls in midseason swaps -- it might make sense to at least consider moving on from the 2024 Pro Bowl lineman. Trading Hunt would open up $19 million in cap space next year, per Over The Cap.

Why Panthers would pass on Hunt trade: The Panthers' offensive line depth is a mess right now. The starting lineup has had its lumps, so it's fair to wonder what Hunt would bring in return, especially as the front office isn't likely to just give him away. While opening up cap space and getting something for Hunt sounds appealing on paper, a team with playoff aspirations probably shouldn't risk moving on from a proven talent in the middle of a postseason push.

Ja'Tavion Sanders, TE, Panthers

Age: 23 | Stats: Healthy inactive for all seven games this season; 62 catches for 532 yards yards and two touchdowns in 29 games (13 starts) in his career.

Why trading Sanders makes sense for the Panthers: The tight end hasn't played all season. Earlier this week, ESPN NFL analyst Benjamin Solak mused about Sanders being sent to the Chicago Bears for a sixth-round pick. Given Sanders' lack of a role, a deal like that might appeal to the Panthers, who have effectively used a rotation of Tommy Tremble, Darren Waller and Mitchell Evans at the position, plus Feleipe Franks on special teams. Sanders, a 2024 fourth-round pick, clearly needs a change of scenery, and his draft pedigree and long-term cost effectiveness (signed on a rookie deal through 2027) could warrant interest from a contender.

Why Panthers would pass on Sanders trade: The Panthers play 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 TEs, 2 WRs) on 28.8% of their offensive snaps, which ranks sixth in the NFL. They play in 13 personnel (1 RB, 3 TEs, 1 WR) on 10.5% of their offensive plays, good for 11th in the league. More than a third of their looks on offense come with multiple tight end sets, so if someone such as Waller, 34, were to go down, the Panthers would need a competent pass catcher to replace him. And as mentioned earlier, Sanders is cheap, so he's not really hurting the Panthers' cap situation.
