At age 22, when Declan Doyle arrived in New Orleans in 2019 shortly after getting hired for his first NFL job as an offensive assistant, he wrote down some of his goals and aspirations on sticky notes that he bunched around a mirror.

One of the messages read: "Youngest NFL coordinator in history, February 2024."

When Doyle was hired to become the Chicago Bears' offensive coordinator in 2025, he remembered that note and thought to himself, "Oh, I was a year late."

Doyle's obsessive determination is why he is leading the charge with the new generation of offensive coordinators, which is a storyline for Thursday's game between the Baltimore Ravens and Jacksonville Jaguars (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video). Doyle, who is in his first season as the playcaller for the Ravens at age 30, and the Jaguars' Grant Udinski (also 30) are among nine NFL offensive coordinators who are 35 years old or younger.

These members of Generation Y represent a young wave in the NFL that has nearly doubled in size in a year. With five offensive coordinators 35 or younger in 2025, that number has grown in 2026 to include Doyle, Udinski, Denver's Davis Webb, Washington's David Blough, Cleveland's Travis Switzer, Philadelphia's Sean Mannion, Atlanta's Tommy Rees, Carolina's Brad Idzik and Los Angeles Rams' Nate Scheelhaase.

Their experiences this season range widely: guiding high-scoring offenses, getting stripped of playcalling duties, going from being celebrated to criticized and dealing with multiple quarterback changes. But all of these millennial minds born in the 1990s have proven to be young and relentless, rising rapidly to the role of offensive architects because of their connections, creativity and sacrifice.

As a student football assistant at the University of Iowa, Doyle worked 100 hours a week while taking a full course load, which meant he drew up scout cards for the football team during his own classes. As a graduate assistant at Baylor University, Udinski had so little money that he lived in his car in a Walmart parking lot.

Now, Doyle is tasked with keeping the Ravens' offense afloat with undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano, who will start Thursday night, and Jacoby Brissett, a veteran journeyman who is expected to be acquired in a trade this weekend. Udinski is the right-hand man of Jaguars coach Liam Coen, helping Jacksonville produce the fifth-most points per game (28.0) this season.

"This is going to be my 11th year coaching, and I've pretty much been younger than every guy in the room I've been in," Doyle said. "I've always been too young for every job I've ever had. And what I've noticed is that it really doesn't matter. Knowledge is power."

Here are the stories of the NFL's nine millennial offensive coordinators:

Offensive Coordinators 35 and under:
Doyle | Udinski | Webb
Blough | Switzer | Mannion
Rees | Idzik | Scheelhaase

Declan Doyle, 30, Baltimore Ravens

Inside Doyle's offensive meeting room is a sign that reads: "Nobody adjusts better than us." His first few months as Baltimore's offensive coordinator have tested that mantra.

Jackson has played only 14 full quarters this season because of ankle and hand injuries. He will have surgery on his right thumb and be placed on injured reserve with "potentially" a season-ending injury, according to coach Jesse Minter.

Backup quarterback Tyler "Snoop" Huntley also suffered a season-ending turf toe injury, which would lead to a rare occurrence: Fagnano will become the second undrafted rookie to start at quarterback in Ravens history.

Plus, the Ravens' top three centers have all suffered season-ending injuries, which has led to six different starting offensive line combinations. 

As a result, the Ravens have been held to 14 or fewer points in three straight games. That hasn't happened in Baltimore in 21 years.

"I've said it to the group, but it's all about just fixing this week's problems," Doyle said earlier this season. "So, you figure out what the problems are this week, how do we minimize those things [and] how do we take advantage of giving our guys that are up and that are playing, the best chance to go win the game and to be able to execute at a high level?"

At 30, Doyle is the NFL's youngest playcaller. Others inside the Ravens' facility have different names for him.

Jackson, who is 10 months younger than Doyle, calls him "a wizard." Flowers refers to him as "a genius." And defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver described him as a "human computer" for the rolodex of offensive plays in his head.

One of Doyle's finest trick plays came in Week 6 in Cleveland when tight end Josh Cuevas lined up between the center and left guard. Cuevas positioned himself a step behind the line of scrimmage, which kept him as an eligible receiver.

This unusual formation confused the Cleveland defense and allowed Cuevas to slip into the open field for a 29-yard catch.

"He's somebody that knows where he's going in life," Ravens tight end Mark Andrews said. "He's not like copycatting guys. He's making his plays, and I feel like he's a trendsetter in the league. He's going to be like that for a long time just because he's so smart."

Some players believe Doyle is too cold-blooded. In the season opener, Flowers scored on a spectacular 54-yard touchdown. When the TV camera panned to Doyle, he sat there stonefaced.

"You are trying to eliminate anything that would cloud your judgment or what is going to happen next," Doyle said when asked about not showing any emotion. "If he gets tackled, [and] we are at the 8-yard line, I have to have a play as fast as I possibly can to get into [Lamar Jackson]. You do not smile until it hits zeroes." -- Jamison Hensley

Grant Udinski, 30, Jacksonville Jaguars

In Jacksonville, Udinski's journey from his first coaching job to offensive coordinator for the Jaguars began in a Walmart parking lot.

When Udinski arrived at Baylor in 2019 to be a graduate assistant under then-coach Matt Rhule he had little money and no place to stay. He also knew nobody in Waco, Texas, so his solution was to hunker down in his car in a store's lot near campus.

That lasted about a week until Baylor's assistant defensive coordinator Phil Snow found out and convinced Udinski to move in with him. A year later Udinski was a coaching assistant under Rhule with the Carolina Panthers lasting two seasons, followed by three seasons with the Minnesota Vikings. Then Jaguars head coach Liam Coen called in January 2025.

Udinski's path from several uncomfortable nights sleeping in his car to the Jaguars' offensive coordinator at only 29 years old took just six years. It's a journey that Udinski acknowledges has been surprisingly quick but also one that wouldn't have happened without help from a lot of people -- and he's grateful for all of it.

"Those are the things that you look back and you almost think the amount of stars to align seems impossible for things like that to work out the way that they did," Udinski said. "Those type of things, you pinch yourself and on the long days and long nights, you remind yourself where you came from."

Udinski doesn't call plays for the Jaguars but his impact on the offense throughout the week and on game day is significant. Coen, who is Jacksonville's playcaller, likes that Udinski is level-headed, which balances out his own ups and downs.

"If something doesn't look good on a Wednesday, I'm typically going to be the one to say, 'Let's throw it out. Why waste our time on that? We have a million other plays,'" Coen said. "Whereas he can then communicate to me, 'Hey, no, no, no. Let's try it again tomorrow.'"

Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence, 27, called Udinski one of the best coaches he has ever had.

"Sometimes I think Grant's double my age, honestly. Not three years older," Lawrence joked. "Just the way he's about his business.

"... He's really sharp, so smart, works extremely hard and I think he's so reliable. When you ask him something, you know how much time he's put into it, so the answer you get, you trust it because you just know he's put the time in." -- Michael DiRocco

Davis Webb, 31, Denver Broncos

It started with such promise in Denver, back in February, when Broncos coach Sean Payton said publicly, for the first time, Webb would call plays in the upcoming season.

Calling Webb "gifted," Payton said he wouldn't have surrendered playcalling if Webb hadn't shown so much potential for the job. That changed after four games when, in nine words, Payton took playcalling duties back in an effort to kick-start Denver's struggling offense.

"We'll make a change offensively, I'll call the plays,'' Payton said in the days before the Broncos' Week 5 game against the Los Angeles Chargers. And even as he said it he offered Webb would be a future NFL head coach.

In four games with Webb as the playcaller, the Broncos were 27th in both scoring (18.5) and yards (280.3). In four games with Payton, Denver has increased its scoring at 24.5 points per game but has produced fewer yards (265.8).

The most troubling part was the struggles of quarterback Bo Nix. With Webb calling the plays, Nix ranked 22nd in QBR (44.3), throwing five touchdowns and three interceptions.

   

For his part, Webb has said he's still "all-in''on Nix. When asked earlier this month if four games was a big enough sample size to show what he could do, Webb said: "Luckily that's not my job, that's (Payton's) job. (But) I think he answered that. I think the world of (Payton), how we've gone about it ... it's not ideal ... Welcome to the league.''

Webb, who went directly from his last season as an NFL quarterback in 2022 with the New York Giants to Payton's staff as a quarterbacks coach in 2023, said he takes it -- including the disappointment of his role changing -- as part of the developmental process.

"I taught myself early to think about the best- and worst-case scenarios,'' Webb said. "And if you're OK with both, then take that job on. It is what it is, nothing I can do about it now except be the best offensive coordinator I can be and that's what I'm trying to do.'' -- Jeff Legwold

David Blough, 31, Washington Commanders

Blough, who is in his first year as the Commanders' offensive coordinator, understands how quickly a playcaller can go from being celebrated to being criticized.

In Week 3, Blough orchestrated an offense that scored 33 points on the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. It was the second-most points allowed by Seattle since the start of last season -- all with Marcus Mariota subbing for the injured Jayden Daniels at quarterback.

Two games later Blough was at the center of a late-game gaffe that cost Washington a chance to beat the New York Giants in overtime. With 50 seconds left in overtime, the Commanders had just been tackled at the Giants' 24-yard line. Because four kicks had been missed that day due in part to rain and slick field conditions, Blough wanted to gain more yards.

But the play took too long to get to the huddle, according to multiple team sources, and the ball wasn't snapped until 12 seconds remained. Once Daniels was tackled, instead of throwing the ball away, the Commanders lost a chance at a game-winning field goal attempt. It was evident the offensive players did not realize how little time remained.

"I'm the one with the last line of communication to the quarterback. It falls on me," Blough said.

It was a hard lesson in handling late-game situations. One person who had coached with Blough in the past called him "very smart" and constantly discussing situational football. But doing so in-game can be trickier.

"For me in particular, it's how do you handle that situation better the next time you're in it?" Blough said.

Washington's players have maintained belief in Blough, with one saying he coaches with "no fear." In the days following that game, Quinn reiterated his confidence that Blough will be an excellent coordinator -- saying so publicly and privately, according to multiple team sources.

For now, Blough has received a crash course in being a coordinator, having to navigate star injuries - Daniels missed two games and multiple starters have missed time -- and a load of second-guessing. 

"We are paid to adapt and be versatile and be fluid," Blough said. "That is our job, to be able to have the contingencies, whether it's at quarterback, whether it's at running back, whether it's at center or guard, like, our job is to adapt and try to find a way in that week to win." -- John Keim

Travis Switzer, 33, Cleveland Browns

Switzer knew "pretty much from the jump I was going to play until they told me I wasn't good enough to play anymore and then I was going to coach." But after leaving the University of Akron as a three-year starter at center and an unsuccessful tryout at Dolphins rookie minicamp in 2015, Switzer's entry into coaching was an unorthodox one.

Switzer was applying to graduate assistant jobs and staying in shape in Pennsylvania at Power Train Sports and Fitness, which is owned by Steve Saunders, the Ravens' head strength and conditioning coach from 2016 to 2022. Saunders trained Switzer through high school and college, and one day asked Switzer about joining the Ravens -- but as an assistant on the strength and conditioning staff. Switzer was hesitant but agreed to leave for Baltimore in 2017.

By 2019, Switzer was moved to the coaching side as an analyst. One of his earliest projects was watching every run play in the NFL over a two-year span and mapping leaguewide trends. Next came a quality control job and then a promotion to run game coordinator during the final two years of Todd Monken's stint as Ravens OC.

Switzer was one of four offensive assistants that Monken brought with him to Cleveland. Though Switzer doesn't call plays on game day, he has a big role in the game plan installation.

"There's a transition period from being an idea guy to somebody that has to make decisions, and that's a step too," Switzer said. "... as you advance, eventually you have to become the one who's the decision maker of, OK, we got some good ideas, we got a lot of good stuff, what are we actually going to do and how are we going to put it together?" -- Daniel Oyefusi

Sean Mannion, 34, Philadelphia Eagles

Like Webb did, Philadelphia Eagles offensive coordinator Sean Mannion has struggled in his first season as an NFL playcaller. Unlike Webb, Mannion hasn't been stripped of that role for now.

The Eagles rank last in offense, averaging 265.3 yards per game. This is Philadelphia's fewest yards per game through eight weeks since 2003.

"I have a high confidence level in everybody in this building," Eagles coach Nick Sirianni said last month. "Sean, that's why I hired him. Right now, we are in a rough spot, as we know. And so it is about controlling the things you can control in this moment and figuring out what the next steps are."

The hype around Mannion got a little out of control this offseason. 

The front office was looking to modernize an offensive attack that had grown stale of late and ultimately landed on Mannion, the 34-year-old former Oregon State quarterback who studied under offensive gurus such as  Sean McVay (Rams), Kevin O'Connell (Vikings) and Matt LaFleur (Packers).

"Sean [Mannion] is an evil genius. That is my first impression," Eagles left tackle Jordan Mailata said. "The guy knows ball. If I were to lock the three smartest people in the facility in one room, Sean would be there."

There was always going to be a needle to thread. Quarterback Jalen Hurts had never majored in a system featuring heavy under center, motion and play-action and it's tough to undergo a transition like this on the fly while maintaining contender status. 

Philly ended up going with a blend of the old and the new, and none of it worked super well.  

Then came the retirement of right tackle Lane Johnson, the trade of center Cam Jurgens, the rash of injuries to the skill position players and then the loss of Hurts for the season, making it near-impossible to have a highly-efficient offense. The learning curve appeared to hit Mannion hard as well, as the offense struggled week after week in the second half in particular, signaling a lack of effective adjustments. 

"I know we're fighting tooth and nail every day to get the results that I know we can get, the results I know we want," Mannion said. "The thing with the work part of it is it really is -- that's the part you love. You love coming in here every day, working your tail off with your staff, with your players, working as a unit to try to achieve the best result possible." -- Tim McManus

Tommy Rees, 34, Atlanta Falcons

Long before Rees was hired as the Falcons' offensive coordinator this offseason, he interviewed for an offensive assistant role with the San Diego Chargers at the age of 23.

Ken Whisenhunt, who was the offensive coordinator for the Chargers at the time, asked Rees a poignant question.

"If you have a 30-year-old receiver roll his eyes at you or tell you to 'F' off, how do you handle it?" Whisenhunt inquired.

Rees said his answer then would be the same as his answer now as the 34-year-old Falcons O-coordinator and playcaller.

"These guys want to extend their career," Rees said. "They want to be great. ... If you can show them [at] any level that you can help them 1%, that you know what you're talking about, then they're going to buy in and listen. And we have young guys on our staff, young girls on our staff now that I talk to, and that's always the message. You have to be on it, because if you slip up, you're going to lose their trust."

Rees and Doyle are close friends and Rees said they have discussed being considered young for their roles in Atlanta and Baltimore, respectively. Rees believes younger head coaches might be more apt to hire younger coordinators.

But it's a balancing act, he said. For instance, Falcons offensive line coach Bill Callahan "has been coaching since before I was born." (For the record, the 70-year-old began coaching in 1978).

"And so, there's a level of respect that you always want to approach the job with," Rees said. "There's a level of not always having the answer that you want to approach the job with. You have to be humble, and you have to be respectful to the guys in the room, but at the end of the day, you have to make a decision to move forward.

"Everybody thinks it's about calling plays on Sunday. It's not just that. There's so much more that goes into it from planning, from communication, from getting everybody on the same page, from having hard conversations." -- Marc Raimondi

Brad Idzik, 35, Carolina Panthers

While other first-year playcallers have struggled, Idzik has shown promise with the Panthers.

Idzik is in his third season as the Panthers offensive coordinator but coach Dave Canales handed him the playcalling duties for the first time this offseason. Carolina ranks ninth in both scoring (25.4) and yards (363.7).

Idzik has forged a bond with quarterback Bryce Young, 25, over the past three years, as the coordinator and his wife, Emily, have hosted the QB room for dinner every offseason. Idzik views relationship building as a paramount aspect of his coaching approach, and he has taken what he's learned from the likes of former NFL coach Pete Carroll and Dallas Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer and put his twist on their lessons.

"Taking those experiences and then relying on the connection with the players," Idzik said. "Anytime you're a little bit closer in age with some of the guys, there is a cultural connection piece that you feel like you can talk, not eye-to-eye with guys, but making sure that you're receptive to how they're communicating with you and their forms of communication, which has definitely changed over the years." 

The former Wake Forest wide receiver has found common ground with his players through collaboration. Young and his wide receivers, including Jalen Coker and Tetairoa McMillan, have routinely acknowledged Idzik's tendency to seek out player feedback. 

"He gives everybody a chance and an opportunity at the ball," McMillan said following a Week 4 win against the Detroit Lions in October. "And he's good at communicating throughout the week just to see what everybody's feeling, see what we like, see what Bryce likes. He likes to communicate in that way as far as [getting] our opinions. He's humble in that way ... ." -- Mike Kaye

Nate Scheelhaase, 35, Los Angeles Rams

Just two years ago, Scheelhaase was in his first season as an NFL coach, serving as an offensive assistant and pass game specialist on the Rams coaching staff. Since then, it has been a quick rise for Scheelhaase since he was hired by the Rams in February 2024 after spending the previous six seasons at Iowa State.

During the 2024 season, Scheelhaase drew plays for head coach Sean McVay, helping the young coach learn the intricacies of the complex offense run by quarterback Matthew Stafford. Scheelhaase made an immediate impression on McVay and others in the NFL. That offseason, he interviewed with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers for their open offensive coordinator role.

"It was just two years ago where it was my first time being around Sean, being around this offensive, being around this environment and there was so much learning," Scheelhaase said. "I felt like every day, I was putting my nose down, going to work, listening to the coaches coach, listening to how things were taught, trying to be as disciplined as I could with my notetaking and reviewing and studying. To be able to find a way to then add value at some point."

After serving as the Rams' pass game coordinator in 2025, Scheelhaase again received interview requests, this time for head coaching positions. The 35-year-old interviewed with the Baltimore Ravens and twice with the Cleveland Browns.

The Rams promoted Scheelhaase to offensive coordinator after Mike LaFleur was hired by the Arizona Cardinals. After he was elevated, Scheelhaase acknowledged that it's "rare" as a coach to get to continue to add responsibilities and stay in one place. 

"Being here, it is a great place to just learn to ask questions, to hear things taught in a way that you feel like really makes an impact for our players," Scheelhaase said.

The new role has meant Scheelhaase has worked even more closely with Stafford and McVay.

"I think he's sharp," Stafford said. "Obviously, he's a young guy in the NFL, but a really smart mind. A guy that's really well thought out. He's a really good communicator, calm personality, but in front of the room, he does a really nice job commanding the eyes and ears of everybody that's in there listening to him." 

McVay praised Scheelhaase's emotional intelligence and his "ability to be able to connect with a variety of different people because he actually listens to understand."

"And when he wants to communicate, he's trying to connect," McVay said. "That's who he is all the time. I think he has a good swag and charisma about himself too that people can relate to." -- Sarah Barshop

headlines.story: DETROIT -- — Nick Woodford ran for three touchdowns and Central Michigan rolled past Eastern Michigan 35-7 on Wednesday night at Ford Field. The Chippewas (4-5, 2/3 Mid-American Conference) had a total of 235 yards rushing, 123 by Woodford, who scored on runs of 11, 2 and 1 yard. Jadyn Glasser completed 14 of 19 passes for 175 yards, including an 8-yard touchdown pass to Nasir Williams for the game's first score. The Chippewas had more than double the total offense of the Eagles, outgaining them 418-177. Eastern Michigan got on the board with 10 seconds remaining when backup quarterback Jace Stuckey and Harold Mack connected on a 6-yard touchdown pass. The Eagles (4-6, 3-3) had 103 yards passing and 74 yards rushing. Eastern Michigan won 61-58 in four overtimes the last time these two played at Ford Field, in 2004. Central Michigan has a 66-32-6 advantage in the series that dates to 1902. Up next Central Michigan: vs. Sacramento State next Wednesday. Eastern Michigan: at Western Michigan on Nov. 17. ------ Sign up for Top 25 poll alerts here, visit the Top 25 here and see AP’s full college football coverage here.

headlines.story: AMHERST, Mass. -- — William Watson III broke loose for a 13-yard touchdown run in overtime to give Massachusetts a 31-30 victory over Ball State on Wednesday night. Ball State quarterback Keldric Luster scored on a 2-yard run with 25 seconds left in regulation to end a nine-plane, 75-yard drive that tied it 24-all. Jalen Bonds, who finished with 132 yards rushing on 17 carries, scored from a yard out for the Cardinals on the first possession of overtime, but Brody Boehm’s extra-point attempt was wide left. Derek Morris, who missed a 36-yard field-goal attempt in the first quarter but was good on a 23-yarder in the third, converted the extra point in OT for UMass. Watson completed 17 of 25 passes for 302 yards. He tossed a 64-yard touchdown pass to Jabari Lewis just before halftime to give UMass a 14-10 lead, and his 1-yard TD run gave the Minutemen a 21-17 advantage with 2:31 to play in the third quarter. Curtis Kimmons had 85 yards rushing and Elijah Faulkner scored from a yard out for UMass (5-4, 2/3 Mid-American Conference), which snapped a four-game losing streak. Luster was 17-of-27 passing for 182 yards and threw a touchdown pass for Ball State (3-6, 2-3). Up next Ball State: Hosts Buffalo next Wednesday. UMass: At Toledo next Wednesday. ------ Sign up for Top 25 poll alerts here, visit the Top 25 here and see AP’s full college football coverage here

headlines.story:
Star running back LJ Martin of No. 9 BYU is trending toward dressing and being available to play in the Cougars' showdown against No. 3 Utah in Salt Lake City, sources told ESPN's Pete Thamel on Wednesday.

Martin is officially doubtful for the game, per the initial Big 12 availability report released Wednesday night, but sources said the reigning conference Offensive Player of the Year is trending toward playing Saturday and having some impact on the game, although he's not expected to be 100% if he does go.

A final decision will be made later in the week.

Martin has been sidelined since suffering a lower-body injury in a 17-10 win at TCU on Oct. 3. He was expected to miss four to six weeks, sources told ESPN at the time.

The Cougars have gone 3-1 in his absence, the loss by 39-31 in double overtime at UCF a week after they knocked off Notre Dame. Sione Moa and Preston Rex have mostly filled in during Martin's absence.

A 6-foot-2, 225-pound senior, Martin rushed for 1,305 yards and 12 touchdowns in 2025 while helping the Cougars win 12 games and reach the Big 12 championship game. He had 344 yards rushing and three scores on 7.8 yards per carry this season before the injury.

BYU has won three straight in a Holy War rivalry marked by close games. Utah's losses in that run have come by an average margin of 4.3 points.

headlines.description: — CJ Miller ran for 135 yards, Autavius Ison had 101 yards and a touchdown, and Toledo defeated Sacramento State 20-17 on Wednesday night.
headlines.linkText: Miller, Ison lead ground game and Toledo slips past Sacramento State 20-17
headlines.story: SACRAMENTO, Calif. -- — CJ Miller ran for 135 yards, Autavius Ison had 101 yards and a touchdown, and Toledo defeated Sacramento State 20-17 on Wednesday night. The Rockets (7-2, 4-1 Mid-American Conference) climbed into a tie for second-place and remain in the running for the MAC championship game. After trailing 10-7 at halftime, the Rockets scored 13 points in the second half. Ison scored on a 19-yard run late in the third quarter and Reice Griffith kicked two field goals. Toledo led 20-10 deep into the fourth quarter. Sacramento State's Jamar Curtis scored on a 3-yard run that capped off a 12-play, 75-yard drive but it left only two minutes on the clock. The Hornets got the ball back at their own 16-yard line with 55 seconds remaining but they gained only a few yards before being stopped on fourth down. Quarterbacks Jackson Sharman and Brian Salazar Jr. combined for 216 yards passing for Sacramento State (2-8, 1-6) but the Hornets had only eight yards rushing. John Alan Richter passed for only 60 yards for Toledo and the Rockets had a total of 230 yards rushing. Sacramento State honored Native American Heritage Day by wearing uniforms specially created in consultation with the Wilton Rancheria tribe. It was Senior Day for Sacramento State and the team recognized 27 seniors before the final home game of the season. Up next Toledo: vs. UMass on Nov. 11. headlines.story:
LSU star linebacker Whit Weeks, who missed the past four games with a fractured leg, is doubtful to play in Saturday's home matchup against Alabama, according to Wednesday night's SEC availability report. 

Tigers coach Lane Kiffin expressed optimism about Weeks' return before the team's bye last week. In four games this season, the former All-SEC linebacker has 23 tackles.

Meanwhile, Alabama is looking to get back several of its injured starters as wide receiver Ryan Coleman-Williams, center Racin Delgatty, cornerback Zabien Brown and defensive tackle Terrance Green are all listed as questionable for Saturday's game. 

Coleman-Williams, the former freshman All-American, was the team's leading receiver prior to undergoing arthroscopic knee surgery.

Brown, a preseason All-America pick, was injured early during a loss at Tennessee and did not play the following week vs. Texas A&M.

Like LSU, Alabama had last week off, allowing for extra recovery time.

Also questionable for the Crimson Tide is running back EJ Crowell. The former five-star prospect is arguably the team's most explosive back as he averages 6.8 yards per carry and has four rushing touchdowns this season.

headlines.story:
HENDERSON, Nev. --- It took eight weeks into Kirk Cousins' tenure with the Las Vegas Raiders for the veteran quarterback to unlock his alter ego, "Kirko Chainz."

The Raiders defeated the New York Jets 38-33 in comeback fashion on the road Sunday, snapping a four-game losing streak and improving to 4-4 -- the first time the team has been .500 or better through eight games since 2021. The accomplishment caused much-needed celebration, so on the long flight back to Las Vegas, Cousins took off his shirt and let his teammates place several expensive chains around his neck and watches on his wrist.

"It's been a while. The longer the flight, the more likely the chains," said Cousins, who recorded four total touchdowns in the win.

"Kirko Chainz" originated in 2022 when he started for the Minnesota Vikings. Cousins helped complete a comeback win over the Washington Commanders to improve to 7-1. On the return trip, Cousins went viral when a video of him swaying to Florida rapper Real Boston Richey's song, "Bullseye 2," while wearing his teammates' jewelry, circulated across the internet.

Raiders running back Dylan Laube was on the New Hampshire Wildcats when Cousins first channeled his alternate personality. Laube said it was cool to see at the time, but seeing Kirko Chainz in person was "funny."

"I mean, he loves the attention," said Laube, who was named AFC Special Teams Player of the Week. "... He's just an unreal person."

Raiders starting cornerback Eric Stokes said he "threw a little something" on Cousins' wrist. The large Millennium Ring necklace, which is from the iconic Japanese anime television series "Yu-Gi-Oh," came from defensive tackle Adam Butler.

All-Pro defensive end Maxx Crosby said he contributed in a big way, giving Cousins multiple watches and chains.

"Kirk is the man. ... One of the funnier dudes you'll ever meet," Crosby said. "He probably [has] the most dad vibe energy on the planet."

The return of Kirko Chainz is one of the ways Cousins has brought joy to the Raiders this season. He generated smiles and laughter in the locker room with his "wellness" celebration after he snuck into the end zone for a touchdown in the third quarter against New York.

Postgame, Cousins said his touchdown dance was a nod to the team's training staff. On Wednesday, he admitted Laube created the dance.

"I don't get my own jokes, I steal them from other people, and then I'm just a better megaphone," Cousins said. "Dylan came up with it, and then I was like, 'I'm going to use that.'"

Cousins has also led trips to In-N-Out Burger after every win. He invited more players each time, but the trips halted for a month during the team's losing skid. As the weeks grew and the losses mounted, Cousins said In-N-Out started sounding better.

He promised his teammates a visit to In-N-Out near the team's training facility if they won. On Sunday night, Cousins treated No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza, left tackle Kolton Miller, tight end Brock Bowers, Laube and others to a postgame meal.

"In-N-Out's not that expensive," Cousins said. "You put your card down; it doesn't go too far, which is nice."

Before the Raiders win over New York, head coach Klint Kubiak asked Cousins to speak to the team about playing with joy. Cousins told his teammates that comparison is a thief of joy. And don't allow the league, which consists of making a ton of comparisons, to strip away their joy for the game.

"He brings that joy every single day," Laube said. "This guy is 38, and he's still bringing that same energy as if he was a kid."

headlines.linkText: Florida suspends DT McCloud 1 game for detrimental conduct
headlines.story:
GAINESVILLE, Fla. -- No. 25 Florida suspended starting defensive tackle Jeramiah McCloud for one game on Wednesday for conduct detrimental to the team.

McCloud will miss Saturday's home game against Oklahoma (4-4, 2-3 SEC).

"His status with the program will be reevaluated after this week's contest," the team said.

McCloud, a 6-foot-3, 294-pound sophomore from Sylvester, Georgia, started five of Florida's eight games this season. He has 22 tackles, including 1½ for loss. Earlier this season, McCloud was caught on video making an obscene gesture toward fans late in a loss at Missouri.

Also Wednesday, the Gators (5-3, 3-3) ruled out starting right tackle Emeka Ugorji and backup linebacker Jaden Robinson because of injuries.

Receiver Vernell Brown III, who has missed the past four games with a sprained right knee, was listed as doubtful. He had his knee drained of extra fluid late last week and then had a platelet-rich plasma injection Monday.

Defensive end Emmanuel Oyebadejo and receiver Bailey Stockton, two of the team's best players this season, were listed as questionable with injuries.
